POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:50:32 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 Effort to regulate ‘killer robots’ delayed to 2028 https://www.politico.eu/article/effort-regulate-killer-robots-delayed-until-2028-ai-un/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:43:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9367200 U.N. talks on regulating AI-powered killer robots ended without a negotiating mandate Saturday, as countries decided to extend discussions until 2028.

It’s a result that NGOs called “disappointing.”

Countries party to the U.N.’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons spent five days in Geneva trying to reach an accord to elaborate legally binding rules for weapons that can select and attack targets without human approval.

But resistance from several countries, and especially Russia, blocked those efforts. In the end, the 128 member countries agreed to launch “the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems,” over the next two years, Julien Thöni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the talks, told reporters.

The issue is of growing importance as AI gains new capabilities and autonomous systems become increasingly powerful. Ukraine, Russia, Israel and others are using drones and robots in warfare, although they insist that humans still have ultimate control over pulling the trigger.

However, Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organizations, said such systems have already been tested or deployed, including in Ukraine and Gaza.

“Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield — delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” said Nicole van Rooijen, the executive director of Stop Killer Robots.

Informal talk

Because consensus is required for any decision, Russia was able to block formal negotiations all week, refusing to allow observers — including the European Union — to take part in the talks. Instead, negotiations were held informally to circumvent Russia’s veto.

A Brazilian diplomat suggested it wasn’t only Russia trying to block the effort. “You can blame Russia, but they are not the only ones. Some people are hiding behind Russia,” the diplomat said.

Two EU diplomats listed the U.S., the U.K., South Korea, Japan, Turkey and Israel as countries also resisting an effort to agree on a binding regulation.

In an effort to find a consensus, France called for a “hybrid document” — with both non-binding and binding elements. Germany advocated for an “international instrument” as opposed to a legally binding protocol.

In the final hours of the conference, countries pushing for a regulation on autonomous lethal systems, such as Ireland, Brazil, Belgium and Austria, watered down their positions out of fear of “leaving the conference empty-handed,” the Brazilian diplomat said. They settled for further talks, without calling to adopt a legally binding treaty by 2028.

The final decision seen by POLITICO proposes to “elaborate” an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems in the context of international humanitarian law. A group of intergovernmental experts should report its conclusions to a 2028 meeting of countries party to the treaty.

As AI and automation transform warfare, civil society groups said the conference fell short of expectations.

]]> en Costa cuts proposed EU budget by €44B https://www.politico.eu/article/costa-cuts-proposed-eu-budget-by-44billion-euros/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 21 Nov 2026 10:44:05 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9365286 BRUSSELS — António Costa aims to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, according to a fresh set of numbers unveiled on Saturday.

For the first time since the budget negotiations began last year, EU regional spending, known as cohesion policy, is a target for reductions. The European Council president proposed reducing it by €8 billion compared with the last proposal, while farmers’ subsidies remained untouched.

This is a major setback for a coalition of 17 countries from Eastern and Southern Europe — including Poland, Italy and Spain — who rejected potential cuts to cohesion policy only a few days ago. However, the plan was welcomed as “a first step” by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who urged further cuts.

“This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act,” Costa said on Saturday morning.

Costa, who is guiding discussions over the 2028-2034 budget which needs to be agreed by all EU governments, suggested the reductions, which are based on current prices, from the previous proposal presented by Ireland, in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, last month.

Overall, the cuts amount to a reduction in size of the budget by €204 billion, or 10.2%, from the European Commission’s original proposal in July last year.

In another major development, Costa suggested introducing a new tax on large digital companies such as Google and Meta to help finance the budget over the coming years.

However, budget savings also came from foreign aid which was cut by €7 billion, and competitiveness which was axed by €20 billion.

The proposed digital levy will cover online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data for companies.

It is expected to generate around €5 billion per year, according to an EU official.

Most governments opposed CORE — a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — over fears that it would undermine EU competitiveness.

The proposal also envisions a higher share of a carbon imports’ tax that flows to the EU cash pot to 100% from the current 75%, and exploring levies on crypto firms and national spectrum auctions.

Costa argued that the new proposed taxes will keep national contributions to Brussels under control.

“With this proposal we have managed to come very close to the current level of national contributions,” he said.

]]> en The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals https://www.politico.eu/article/the-winners-and-losers-of-the-eu-uk-summit-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:24:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9366021 BRUSSELS — U.K. and EU leaders on Friday hailed a “win-win” as they announced long-awaited deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth visas scheme. The reality is more complicated.

A summit press conference failed to resolve questions over whether the much-lauded deals are contingent on a tuition fees agreement set to be negotiated over the next six months.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that the deals are “done” and tuition fees are still to be negotiated — despite EU claims to the contrary earlier on Friday.

If all the agreements take effect, there will be winners and losers on both sides of the English Channel and beyond. We take stock of who’s up and who’s down.

Winners

Students 

British and EU students are among the biggest winners from today’s announcements, benefiting from both a youth experience scheme and the planned tuition fee deal.

Under the new scheme, 100,000 young people will be able to spend up to three years working or studying in Britain or the EU respectively — a significant improvement on current visa requirements.

Under a deal yet to be thrashed out, students could also benefit from lower tuition fees when studying abroad. Two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, said London had so far offered fees of £12,000. The EU would lower its fees too.

If agreed, this would be a significant win for Brussels, with EU students currently subject to international student rates of up to £38,000 per year in the U.K.

British supermarkets

U.K. supermarkets — many of whom import from and export to the EU — were among the first to praise the agrifood deal, with major brands like Tesco and M&S saying the deal would make it easier and cheaper to trade with Europe.

The deal will see Britain align with EU food and agriculture rules by 2028, removing the need for costly certification requirements and checks in a move the U.K. government claims could add up to £5.1 billion a year to the British economy. 

“Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said M&S managing director Alex Freudmann. “When this deal comes into force, it will remove this bureaucracy.”

That said, there are questions over whether retailers will be in a position to pass on any savings to the customer amid spiraling energy costs.

Renewables providers

British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers. 

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,”  RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.”  EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry

The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.

The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.

The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.

Of the more political parts of the agreement, the youth visas scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

The City has been shut out of EU markets since Brexit, with only London’s clearinghouses, a key part of the plumbing of the financial system, maintaining the ability to directly serve European clients. Brussels for years refused to even talk to Britain about financial services until issues on the Northern Ireland border were resolved.

Now, as Burnham pushes for better, financial services could yet benefit. While the City is in no great rush to give up the new U.K. regulatory regime developed since Brexit, there is hope of more collaboration in areas like investment, particularly for defense and start-ups, where both sides face a lack of cash and fears over economic resilience

Losers

British universities

With so much potentially hinging on a tuition fee deal, the U.K. government is under increasing pressure to get this agreement over the line. 

But it’s also under a lot of domestic pressure from universities, which have warned the move could cost them £500 million a year — money that they say would otherwise be used to help fund research, teaching and jobs.

Currently, tuition fees for EU nationals studying in the U.K. can reach up to £38,000 per year, in line with other international students, while British students pay a maximum of £9,790 a year in England.

Hollie Chandler, director of strategic policy at the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said any reduction in EU student fees would “put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.”

Chinese carmakers

It could have been worse for Chinese carmakers, but they aren’t in the clear just yet.

The EU wanted the U.K. to agree to a commitment binding it to the EU’s tariff regime on Chinese cars and other imports. The U.K. successfully pushed back, instead saying it would “ensure outcomes consistent with the relevant EU measures in order to ensure that the supply chain in question is protected in a consistent way” across the two markets and “guard against potential risks of circumvention.”

But as talks over British access to the EU’s Made in Europe industrial scheme continue over the coming months, that phrasing leaves the door open to raising tariffs in the future.

China experts Gregor Williams and Noah Barkin had previously warned that “acting before the terms of Made in Europe access are settled would weaken London’s negotiating leverage.”

“The UK has an incentive to signal a willingness to align with the EU while stopping short of imposing immediate restrictions on Chinese imports, not least given Beijing’s threats of retaliation,” Williams and Barkin added. They expect “some form of UK trade action on Chinese vehicles will come in the next 12 months.”

Food manufacturers

A major selling point of the SPS deal is the idea that it will bring down food prices for British consumers — one that government ministers have pounced on during the cost-of-living crisis fueled by the Iran war. 

But U.K. food firms have taken issue with this framing, pointing out that alignment with EU rules will mean costly changes for manufacturers as they align with EU requirements on issues like food safety, packaging, labeling and pesticides.

In guidance published alongside the summit statement, the U.K. government sets out a series of transitional arrangements aimed at helping firms adapt to the new changes.

While she welcomed the prospect of closer trade ties with the EU in the longterm, Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, warned that “the timing remains tight.” She urged the U.K. government to pass the relevant legislation and publish detailed business guidance “as quickly as possible” to give firms time to make necessary changes.

British steelmakers

The deal might be a win for steelmakers in the long-run, but the sector will have to wait some time to feel the benefits.

While the emissions trading scheme deal will ultimately spare Britain’s steel producers from the EU’s carbon border tax regime, it won’t take effect until 2028, leaving British producers exposed for at least another year.

Brussels and London are also still in talks to forge a steel alliance that would see the two sides harmonize new quota and tariff regimes imposed in July after they slashed market access for each other. But they couldn’t get things wrapped up in time for the summit and talks are proving challenging.

Defense firms

Although the two sides committed to immediately setting up a new Dialogue on Economic Security to tackle shared economic dependencies, they said little about defense sector collaboration.

Reviving talks for Britain to get access to the EU’s €150 billion SAFE fund for joint defense procurement loans “isn’t part of the summit negotiation,” Britain’s Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said Friday. But if the EU “wanted to return to it, I’d certainly suggest we’d be willing to do so,” he told Sky News.

Potentially significant language in the joint statement includes plans to “enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues,” including the prospect of British involvement in the EU’s “Capability Coalitions” — groups of member states which pool resources and coordinate investment in making new defense capabilities.

]]> en Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-eu-uk-summit-reset-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9365667 BRUSSELS — Hours before Andy Burnham arrived at a long-planned U.K.-EU summit Friday, it seemed like it’d be a humdrum victory lap.

Talks ran late Thursday but that always happens; Britain seemed to believe everything was wrapping up as planned; Burnham even brought a super-delegation of seven Cabinet colleagues. “Deal done,” texted one U.K. official at 14 minutes to midnight.

The spin war only came Friday morning — and not for the first time in Britain’s long Brexit saga, it arrived in a dry technical briefing in the European Council’s Europa building HQ.

A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling.

Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa.

They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what. 

Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.”

“The U.K. wanted to get something on Made in Europe, so that meant tuition fees being delayed as well. Somehow this has turned into a great defeat for the U.K. government because everything would be at the mercy of tuition fees,” he said. “That was what the U.K. government actually wanted.”

Opposition politicians seized on the row, with Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage calling Burnham “naive.” Oliver Lewis, the former Conservative Brexit aide who has founded a new anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, said he had “been played like a fiddle by Brussels.”

Brussels waffle

If intended to seize the narrative, the statement worked. 

Other EU officials tried to downplay its significance as the morning unfolded — the key phrase “equal treatment” was, in fact, not in the final summit text — but the issue still dominated questions at a joint press conference by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

U.K. officials sprang up an unplanned briefing to counter-spin while Downing Street aides texted journalists with lines from a government spokesperson saying the deal was done. Burnham himself told the press conference: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done. It’s there in black and white.”

A senior U.K. official insisted to POLITICO that the three deals on food standards, emissions and youth experience were not contingent on a pact on tuition fees.

Yet EU diplomats continued to suggest they were part of a “package,” a concept neither Costa nor von der Leyen tried very hard to shoot down. (Von der Leyen told journalists merely that the tuition fees deal was “on a different sheet of paper,” before Burnham was treated to a battered fish lunch with a dessert of fruit with actual Brussels waffle.)

Later Friday, Britain’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO he was “confident” that a tuition fees deal would be reached over the next six months.

But the risk is not negligible. The six-month deadline to ink an agreement includes a French presidential election; if the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins it could have unpredictable results for the EU’s legislative agenda, including Made in Europe. And negotiations on the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (the legislation behind Made in Europe) are behind schedule, with talks between the Council and European Parliament yet to begin and disagreements over the automotive package adding to the complexity.

Lower tuition fees, please

The Commission and Council statement Friday morning seized the headlines for two reasons.

The first was that it indicated the three deals tied up on Thursday night would not go ahead if Britain broke its promise to cut tuition fees. EU officials insisted they were not holding Britain “hostage,” but it was difficult to interpret the statement otherwise.

The second was the phrase “equal treatment” — which appeared to suggest the whole deal was contingent on something Britain was not even willing to offer.

Britain has signaled it will cut the international fees charged by U.K. universities — often well over £30,000 per year — to a lower level for students coming from the EU. 

But crucially, the U.K. has resisted European demands to match EU students’ fees with the £9,790-a-year “home fees” paid by U.K. students. Instead both sides have talked about a figure somewhere in the middle; negotiators have discussed a possible figure of £12,000 in private, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, who like others cited in this story were granted anonymity to share candid details.

This is a deeply personal issue for many European politicians and diplomats, who either spent their youths at Britain’s famed elite universities — think Oxford, Cambridge or the London School of Economics — or now have children attending them, or hoping to, at least.

There were immediate suspicions on the U.K. side that the EU’s statement was a piece of spin in the midst of a negotiation.

The U.K. is holding its cards close on tuition fees to keep leverage over Made in Europe. A resolution on both issues was delayed because Made in Europe, designed to protect the bloc’s industries from a flood of cheap imports, remains in its early stages. The summit text agreed by the U.K. and EU contained no direct reference to the scheme, merely a pledge to “limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains.”

Despite this, there was a view in the British contingent that the U.K. pushed the EU successfully for assurances on Made in Europe — meaning the EU had to flex its muscles somewhere else.

“It was a pretty complicated discussion, and the British took a very hard line,” said one EU diplomat. This person added: “The discussion on tuition fees fell out because of the issue related to equal treatment… Ultimately, it’s not the statement we would have wanted, but with a partner like this, it’s important to maintain dialogue.”

‘Dear Andy’

Both sides put on smiles at the press conference, with Burnham calling the deals a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe.” Von der Leyen heaped praise on the man she referred to from the podium as “dear Andy.”

Ultimately, the most important question about Friday’s row will be whether the deals Burnham announced are at any genuine risk of falling apart. 

“Six months seems a bit short to me” to sort out the tuition fees issue, said the EU diplomat quoted earlier in this story. British officials insist there is no issue.

To make matters more complicated, Brussels is also pressing London to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, potentially tying this to Made in Europe provisions. The U.K. has yet to decide, though there is a widespread expectation among Labour MPs and some ministers that Britain will end up raising tariffs on Chinese EVs.

If Friday’s deals do go ahead, the spin battle will be filed alongside countless other technocratic spats of the Brexit wars that fade into background noise.

But even so, the deals are not expected to see the light of day until at least 2028 — undercutting Burnham’s pitch to the British public that they will cut food costs and ease business red tape. (The prime minister highlighted Treasury analysis that showed Friday’s deals could add 0.5% or £17 billion to U.K. GDP.)

Implementation of the agrifood deal is not planned until March 2028, while a deal to link the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems is only expected in the same year — meaning British firms will see no immediate relief from EU carbon border taxes, a further blow to the struggling steel industry.

With the youth experience scheme not expected to be up and running until 2030, there are also questions over whether the program will survive the next election, which must happen before August 2029.

There will be other challenges in selling the deal too. The U.K. claimed a late breakthrough on Thursday night in securing a role in shaping EU food standards rules — but hours later, Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds suggested Britain’s role would be limited. “We’d have experts in the room. We’d have the ability to put our point of view into that process. We’re not getting a vote because we’re not a member of the EU,” Reynolds told the BBC.

Farage seized on this Friday, saying Britain would be forced to follow European rules on agricultural technology and pesticides rather than forging its own path.

‘Informal brainstorm’

Perhaps most importantly, Friday’s spin war is a reminder that nothing in Brussels is ever easy. It is a collision between Burnham’s big-picture way of doing politics and the EU’s hard, rules-based world.

This will matter for a prime minister who plans to stake much of his campaign at the next election on a battle for hearts and minds over Europe. That ballot isn’t due until July 2029, but Farage predicted on Friday that the election would come as soon as May 2027, about a year after Burnham’s ascent from the Greater Manchester mayoralty to Westminster.

As POLITICO reported this week, the personally pro-rejoin Burnham has not decided exactly what to promise the British public — and is caught between his aspirational rhetoric and the reality of a divided Cabinet. Now he can throw in the difficulty of dealing with the EU too.

Costa reflected this neatly in the press conference, telling Burnham he was “always welcome in the EU” — but almost in the next breath, reminding him that the EU’s principles, including the “indivisibility” of free movement from access to the single market, would “guide our engagement with the United Kingdom.”

Burnham plans to set out the options he believes are available for the future relationship next month, tied in with his promised “10-year plan” for Britain. It will kick-start a conversation that will likely culminate in a Europe-shaped offer to the public in Labour’s election manifesto.

But he also indicated Friday that he would not seek more policy-by-policy deals with the EU ahead of the next election, instead favoring a broader conversation. Even Starmer promised “iterative” deals once per year.

The U.K. prime minister also continued to be vague about how that process would unfold. He spoke of “informal brainstorming” with the EU ahead of another summit next year. “We are open for brainstorming,” Von der Leyen replied.

Sebastian Starcevic, Sam Francis and Sam Blewett contributed reporting.

]]> en France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership https://www.politico.eu/article/france-germany-complete-political-deal-for-ecb-leadership/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:50:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9348045 FRANKFURT — France and Germany on Friday submitted their candidates to fill two looming vacancies on the European Central Bank’s Executive Board, completing a political package that’ll decide the institution’s leadership for years to come.

Berlin presented Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, as the ECB’s next chief economist, after the Irish incumbent Philip Lane concludes his eight-year term on May 31.

Paris put forward Laurence Boone — a former minister of Europe and political ally of President Emmanuel Macron — who is now head of corporate and investment banking at Santander, to take over the ECB’s markets portfolio. That post will become available on Jan. 4, when Isabel Schnabel leaves the ECB for a job at the International Monetary Fund.

The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7.

The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said.

If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year.

In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets.

“I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.”

Fewer politicians

A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency.

De Cos and Vice-President Boris Vujčić are seasoned central bankers, as is Piero Cipollone, who heads the payments department. Before becoming a politician, Boone had been chief economist at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

While the reshuffle will leave the six-strong board looking more apolitical, the game of ECB musical chairs has been anything but, according to ING’s head of macro, Carsten Brzeski.

“It looks like another masterpiece of French diplomacy and strategic personnel policy,” he said. “With the move to opt for the markets operation, France gave the impression of passing the more important job of chief economist to Germany.”

“However, with a Spanish president and France holding the markets operation, the risk of a more dovish ECB has clearly increased,” Brzeski said.

Kulbergs warned that Russia’s hybrid attacks on NATO’s eastern flank were intensifying. “The situation is escalating,” he said, adding that Latvian and Estonian special forces had arrested eight people on Estonian soil last weekend who had “concrete instructions to attack a production facility in Estonia that supports Ukraine.” Russia, he said, “is behind this.”

He called the coming months “a winter of truth,” arguing that Russia was striking Ukraine’s water, heating and power supplies because it was making little progress at the front, while also trying to sway public opinion in Germany and elsewhere. “Putin wants the Germans to be frightened and to demand that their government stop supporting Ukraine,” he said.

The Yalta summit in February 1945, where U.S. President Franklin D. ]]> en French billionaire hunter takes fight global after California tax defeat https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-zucman-billionaires-california-taxes/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:15:46 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9364740 PARIS — Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world’s billionaires on notice.

The 40-year-old French economist, who has spent more than a decade designing ways to tax the ultra-rich, hosts a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. It comes less than three weeks after California voters rejected a billionaire tax he backed, in a campaign where Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other opponents spent more than $300 million to thwart the initiative.

“Everywhere, we see very, very strong popular support for taxing billionaires,” Zucman told POLITICO this week, arguing that his loss in California was only a minor setback. “That’s true even in the United States.”

Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the U.S. midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races.

“Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. “The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world,” he told POLITICO.

Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) are due to speak at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue off the Champs-Élysées loaned for the occasion by Emmanuel Grégoire, the socialist mayor of Paris.

Left-wing leaders from Italy, Brazil, Spain and the U.K. are also expected to attend. A “Paris Manifesto” published Friday calls for a minimum tax on the largest fortunes, protections for independent media and rules for artificial intelligence.

The question is whether anyone outside the theater will buy into Zucman’s ideas. His signature proposal, a minimum annual tax of 2% on the largest fortunes, was rejected by the French Senate last year.

“It’s a real program to save our democracy,” said Eva Joly, a former French investigating judge who jailed the boss of oil giant Elf in the 1990s and later served as a European lawmaker for the Greens. Zucman “carries it brilliantly,” she told POLITICO.

The fight goes on

Global talks on taxing the super-rich have stalled this year under the U.S. presidency of the G20, according to Zucman, who expects the impasse to persist as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. Still, he hopes to revive the debate when Britain takes over the G20 presidency next year.

In Brussels, meanwhile, tax legislation generally requires the unanimous agreement of all 27 EU governments, making a bloc-wide solution difficult.

Rather than wait for international agreement, Zucman expects individual governments to take the lead, just as France did with value-added tax in the 1950s and several EU countries have done more recently with digital services taxes.

Bills to tax the wealthy are in the works in the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, he said, while the British government has begun looking at the idea.

Joly is less ready to write off Brussels, calling the EU “a field of possibilities.” She argued that low taxes on multinationals distort competition with domestic firms and said it was the responsibility of the European Commission and Parliament to address the problem.

There are also signs of movement on corporate taxation. European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on U.S. tech giants to help fund the EU’s next seven-year budget, POLITICO reported Thursday, after Trump’s poor showing in the midterms eased fears of retaliation by Washington.

“Europe cannot afford to calibrate its tax policy to America’s mood swings,” said Paul Monaghan, chief executive of the U.K.-based Fair Tax Foundation, which campaigns on corporate tax conduct.

At the United Nations, negotiators will meet in Nairobi from Nov. 30 to Dec. 10 for the next round of talks on a global tax convention, with a final text due in 2027.

Beyond the left

In California, Zucman said, billionaires flooded voters with “disinformation” that the tax would bankrupt the health system, even though 90% of the revenue raised would have gone toward health care.

But money was only part of the story. Unions split over the measure, POLITICO reported, and Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned against it. A state-only wealth tax “creates economic incentives for money and jobs to leave the state,” his chief of staff, Nathan Barankin, said.

Zucman rejects the notion that Saturday’s gathering is a rally of the left. He said he had invited former EU competition chief Margrethe Vestager and former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi, but both declined. A spokesperson for Vestager declined to comment.

Yet in France, the far-left France Unbowed party and the Greens were the only ones to fully embrace Zucman’s proposed 2% annual wealth tax ahead of next spring’s presidential election. MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, who is running for a left-wing coalition that includes the Socialists, has instead proposed to raise the tax rate for inheritances above €1.8 million, and a one-off 5% levy on fortunes over €100 million.

François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po’s OFCE, has challenged Zucman’s arguments. In a paper updated last month, he argued that Zucman had exaggerated the extent to which billionaires are undertaxed and proposed a remedy that could do more harm than good.

Geerolf acknowledged that the ultra-rich can use holding companies to shield income from taxation, but argued for closing the loophole instead of imposing an annual tax on fortunes. He also questioned estimates that the tax would raise €20 billion a year in France, putting the likely proceeds at just €2 billion to €6 billion. His verdict: “A real problem, a false diagnosis, a bad remedy.”

Other critics have also been mobilizing. Trop c’est trop (“Enough is enough”), a campaign group backed by business executive Eric Maumy, presented a study Wednesday characterizing Zucman’s tax proposal as confiscatory and unconstitutional.

But Zucman believes it is the status quo that is untenable. “Do you think it’s normal that billionaires can pay zero personal tax?” he said. “It’s the current situation that is radical.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 21 Nov 2026 17:19:43 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit https://euobserver.com/250481/costas-eu-budget-plan-for-10-percent-cuts-pits-frugals-against-cohesion-group-ahead-of-crunch-summit/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 17:18:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250481 Antonio Costa's plan tries to find a careful balance between the demands of 'frugal' states and 'friends of cohesion' ahead of an EU budget summit in Brussels on Thursday.]]> European Council president Antonio Costa on Saturday (21 November) set the stage for a major clash between EU governments and MEPs over the next seven-year EU budget, after setting out plans to cut the EU commission’s spending plan by 10 percent.

The cuts, which follow a series of meetings between Costa and diplomats from EU states, go significantly further than the proposal by the Irish government, which currently holds the EU’s six month rotating presidency.

Dublin had proposed cuts of eight percent compared to the commission’s initial plan for €1.76 trillion in spending for 2028-2034, but Costa’s plan is worth 10.2 percent in cuts. 

Even so, EU spending under the Costa plan would still, at €1.58 trillion, be far higher than the €1.25 trillion 2021-27 package, though €158bn has been earmarked for debt repayments on the Next Generation EU fund which support national economies following the Covid pandemic. 

The Irish government’s cuts had focused on the EU’s competitiveness fund and foreign spending but spared farmers and the EU’s poorest regions.

For his part, Costa has proposed cuts across the board, including a 6.5 percent cut to the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), which guarantees minimum incomes for farmers.

]]> [Infographic] Plastics export ban begins: How much more of EU’s 22 million tonne per year trash mountain will go into landfills? https://euobserver.com/250119/infographic-plastics-export-ban-begins-how-much-more-of-eus-22-million-tonne-per-year-trash-mountain-will-go-into-landfills/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 10:01:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250119 With record plastic waste and shrinking recycling capacity, Europe’s new export ban risks quietly diverting mountains of rubbish into incinerators, landfills and poorer neighbours’ backyards.]]> From 21 November, the EU will have to find new destinations for half of the plastic waste it currently exports outside the bloc. Under the EU’s new Waste Shipment Regulation, adopted in 2024, exports of plastic waste to non-OECD countries will be banned for at least two and a half years, with the aim of preventing environmental damage and ensuring waste is managed safely.

In 2025, non-OECD countries received 735,000 tonnes, around half of the 1.46 million tonnes of plastic waste the EU exported outside the bloc.

Turkey, the EU’s largest OECD destination for plastic waste, could absorb much of this redirected volume.

However, environmental groups such as the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) have raised concerns about the country’s waste management and enforcement, questioning whether it should continue receiving EU plastic waste.

The commission itself expects “a shift in destination countries”: part of the waste will find its way into EU recovery capacity, while “a certain amount will be diverted to treatment in OECD countries outside the EU,” a commission spokesperson said.

So, when November ends, where will Europe’s plastic waste go?

A ban with a waiting list

No non-OECD country will receive EU plastic waste for at least two and a half years.

From May 2029, under the Waste Shipment Regulation, countries can apply to resume imports if the commission is satisfied they can manage it sustainably.

Exports to OECD countries remain legal but are subject to stricter controls. Since 21 May 2026, all plastic waste exports to third countries have required prior notification and consent, processed through the EU’s Digital Waste Shipment System (DIWASS).

The next step comes in May 2027, when exporters will also have to demonstrate that destination facilities have passed independent audits.

Read more

How the EU lets plastic be labelled ‘recycled’ at just 2.5% re-used content

China and Hong Kong received around three-quarters of Europe’s plastic waste exports in 2016, before Beijing’s import ban pushed shipments towards Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Turkey. Of these, only Turkey will still be able to receive EU plastic waste after 21 November 2026.

Can Turkey safely manage Europe’s plastic waste?

Turkey was the EU’s largest single destination for plastic waste in 2025, receiving 503,000 tonnes, mostly from Germany (155,000) and Belgium (107,000). Both also rely on markets that close in November: Germany sent almost half of its plastic waste exports outside the EU to non-OECD countries, and Belgium 43 percent. Spain and the Netherlands, also among Turkey’s top suppliers, are even more exposed to the November ban, at 70 and 77 percent.

The commission’s assessment of Turkey, published on 18 September, acknowledged that Ankara had strengthened its import controls but highlighted a “lack of transparency” in waste data, insufficient information on enforcement and unclear governance.

The commission nevertheless kept exports open, while pledging to continue monitoring the situation.

Lauren Weir, Senior Campaigner at the EIA, sees a gap: “We think that there’s a disconnect between the commission’s application of the regulation and what that regulation actually says needs to happen.”

“It should not happen, but given the conclusions of this recent commission assessment, it may in the short term,” she said.

In Adana, where around 60 percent of imported plastic waste is processed, researchers found up to 132 times more microplastics in irrigation canals downstream of recycling plants than upstream. 

Fires are another warning sign. Blazes at recycling facilities rose from six a year in 2017 to 125 a year in 2022, according to a policy brief by Sedat Gündoğdu, a marine biologist at Adana’s Çukurova University.

“All the fires are happening behind the facilities in storage parts, not the machinery or office parts,” he said.

Read more

The EU should stop exporting its plastic waste, period

Turkey caps each facility’s imports at 50 percent of its certified annual processing capacity, according to the commission’s assessment.

But Gündoğdu claims the capacity figures can easily be manipulated. “You can enlarge your area by fencing some places for storage. That’s all,” he explained.

Audits may not close the gap. In 2021, a German inspector found that 2BPlast, a recycling plant in Düzce certified to receive German packaging waste, had been dismantled months earlier while shipments kept arriving.

“Everything will be based on papers. But the real extent of this business is handshaking business. All things are happening behind the doors,” Gündoğdu warned. If independent auditors start inspecting Turkish plants from May 2027, he expects few to succeed: “I don’t believe that more than 10 percent of the facilities can pass this auditing process.”

Turkey already generates around 3.3 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. The government says it recovers 30 percent of its municipal waste, but World Bank data puts the figure at 11.9 percent, according to Gündoğdu’s policy brief.

“How can this country soundly manage waste that belongs to other countries? This is pollution transfer,” Gündoğdu said.

Can Europe handle its own plastic?

]]> COP31 in Antalya: five takeaways from the ‘implementation’ climate summit https://euobserver.com/250385/cop31-in-antalya-five-takeaways-from-the-implementation-climate-summit/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 08:12:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250385 After three decades of UN climate summits, and little progress on climate finance, this year’s meeting (COP31) in Turkey, is likely to be remembered less for what negotiators agreed than for the deals struck on the sidelines.]]> After three decades of UN climate summits, this year’s meeting (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, is likely to be remembered less for what negotiators agreed than for the deals struck on the sidelines. 

Since the first Conference of the Parties gathered in Berlin in 1995, the annual talks have produced the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C goal, a pledge in Dubai to “transition away” from fossil fuels, and, last year in Belém, a push to turn those commitments into action. 

But delegates from more than 190 countries remain split over who should pay to help the poorest nations cope with climate disasters, while mentions of a fossil fuel phase-out were barred from the final text. Instead, global leaders leaned on a Turkish-backed goal to boost electrification.

Notably, the US did not take part in the talks.

“Consensus often only delivers the lowest common denominator,” Linda Kalcher, co-founder of the climate think-tank Strategic Perspectives told EUobserver. But in the context of trade tensions, wars, and conflicts, she said it is positive to see that “multilateralism still delivers.” 

Turkey, the host country of this year’s COP, is expected to receive billion-dollar investment deals, a preliminary $15bn renewable energy deal with China, $5.1bn in financing from development banks, and accords with Saudi Arabia and Canada.

Post-Iran impact

Global energy shocks linked to the war in Iran, which effectively saw the Strait of Hormuz shut down, have also complicated energy talks.

]]> Russian missiles over Poland, European troops in the mud: Ukraine’s defence force is taking shape https://euobserver.com/250435/russian-missiles-over-poland-european-troops-in-the-mud-ukraines-defence-force-is-taking-shape/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:33:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250435 Just hours before the European war games in Poland began, Russian missiles and a drone tore through its Nato airspace.]]> The air raid sirens came at around 6.30AM on Friday (20 November) near Nowa Dęba, a small town in south-east Poland, roughly 100km from the border with Ukraine.

At least two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone had violated Polish airspace during the morning even as troops from 11 European countries had gathered in a large field surrounded by tall pine tree forests nearby.

The Russian cruise missiles and drone hit areas in south-eastern Poland, one 50km from Ukraine’s border. Nobody was killed.

“Common sense suggests there are no coincidences in such incidents. I think it was some kind of incident linked to our presence here,” Dariusz Mendrala, a major general in the Polish Armed Forces and the chief of the Armed Forces Support Inspectorate, told reporters.

“It won’t stop us from preparing to carry out our mission. For us, for the Polish state, for the Polish Armed Forces, these things have not been entirely exceptional for some time now,” he added.

Behind him, some 48,000 square meters of military infrastructure and logistics facilities had been erected by the Polish forces in the thick mud and rain, as part of the first major exercise by the Multinational Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), a non-Nato European military force, led by France and the United Kingdom, which is to be ready to deploy to Ukraine once a ceasefire has been announced.

Named Koalicja (coalition in Polish), the exercise had attracted scores of journalists, some as far away as Japan, as well as high-ranking officials and defence ministers from Estonia, France, Lithuania, Poland, and the United Kingdom.

With its 2,800 troops and jet fighter flybys of French Rafales, British RAF Typhoons, and Tiger helicopters, the MNF-U intends to provide reassurance for a Ukraine that was itself pounded overnight by a large-scaled Russian air barrage, targeting bridges in Kyiv and killing at least eight people.

    A coordinated operation

    Early last Saturday, several people smashed windows at the premises of Threod Systems, a company in the town of Viimsi that manufactures long-range strike and reconnaissance drones. Its website lists Ukraine and Nato member states among its customers.

    Palloson also said that no one was injured in the incident, the company was not damaged in any way, and its production and supply capacities were not disrupted.

    Although police detained eight people, only five were remanded in custody.

    “Estonia has long sought to be as transparent as possible in informing the public about Russia’s hostile activities,” Estonian security expert Henrik Praks of the International Centre for Defence and Security (CDS) in Tallinn told Euobserver.

    Although the attack took place on Saturday morning, Estonian authorities and politicians attributed it to Russia as early as the following day.

    Responding to the attempted sabotage, Michal announced that the country would close all its land border crossings with Russia.     It requires companies in the energy sector to monitor and measure methane emissions from their operations, for example, during gas production. It also restricts venting and flaring.     As repression increasingly hits press and NGO freedoms in Europe and beyond, laws that seek to police the vocabulary of crucial democratic debates risk pushing our societies back into dark times, which our grandparents fought to end.

    In 2024, the German parliament passed a non-binding resolution backing the IHRA definition. Two years later, Germany is considering a law that would make denying Israel’s right to exist a crime, with up to five years in prison.

    UK prime minister Andy Burnham wants to prove that he is delivering the EU ‘reset’ that his predecessor Keir Starmer had promised.  

    But there are limits to the number of sectoral agreements – or cherry picking – on offer. Ahead of the summit, EU officials have warned that there’s not much more fruit left to pick.

    A draft joint summit statement points to further discussions on the UK linking up with the EU’s energy single market, as well as on co-operation on migration control, and a closer defence and security relationship. 

    Read more

    ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit

    The UK needs to decide whether it wants to join the single market, rejoin the EU, or accept the status quo, say EU diplomats. 

    In a fact sheet published earlier this week, the UK government said that the ‘food & drink’ trade deal “could add up to £5.1bn [€6.1bn] a year to our economy, cutting back on paperwork for businesses and easing pressure on prices.” 

    The agreement to align agrifood standards will scrap border controls and certification requirements for “the vast majority” of animal and plant products traded between the UK and the EU from 1 March 2028. 

    The factsheet adds that an emissions linking agreement could add up to £3.8bn a year, and protect critical industries, such as steel and aluminium, from the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), on approximately £6.5bn in exports.  

    The EU and UK are also to launch a digital partnership in early 2027 covering secure connectivity, artificial intelligence, and digital identities. 

    A Youth Experience Scheme (TES), meanwhile, will let young people live in each other’s territories for up to three years to work or study. The aim is to seal the agreement by 2028 and have the scheme running by January 2030. The total number of participants has not been decided yet, although sources say it is likely to be around 100,000. 
     
    But the UK will probably have to wait for an agreement on its main priorities: inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ industrial support scheme, and participation in the EU’s €150bn ‘Security Action for Europe’ (SAFE) instrument for common defence borrowing.  

    The talks on ‘Made in Europe’ are more complicated than simply aligning regulation. The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act, which sets out the rules on supply chain inputs, is still being negotiated by EU governments and MEPs and is unlikely to be finalised before early 2027.  

    Any deal between London and Brussels would need to be based on the EU law that is eventually adopted.

    It would also need to be in line with the demands of a Franco-German paper from October, which proposed Britain be granted special status for automobiles, subject to “dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures”. 

    That will likely require the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and curbing imports of Chinese hybrid cars, in line with the EU.

    ]]>         Hungary’s new government claws back motorways and tobacco monopoly after years of taxpayer‑funded Orbán luxury travel (Day 191 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/250131/hungarys-new-government-claws-back-motorways-and-tobacco-monopoly-after-years-of-taxpayerfunded-orban-luxury-travel-day-191-of-the-tisza-government/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:04:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250131 Hungary’s new leaders rip up motorway and tobacco deals that once enriched Orbán’s allies, raising the prospect of a massive financial and political reckoning. ]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Viktor Orbán travelled in luxury on trips abroad
    • Treasure hunting, Hungarian style
    • The state is taking back motorway operations from Mészáros and Szíjj
    • The government moves to dismantle part of Hungary’s controversial tobacco concession system

    It has been an eventful week in Hungary. As investigators seized billions of forints in cash buried in forests and hidden in safes, the government began dismantling some of the most controversial concessions awarded under its predecessor.

    The state is taking back motorway operations from the consortium linked to Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj, and the government has moved to end the monopoly on supplying tobacco shops. Meanwhile, foreign ministry records obtained through a court case have revealed how much Viktor Orbán’s luxury travel cost taxpayers.

    Orbán luxury travels

    The news outlet 444.hu obtained records from the ministry of foreign affairs and trade through a freedom-of-information lawsuit. The records detail the cost and circumstances of former prime minister Orbán’s official trips by air between 2015 and 2025. Who paid for his foreign travel had been a recurring question since 2010. Reports suggested he travelled on private jets belonging to OTP Bank or to various oligarchs, while others suggested he paid his own way.

    The records show that the ministry alone spent HUF 4.8bn (€13.03m) in public funds over 10 years, covering all or part of the cost of 327 trips by air. The figures exclude trips on military aircraft. The ministry covered an average of 32 trips a year, with both the number of trips and spending peaking in 2024, when it paid nearly HUF 800m (€2.17m) towards 44 trips.

    The ministry’s flight costs fell sharply after the Hungarian Defence Forces acquired two Airbus troop transports and two luxury Dassault Falcon jets in 2018. The cost of using military aircraft was charged elsewhere. The foreign ministry’s overall travel spending rose sharply again from 2022 as hotel bills and “other” expenses, including meals, official hospitality and car hire, increased. In 2025 alone, the ministry spent HUF 450m (€1.22m) on hotels, almost as much as it had spent from 2016 to 2021 combined.

    Brussels was Orbán’s most frequent destination, with 74 trips costing a total of HUF 550m. Warsaw followed with 18 trips and Belgrade with 16. Orbán visited the United States only five times during the period covered by the records, but the size of his delegations made it the second-costliest destination overall, at HUF 380m.

    The five most expensive trips:

    • Vietnam and Singapore, 2017 — HUF 180.4m (€490,000). The 23-member delegation stayed four nights. Flights accounted for most of the cost.
    • Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2023 — HUF 159m (€431,000). A delegation of 27 stayed three nights for Javier Milei’s inauguration. Expenses included luxury hotels, HUF 12 million in catering and a meal at a Michelin-starred restaurant.
    • Doha, Qatar, 2022 — HUF 131.8m (€358,000). The four-person trip included stops in Europe between the FIFA World Cup semi-final and final. The foreign ministry paid HUF 126 million of the total in hotel bills.
    • Washington and Palm Beach, United States, 2024 — HUF 127m (€345,000). The 73-member delegation stayed two nights. The trip included a meeting with Donald Trump and had no official government programme.
    • Beijing and Shenzhen, China, 2023 — HUF 106.5m (€289,000). The 26-member delegation stayed five nights. The trip included the Belt and Road Forum and meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.

    Travel requests from the prime minister’s cabinet office often left out the name of the event, the mode of transport or the point of departure. In some cases, it is still impossible to establish exactly why the trip took place.

    In others, the circumstances point to private engagements or sporting events for which the foreign ministry covered the cost of a private, high-security airport lounge reserved for government use or a stay at a luxury hotel. The line between official and private travel often blurred.

    Read more

    Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták

    The 444.hu report also recalls that government ministers, Orbán himself and Sándor Csányi, who chairs both the Hungarian Football Federation (MLSZ) and OTP Bank, gave conflicting accounts over the years of who paid for private flights to football matches or holiday destinations.

    In 2019, Csányi said Orbán had always paid for his own trips. In an interview in autumn 2025, Orbán acknowledged that the Hungarian state paid for his private flights to national team matches abroad, citing invitations from the federation. The newly released ministry records corroborate that account.

    Treasure hunting, Hungarian style

    Investigators from the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) found nearly HUF 6.5 billion (around €17m) in cash in the course of criminal proceedings involving Miklós Seszták. The money had been buried in forests and concealed in warehouses and a hidden safe.

    Read more

    Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták

    The office says it is still unclear who owns it. Hungarians were confronted with the sight of a sum that someone earning an honest living could hardly make in a lifetime, hidden underground, in buildings and in safes.

    ]]>         EU gives oil and gas importers until 2029 on methane checks, rules out more delay https://euobserver.com/250022/eu-gives-oil-and-gas-importers-until-2029-on-methane-checks-rules-out-more-delay/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 15:07:11 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250022 After all-night talks, EU governments and MEPs agreed to delay methane regulations until 2029, but scrapped the legal possibility for further fob-offs, in a win for centre-left politics. ]]> EU governments and the European Parliament agreed, in the early hours of Thursday (19 November), to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil, gas, and coal importers by two years, which is double the lag that the European Commission had proposed. 

    Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that traps around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over 20 years. 

    A lot of it leaks into the atmosphere from wells, pipelines, and coal mines, which the EU rules aim to address.

    Originally, they were to kick in on 1 January 2027, but under the new provisional deal, the rules for importers will now apply from 1 January 2029.

    Importers and EU producers will also get two more years to report the methane intensity of the fossil fuels they sell in the EU, now from 5 August 2030. 

    The agreement settled halfway between an earlier compromise by member states, which wanted a one-year delay earlier this month, and parliament, which voted for a three-year delay in October.

    But gone was the option, pushed by member states, to extend the delay again. Centre-left MEPs had warned it could be used to postpone the rules indefinitely, after centre-left MEPs pushed back against it, warning that it could be used to delay the rules one more time after 2029, or keep postponing them for ever. 

    Instead, the commission will only look at how the law is being implemented at the start of 2028 and whether there is any risk to security of supply. 

    And any further delay would need a whole new methane law, which came as some relief to campaigners. 

    “Despite the delay, the integrity of the regulation is preserved in the final deal,” said Léa Pilsner of Environmental Defense Fund Europe in Brussels, adding that governments had “bought themselves two years the regulation never needed”.

    But Pilsner also said 24 billion cubic metres of methane will leak into the atmosphere during the extra two-year delay, which equals two-thirds of what France uses in gas in a year. 

    Governments said the delay was needed due to supply risks and worries over high fuel prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted Gulf oil and gas supplies.

    “We are not suspending the Methane Regulation; we are ensuring that it can be effectively implemented,” said Greek centre-right MEP Dimitris Tsiodras, who led the talks for parliament’s environment committee. 

    His Polish centre-right colleague, Borys Budka, the lead MEP for the industry committee, said that “security of supply comes first”.

    Meanwhile, the cost of adapting fuel infrastructure to align with EU rules is relatively low. 

    Modelling by Rystad Energy in Oslo puts the cost of the rules at a few euro cents per million British thermal units, or about 0.3 percent of the current gas price. 

    And the International Energy Agency in Paris, in its most recent projections, sees overseas gas markets remaining tight next year, it still expects a gas glut to arrive relatively soon, due to a very large increase in gas export capacity, primarily in the United States.

    A separate analysis by Data Desk, commissioned by the European Climate Foundation in The Hague, found in September that some central and eastern European countries reliant on Russian gas could face supply challenges, but also argued that “in no case are these sufficient to disrupt the implementation of the regulation in its current form”.

    Thursday’s decision to delay follows an intense and years-long campaign led by US president Donald Trump administration and the oil and gas industry. 

    Internal commission documents, reported by EUobserver earlier this month, showed how the commission tried to placate Washington with technical fixes, while US officials and industry lobbied national capitals directly.

    Seven of the eight central and eastern European member states courted by Trump’s energy officials at a Washington summit in February later backed a three-year delay.

    Parliament is due to vote on the deal next week, and member states still need to formally sign off before the end of the year, when the original rules are due to otherwise kick in. 

    ]]>         MEPs gut EU Commission plan for regulating space industries https://euobserver.com/249952/meps-gut-eu-commission-plan-for-regulating-space-industries/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:00:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249952 Brussels is racing to keep up in the global space race, after MEPs slashed green demands from the EU’s first Space Act, in a bid to win over capitals and industry. ]]> Substantially watered down EU rules on safer and more competitive space activities came a step closer to life on Thursday (19 November), when the European Parliament’s industry, research, and energy committee (ITRE) voted on its position on the proposed EU Space Act.

    The vote allows the full parliament to move towards establishing its negotiating mandate, paving the way for ‘trilogue’ talks with the EU Council of member states and the European Commission.

    The draft report was adopted with 72 votes to 1, with 2 abstentions. With the same majority, MEPs also voted to start negotiations with Council.

    “If everything goes fine next year with the proposal, we have another three years and a half to be implemented,” said German MEP Angelika Niebler, of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) and shadow rapporteur on the file.

    The new EU space rules are to replace a patchwork of national regulatory measures, but the text approved by ITRE differs significantly from the commission’s original proposal.

    It is around 22 percent shorter, with the number of articles reduced from 119 to 97, according to Italian MEP Elena Donazzan, the lead rapporteur for the rightwing European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group.

    The proposed Union-level legal framework  – a harmonised set of rules governing safety, resilience, and environmental sustainability for space activities – has been removed, Donazzan said, arguing that it would have added costs for companies and member states.

    This means the commission’s vision of a common legal baseline failed, leaving regulatory flexibility for member states.

    The mandatory environmental certificate has also been dropped, while a standalone cybersecurity regime has been removed, as space-related cybersecurity requirements are now addressed through amendments to the NIS2 directive.

    The changes come amid growing pressure for Europe to strengthen its position in an increasingly contested space sector.

    Read more

    [Interview] Europe’s labs are chronically underfunded and sovereignty is at stake, says French Academy chief Françoise Combes

    “The EU Space Act means greater clarity, predictability, and less fragmentation,” Maria Fernández Molinero, head of unit for Space Policy at the commission’s directorate-general for defence industry and space, told the Space Tech Expo Europe in Germany on Wednesday.

    “Across Europe, countries face different regulatory arrangements. A common framework can address those challenges,” she said.

    “Maintaining the status quo as we see it now, while impressive, is not enough for the decade we see ahead of us,” Molinero added.

    “Europe’s response to changing geopolitics must match a new reality,” she also said, while warning that greater dependence on space also created new vulnerabilities. Europe, she added, must not only innovate in space, but also protect what it builds.

    For the shadow rapporteur, Niebler, the incoming legislation still marked a “historic moment” in the EU’s approach to space policy.

    The commission’s original proposal envisages the rules applying from 1 January 2030, a timeline which Donazzan, the lead MEP, described as “realistic”.

    The Council position on the Space Act will not be finalised during the Irish presidency, which ends on 31 December, but a progress report will be submitted at a “Space Council” in early December, and the file will be handed over to the Lithuanian presidency next year, said Peadar Ó hÚbáin, an Irish spokesperson.

    ]]>         Erdoğan is strangling Turkey’s last free media, as EU turns a blind eye https://euobserver.com/249968/erdogan-is-strangling-turkeys-last-free-media-as-eu-turns-a-blind-eye/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:50:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249968 Turkey's state takeover of independent broadcaster Sözcü TV was met by loud EU silence, in a broader pattern of appeasement, as Erdoğan strangles what is left of free speech.]]> “Free media in Türkiye is dead,” Europe’s Socialist and Democrats (S&D) party declared on Tuesday (17 November), after a Turkish pro-opposition media, Sözcü TV, was raided by police in Istanbul.

    One of the last critical news channels standing in Turkey has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey’s broadcasting regulator, as president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s government keeps up pressure on its opponents ahead of the next general elections, expected in 2028. 

    Sözcü TV had earlier gone dark for 10 days, in July 2025, after getting a ban from Turkey’s broadcasting regulator following its coverage of protests sparked by Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu’s arrest.

    After police searched Sözcü TV’s building under a court order on Tuesday, authorities replaced the broadcaster’s direction with a government trustee.

    And for many European observers, the raid was a further step in a vicious crackdown, which has seen independent media toppling into the hands of state control.

    Ankara also placed Erdoğan-sceptic news channel Halk TV under state trusteeship in October, while the opposition-leaning TELE1 broadcaster was given a state trustee a year before, due to espionage allegations lodged against its editor and chief. 

    Read more

    EU and Turkey explore closer trade ties to reduce dependence on China

    With state sanctions affecting most major broadcasters across the country, what remains of independent journalism is some print news, niche online outlets, and independent digital publications.

    “As writers and journalists in Turkey we often feel things can’t be any worse for us, that we have reached the bottom, but the government continues to prove us wrong, and freedom of expression manages to shrink even more,” said Kaya Genç, author of The Lion and the Nightingale, chronicling Turkey’s crackdown on the country’s creative communities.

    The European press prize laureate found the Sözcü takeover particularly unsettling, as it broadened expectations among his colleagues that Ankara may be prepared to remove all critical media. 

    “I watched Sözcü TV this morning. The caretakers of the network had managed to surgically remove the political coverage, leaving space only for news about crime and traffic,” Genç told EUobserver from Istanbul.

    The writer fears that the crackdown will push more Turks to get their news from WhatsApp groups and YouTube streams of opposition journalists, such as the formerly imprisoned Fatih Altaylı, who “has a social media following and views larger than all pro-government media combined,” instead of reading professional and independent journalism.

    Read more

    Could Islamophobia one day become EU law?

    Meanwhile, the increased silencing of media, NGOs, and associations, is enshrined in Turkish law. Article 299 of the penal code foresees one to four years’ imprisonment for insulting the president, while article 301 criminalises “denigrating the Turkish nation”.

    The result has been a “chilling effect” on all forms of civil society, according to Amnesty International, and the law has meant that 17 journalists and media workers are currently in prison.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-markets-slump-anthropic-ipo-ai-sell-off</link>
      <description><p>The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/19/who-are-anthropic-founders">Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?</a></p></li></ul><p>As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it.       <description><p>Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream</p><p>On a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts.       <description><p>Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat</p><p>From <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/jan/04/profumo-scandal-trial-of-christine-keeler-bbc">Profumo</a> to <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-20317995">Petraeus</a> to <a href="https://www.americanheritage.com/content/30-years-ago-gary-harts-monkey-business-and-how-candidate-got-caught">Gary Hart</a>, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-bill-gates-relationship-with-jeffrey-epstein-as-he-is-interviewed-in-house-probe">Bill Gates</a> and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/clinton">Bill Clinton</a>, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/nvidia">Nvidia</a> CEO, Jensen Huang.</p><p>These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us.
