<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 22 Nov 2026 02:27:55 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Alarm bells will have gone off in Dublin after António Costa’s digital tax plans]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/21/ireland-will-not-like-antonio-costas-digital-tax-plans-for-two-standout-reasons/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/21/ireland-will-not-like-antonio-costas-digital-tax-plans-for-two-standout-reasons/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 17:00:00 +0000Alarm bells will have gone off in Dublin at the proposal from European Council president António Costa for the imposition of a digital sales tax on big multinational companies.

This was part of a revised plan for the next seven-year EU budget starting in 2028, on which talks have been highly contentious. Costa sees the tax as a way of raising money directly for central EU coffers, helping to close a financial hole in the proposed budget.

Ireland will not like the plan for two reasons. One is that it threatens to ignite a new row with US president Donald Trump, who hates the idea of digital sales taxes on US firms.

Costa insists the plan does not specifically target US companies. But as it applies to those with a digital turnover of €750 million worldwide and at least €50 million in Europe, the reality is that many of the big US players will be in the frame.

Ireland is the European headquarters of many of these big companies and thus will be central to any developing row. Briefings from Brussels suggest that Costa has proposed the move now because Trump is weakened after the midterm elections. Whether member states agree remains to be seen. They may not want to give Trump an excuse to tear up the EU/US trade agreement. It is very much in Ireland’s interest for this agreement to hold, given the State’s strong trade and investment links with the US.

The Government will also be concerned that more money for EU coffers from the big digital firms such as Google and Facebook could mean less money for Ireland. At the moment big tech pays tax in Ireland on profits earned around the world. If more is levied via this charge for the central EU budget, there may be less tax to be paid here.

Much will depend on the detail of how the charge – set at a rate of 3 per cent on digital revenues – would work. But the part of the OECD corporate tax plan which would have involved more tax being paid by the digital giants in bigger EU markets was seen as likely to cost Ireland more than €2 billion a year. In the event, this part of the OECD deal collapsed.

Ireland had signed up for it – hoping it would settle global corporate tax rows – but has always opposed plans at an EU level, saying that a global solution was the way forward. Over many years a variety of EU plans have come up, with different versions of centralised tax plans at the expense of countries such as Ireland, but none has won the necessary unanimous approval.

António Costa revives EU digital tax proposal in bid to reach agreement on budget

The latest version may not either, and Ireland will hope that other countries will join it in opposing the digital sales tax proposal. The plan will get some support, however. Germany reacted reasonably positively to the Costa plan initially and France has long supported more taxes on big tech. So the coming diplomatic moves will be interesting to watch.

Elsewhere, Costa has not taken any more out of the budget for the Common Agricultural Policy, though the Irish Farmers’ Association points out that spending in this area is set to fall compared with the present budget. EU leaders are due to discuss the new budget plan in Brussels this week. A plan that wins the necessary unanimous support will not be easy to find.

]]>Paulo Nunes Dos Santos<![CDATA[David McWilliams: The economics of the AI boom are actually quite old-fashioned]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000This week saw the largest share offering the world has ever seen. Anthropic, the AI company that makes Claude, floated on the US stock market with an initial value of just over $1 trillion – a thousand billion dollars. Founded only six years ago, it is today the 10th most valuable corporation in the US.

With the share offering coming a week after the Jensen Huang scandal, it seems that the world is captured by some AI story or another. Even global politics is in thrall to this new technology. On Thursday, when Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat together, it was clear that the new cold war was as much about tech as arms. We are looking at an industrial transformation on the scale of the move to oil and gas in the early 20th century. It will change the world, but that doesn’t mean everyone can profit from it.

Despite all the money flooding into what is known as “the AI trade”, there seems to be precious little understanding of the economics underpinning the AI boom. Where is the money going, why is everything so expensive and what are the risks that it collapses following one big speculative mania?

When so few people have the answers, it makes sense to ask the questions.

The AI story is portrayed as a high-end technology story, but when you drill down a bit, the economics of AI seem close to old-fashioned heavy industry. It involves pouring concrete, connecting power grids and buying manufactured microchips at a large scale. The lion’s share of the money goes on imported hardware. Very little of the spending is creating new tech jobs. And a growing share of the AI buildout – estimated to be $1 trillion this year – is being financed with borrowings that will need to be paid back sooner or later.

Who is profiting at the moment, who is paying, and how long can it last?

Most of the profits are being made by chipmakers largely based in Asia. Most of the cost is borne by the companies in the US doing all the borrowing, those building or renting the data centres. In addition, as almost everything uses chips – your phone, your car and your fridge – we are all paying through higher costs in our data-driven economy. The amount of new debt means the AI boom is dependent on the rate of interest, the patience of lenders and the tolerance of local communities for data centres, which were a big issue in the US midterms, as was a general dislike of the tech titans who dominate the AI world.

A data centre needs four things: chips, land, water and electricity. Building a new facility can take about two years. There’s a lot of concrete to pour. The amount of money, water and electricity required is enormous. Consider a 1 gigawatt (GW) campus of data centres. Granted, this is a huge data centre but it gives us an idea of the scale of the industrial transformation in front of us. One GW of electricity roughly corresponds to the output of a nuclear power plant or the annual electricity for some 650,000 houses – bigger than Dublin. About 10.5 billion gallons of water are needed to cool the machines, about enough for 100,000 households, and it needs around 700-1,100 acres of space, about half the total size of Phoenix Park. Are you beginning to grasp the scale?

There is little indication we have a plan for what to do if the AI bubble bursts

Most data centres are not this big, running on the megawatt rather than gigawatt scale, closer to 100-250MW of energy, but the demands of AI mean this figure is trending relentlessly upwards, which makes it worthwhile to look at the jumbo data centre.

A 1GW data centre costs about $50 billion – roughly $15 billion for the facility and $35 billion for the compute to power it. Chips make up roughly 70 per cent of the total cost. Because chips dominate the cost, the profits flow to whoever makes them. Nvidia and the amorous Jensen Huang may well design these chips, but they do not manufacture them. Rather, the likes of SK Hynix, TSMC and others do, with Korea, Taiwan and Japan controlling manufacturing. Others will want to get in on the game.

AI fever is producing some strange symptoms

The hyperscalers, companies such as Google and Meta, are designing their own chips, elbowing in on Nvidia’s turf. Geo-strategically, rival suppliers, particularly in China, will emerge. Greater supply of chips will bring down the cost and as the cost of chips falls, the price of using AI will fall. The dilemma for companies such as Anthropic is that if the price of using it falls, its revenues will fall, undermining its new position as the 10th most valuable company in the US.

Not only is the industrial model changing rapidly, with new competitors emerging at every stage of the supply chain, but maybe – more critically – the financing of the AI transformation has changed from cash flow to debt and equity. The hyperscalers, such as Google, used to finance their AI businesses from their large cash flow but, as the costs have risen, even a big company such as Google has had to start borrowing money.

About 10 per cent of all global investment-grade bonds are already related to AI, possibly rising to 16–19 per cent by next year. The AI borrower is in a highly competitive market. For example, the US government bond yields roughly 5 per cent with essentially no risk, so every data centre bond competes with sovereign debt.

Moreover, central banks that are trying to bear down on inflation are raising interest rates, pushing up rates everywhere. Markets are already getting nervous. Hyperscalers with other subscription businesses can borrow cheaply, but others such as Oracle are paying the widest spread. There is also another group of AI-related businesses called neo-clouds that offer cheaper data centre services than Google, Meta, Amazon or Microsoft. You might have heard of names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe. They are paying much higher interest to get money and are most exposed to any change in interest rates or market sentiment.

Over the past few weeks, the huge amounts of money involved have put the wind up financial markets. Can the AI companies such as Anthropic that have yet to make a profit generate money to validate their huge valuations? Will the hyperscalers continue to bankroll our datacentres? Will banks start to call in loans? And can all this credit continue to flow into a sector that is spending so much but – at least so far – is earning so little?

We’ve seen boom and bust before. Will this be the biggest one?

]]>imaginima<![CDATA[Italian wile trumps German ineptitude to secure Commerzbank deal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/italian-wile-trumps-german-ineptitude-to-secure-commerzbank-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/italian-wile-trumps-german-ineptitude-to-secure-commerzbank-deal/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:01:00 +0000To lose one bank is bad luck, as Oscar Wilde once almost said, but to lose two – and to the same Italian group – seems careless.

So it was on Thursday, when German ineptitude and Milanese wile coalesced in favour of UniCredit.

A decade after it swallowed Bavaria’s HypoVereinsbank, the Italian bank has finally won its hostile takeover bid for Germany’s number two lender.

After 156 years, Commerzbank’s days as an independent institution are numbered after Germany’s federal finance ministry put an end to a months-long protest that was as pride-filled as it was powerless.

A joint agreement will see UniCredit keep the German lender’s Frankfurt headquarters while Berlin – which still holds a 13 per cent stake, a bailout-era holdover – has agreed to drop its demand for two representatives on the future board. Instead, it has climbed down and will be happy with two German nationals.

The capitulation marks the end of a two-year saga triggered when UniCredit chief executive Andrea Orcel began building a discreet stake, then snapping up a holding sold off at speed by Berlin’s last finance minister, Christian Lindner.

Finance ministry officials use unprintable language when they refer to Orcel, while current federal finance minister Lars Klingbeil is more diplomatic – on the record, at least.

In May, Klingbeil, who is also vice-chancellor, told the foreign press in Berlin: “Commerzbank is a very important actor when it comes to supporting German SMEs abroad and has a huge significance for Frankfurt as a finance marketplace.”

Thursday’s statement reflected that Commerzbank’s new owners promise to maintain its profile as a lender to Germany’s SMEs. But that commitment is aspirational rather than legal, prompting the Wirtschaftswoche business weekly headline: “Commerzbank promises hot air on Commerzbank – the vice-chancellor cheers.”

How UniCredit CEO outmanoeuvred Germany on Commerzbank

The conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine daily was more circumspect. A likely cost-cutting wave by its new owners means Commerzbank workers are right to fear for their jobs. But the fact it has come to this is because Commerzbank executives were “lacking in ambition” a decade ago. And, as a major shareholder at that time, “the [German] state carries its share of the responsibility, too”.

]]>Luis Sander<![CDATA[Meath builder sues developers for €12.8m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/meath-builder-sues-developers-for-128m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/meath-builder-sues-developers-for-128m/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Builder Midland Construction and Engineering is suing well-known developers John McKeon, Brian Kennedy, Liam McSharry and others for €12.8 million in a dispute over an apartment project.

High Court president Judge David Barniville last week ordered the enforcement of a €9.8 million arbitration award to Midland against Baystreet Ltd, now in liquidation, which was found to have wrongly terminated a contract with the construction firm.

Separate to this, High Court documents show Midland has issued proceedings against Baystreet’s directors, McKeon, Kennedy and McSharry, along with its shareholders, for almost €12.8 million, including the arbitration award, interest and enforcement costs.

McKeon runs well-known family-owned property development business MKN, which focuses primarily on home building. He did not respond to a request for comment.

Kennedy and McSharry are involved in the Sheelin McSharry property group, associated with the Embassy House complex in Ballsbridge among other high-profile projects. Baystreet Ltd is a separate company to its directors’ other businesses.

Kells, Co Meath-based Midland will seek to have the case heard by the Commercial Court, a division of the High Court that deals with business disputes, at a hearing scheduled for next week.

Baystreet hired Midland in early 2022 to build a development of 44 apartments at Ashbrook, Howth Road, in Clontarf on Dublin’s northside, for an initial €9.6 million, which the parties subsequently agreed to increase to €10.8 million. Work was due to finish in March 2023.

Difficulties with the site’s water connection, along with several other delays, led to a dispute between the parties, prompting Baystreet to terminate the contract in February 2024 with much of the project built and call in Midland’s bond.

The dispute was referred to arbitration and admitted in March 2025 when Midland filed its initial claim and Baystreet responded.

Details from the residential property price register show that in the meantime the 44 apartments in the Howth Road development sold for a total of almost €23 million, with the last one selling in August last year.

In September 2025, creditors put Baystreet, established to develop the Clontarf site, into liquidation, appointing Tom Murray of Friel Stafford as liquidator. He is a notice party to the case and declined to comment when his office was contacted.

Midland successfully sought a High Court order last October allowing it to continue the arbitration after Baystreet went into liquidation.

In February this year, arbitrator David O’Leary decided that Baystreet had unlawfully and invalidly terminated the contract with Midland and awarded the construction firm €9.15 million in total with interest.

The building firm was confirmed as a creditor of Baystreet Ltd in July. The High Court heard last week that, up to then, Midland had not received any payment from the company on foot of the award.

Barniville granted judgment for €9.86 million, which included interest on the original €9.15 million that O’Leary ordered Baystreet to pay.

John McKeon’s father Sean established MKN in the ‘nineties. Around 20 years earlier, he and Brian Kennedy’s father, John Kennedy, set up Sheelin Homes together. Kennedy senior helped established Sheelin McSharry after he and McKeon senior decided to go into business separately.

Midland Construction and Engineering did not comment.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Shein sold €7.9bn of goods in Europe through Irish entity in 2025]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/shein-sold-79bn-of-goods-in-europe-through-irish-entity-in-2025/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/shein-sold-79bn-of-goods-in-europe-through-irish-entity-in-2025/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Chinese fast fashion giant Shein sold more than €7.9 billion worth of goods through its Irish-registered European arm in 2025, the last full year before the European Union (EU) introduced new charges on purchases of goods from outside the bloc.

Incorporated in 2020, Infinite Styles Ecommerce is the group’s main European entity and sole shareholder in a range of Shein-related trading companies in other EU countries, including France, Germany and Belgium. Its address is listed as Shein’s Europe, Middle East and Africa headquarters in Grand Canal Dock, Dublin 2.

The company paid almost €17.5 million in corporation tax in Ireland last year, according to the consolidated group accounts.

It generated revenues of €8.2 billion, most of which was derived from sales of its products to the European market, which topped €7.97 billion in the year. Year-on-year, its revenues were down by around 16 per cent from €9.8 billion in 2024.

Still, the company reported after-tax profits of almost €117 million last year, down from €137.6 million in 2024. It employed 389 people on average in 2025, up from 254 in 2024.

EU import duty rules previously excluded goods valued at less than €150 from additional charges. However, in July, the bloc fast-tracked a reform of its customs regime, originally due to be implemented in 2028. Since July, goods valued up to €150 imported from a non-EU country are subject to a flat €3 charge.

New €3 charge means online shopping is now a lot more expensive

The new regime is aimed at tackling a surge in online sales of goods from Chinese retail giants like Shein and Temu. The European Commission said almost six billion low-value items were directly shipped from countries outside the EU to consumers in the region last year.

Shein, which listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in September, has continued to expand its presence in Ireland, opening a new 16,000-square-foot ecommerce logistics facility in Greenogue Business Park, Rathcoole, Co Dublin, in May, to act as a regional fulfilment and returns processing centre.

Separately, the group’s other main Irish entity, Infinite Fashion Ecommerce, reported a widening of its accumulated deficit to €367.2 million last year. The entity is an investment holding company, which holds the group’s stake in several US-registered trading and investment companies within the Shein structure.

The Irish Times reported last year the company posted a 30 per cent climb in revenues to €11.53 billion in 2024. However, in the 2025 filings, which were signed off by the directors in late September, the Shein subsidiary did not report revenues.

Shein has been asked for comment.

Combined €21bn revenues pass through fast-fashion giant Shein’s Irish subsidiaries

]]>Lam Yik<![CDATA[McEnaney firm to provide emergency housing at recently acquired €4.3m Dublin property]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/mcenaney-firm-to-provide-emergency-housing-at-recently-acquired-43m-dublin-property/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/21/mcenaney-firm-to-provide-emergency-housing-at-recently-acquired-43m-dublin-property/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000A company linked to former Monaghan GAA manager Séamus “Banty” McEnaney has expanded its property portfolio with the purchase of a home opposite the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin.

]]><![CDATA[Nex Playground review: turning your home into a family-friendly arcade ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/11/21/nex-playground-review-turning-your-home-into-a-family-friendly-arcade/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/11/21/nex-playground-review-turning-your-home-into-a-family-friendly-arcade/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Remember the Xbox Kinect? Microsoft’s system, released in 2010, turned your body into the controller, with a range of casual games that were designed to appeal to a family audience. I loved it, even if it had its quirks. It was something different and it had so much potential.

But it didn’t take off in quite the way that Microsoft had hoped, and the company eventually discontinued it in 2017.

But motion gaming may have a new hero: the Nex Playground. The tiny console turns your room into an arcade, with games for all ages that encourage players to get moving.

Unlike an Xbox or a PlayStation, it doesn’t dominate the room, designed instead as a small cube that fits in the palm of your hand. And unlike its console rivals, the camera is built in rather than existing as a separate add-on. Plus it comes with a lens cover for added privacy protection.

That camera works well. One of the weaknesses of the Kinect was how much room it required, forcing players with smaller spaces to turn to yet more add-ons to try to make it work. The Nex Playground has a wide angle camera that needs about six foot of space in front of the TV to play. That should suit most homes.

Grand Theft Auto: The thrill of breaking bad from the safety of your sofa

The games are equally accessible. The Nex Playground comes with five games on the console to get you started; additional games can be accessed through an annual pass for €99 that will cover all games released on the platform, and any updates that are needed.

That works out at little more than a decent new release for one of the consoles so, as far as value for money goes, it does well.

The range is good too. It also assumes no major shock to the tax base in the meantime – or Irish bond yields blowing out from their current tight range with Germany.

If that happens, Ireland can hardly expect the ECB to be any more willing to ride to its rescue than it is today to France’s.

]]><![CDATA[Spend your gift vouchers as soon as you get them – there’s no point in waiting ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/20/spend-your-gift-vouchers-as-soon-as-you-get-them-theres-no-point-in-waiting/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/20/spend-your-gift-vouchers-as-soon-as-you-get-them-theres-no-point-in-waiting/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:17:11 +0000Until the end of 2019, readers of The Irish Times would frequently make contact with us to complain about the ridiculous terms and conditions that were attached to the gift vouchers they had given or received.

The sector – despite being worth hundreds of millions of euro annually – was almost completely unregulated. That lack of regulation was relentlessly exploited by retailers, restaurants, hairdressers, hotels, airlines and all the rest.

They imposed all sorts of ridiculously consumer-unfriendly terms and conditions on the sale of vouchers and were happy to bury all the unfair rules deep in the T&Cs, knowing we as consumers could do nothing about it.

Vouchers were sold with expiry dates of 12 months, six months, or even less. Shops, restaurants and airlines routinely refused to give people change – even in voucher form – if they bought something for less than the full value of their voucher.

Unfortunate consumers were told they could not use their vouchers during sale periods, and retailers could refuse to accept two vouchers worth €50 each for a product or service that cost €100.

It was insane and saw hard-earned cash turn into overly complicated pieces of paper that sometimes actively worked against our best interests.

Because of the shambolic way the system operated, Irish consumers lost tens of millions of euro every year – while those who sold the vouchers to us laughed all the way to the bank.

There were attempts to fix things. In 2009, the Labour Party proposed the Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Bill, but it was rejected by the government of the day for reasons best known to itself. In 2015, then minister for enterprise Richard Bruton published a draft consumer rights Bill, which contained several provisions for the regulation of vouchers, but it never became law. And an attempt by the Social Democrats to bring another Bill before the Dáil in 2018 also foundered.

But in 2019 everything changed. Then minister for enterprise Heather Humphreys successfully got legislation over the line that imposed consumer-friendly rules on the gift voucher industry.

Profits jump 13% to €7.5m at gift card group One4All

The Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Act set a minimum expiry date of five years for vouchers and banned contract terms that required them to be spent in a single transaction.

If a consumer did not redeem the full amount of the voucher in an initial purchase, businesses were required to reimburse any remaining balance of more than €1 by cash, electronic transfer or voucher.

The law also banned contract terms that limited the number of vouchers that could be used in a transaction.

In passing the legislation, Ireland became the first European country to enact laws protecting consumers in this area. However, more than six years on, some retailers appear to be struggling to come to terms with the changes.

That became clear this week when the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) said it had identified retailers doing business in the State who were not complying with the law on gift vouchers.

It was able to establish this by using recent data from consumer reports to its helpline.

Irish gift voucher legislation is clear, and traders selling vouchers must follow the law

Aoibhín de Búrca of the CCPC

It wrote to traders around the country to remind them of the rules, highlighting a number of issues and drawing attention to the core provisions of the consumer law around gift vouchers.

It called on traders who had sold vouchers valid for less than five years in the post-2019 period to engage with the CCPC and propose remedies for affected consumers.

“We are still hearing from consumers who are experiencing issues with gift vouchers,” said CCPC director of communications and consumer information Aoibhín de Búrca.

“As we approach one of the busiest times of year for the purchase and use of gift vouchers, we are reminding traders of their consumer protection obligations.”

She said: “Irish gift voucher legislation is clear, and traders selling vouchers must follow the law. The legislation is there for consumers and we want consumers to know what their rights are, and to get the full protection and value of the legislation.”

The CCPC did not name any retailers that were in breach of the law. The letter has been sent to a wide range of businesses including hotels, restaurants, takeaways, dentists, sports retailers, clothes shops, salons and spas.

Some retailers are not complying with gift voucher laws, says Irish consumer watchdog

But we know at least a couple that it may have had in mind.

In July of this year, JD Sports issued refunds of €250,000 to consumers following a CCPC investigation that came in the wake of revelations in The Irish Times that it had sold gift vouchers valid for only one year, instead of at least five years.

In recent weeks, this newspaper revealed that British fashion retailer Flannels – which is owned by Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group – had sold vouchers that came with a two-year expiry in line with its UK policies but contrary to Irish law.

It is only right that the CCPC and consumers focus on vouchers now because it will soon be Christmas, and in the weeks ahead millions of euro will be spent on these things.

Recent CCPC research has found that two-thirds of people received at least one the previous Christmas. That research highlights a problem that is beyond legislation and even retailer ignorance of the law. The blame for that other problem may rest with us: as many as one in five people who get a voucher do not spend it in the first year. There is a good chance that if a voucher is not used in the first 12 months, it will go unused forever – and that means we are wasting as much €70 million a year.

Even if we do get around to spending them eventually, we are taking a risk by waiting. The retail space is volatile and shops come and go.

Liquidators appointed to Dundrum Harvey Nichols store

Earlier this year, the Harvey Nichols store in Dundrum Town Centre closed down after the sale of its UK parent to Frasers Group through what is known as a prepack administration process in the UK. Liquidators from Grant Thornton were appointed to the Irish business.

One of the liquidators’ first actions was to post a notice on the store’s website stating that any “orders placed and gift cards purchased before August 13th, 2026, fall under the ownership structure preceding this transition”.

In other words, they were not being honoured.

When a retailer goes out of business or changes ownership as part of an insolvency process, the holders of gift cards and vouchers are ranked among unsecured creditors and are at the back of the queue when seeking payments.

By the time the secured creditors – Revenue and banks – get at least some of their debt repaid, there is rarely anything left for those unsecured creditors.

That is why it is a good idea to spend the vouchers you get as soon as you get them. There is almost no point in waiting.

It’s got form. There were 256 non-employees working in the offices of Dutch lender Knab when Bawag acquired it at the end of 2024. By the end of last year, the number had fallen to 56. Bawag inherited 95 non-employees working on-site at Barclays’s German consumer finance business when it bought that business in February 2025. The Austrian group is widely expected to follow a reduction in PTSB’s non-staff numbers with a voluntary redundancy scheme within the first 12 months of the takeover.

Bawag has promised in the transaction agreement that for at least two years after the deal is completed, it will keep PTSB’s headquarters in Dublin as well as a “meaningful branch footprint across Ireland to continue to provide bricks-and-mortar banking services to the Irish customers of PTSB, including access to cash, in line with applicable regulation”.

Abuzaakouk said earlier this year that he sees the branch network – comprising 98 locations, including 25 acquired from Ulster Bank in 2023 – as “a real asset”, but one that would probably evolve from being transactions-based towards advice, as has been the case with Bawag in Austria over the past 10 years.

Irish access-to-cash rules, introduced late last year to preserve ATM and cash-service provision at 2022 levels, complicate the picture in this State. Bawag sees the PTSB deal boosting its earnings per share (EPS) by 20 per cent within three years of going through. That is without even factoring in potential income growth.

A big play over the medium term will be to increase PTSB’s commercial lending portfolio, according to analysts and industry sources.

Looking at the Austrian group’s loan portfolio provides some useful clues. On the lending front, the group has consistently pitched itself to investors as being “disciplined” on pricing, particularly in mortgages, and unwilling to chase volumes at the expense of margins over the long term.

The case for PTSB to strengthen its offering – currently centred on being a tied agent for Irish Life products – is underscored by the Government’s plans to introduce tax-efficient personal investment accounts aimed at encouraging greater participation in investing.

In its latest financial stability review, the regulator also urged credit union customers to remain vigilant after the recent cyberattack, Joe Brennan writes.

Separately, Joe reports that Cantor Fitzgerald Ireland said its revenues dipped 4 per cent last year to €59.4 million as it exited a “noncore” offering to clients. It’s understood that this relates to a decision to exit so-called structured products.

Ubiquitous though its social media presence is, it’s a common misconception that Meaghers Pharmacy group is nationwide. It’s not, Oonagh O’Hagan, who has led the group for 25 years, tells Killian in our Interview of the Week. But that’s all about to change.

With Christmas coming into view, Ireland’s consumer watchdog says it has identified retailers in Ireland who are not complying with laws around gift vouchers. Conor Pope has the story.

Brown Thomas Arnotts chief executive and chief merchant Donald McDonald has been chosen as The Irish Times Business Person of the Month for October. During the month, the Irish department store group posted record revenues of €345 million for the 52 weeks to January 3rd, 2026.

]]><![CDATA[Chances of Jensen Huang making a Steve Jobs-like comeback go from slim to zero]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/20/chances-of-jensen-huang-making-a-steve-jobs-like-comeback-go-from-slim-to-zero/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/20/chances-of-jensen-huang-making-a-steve-jobs-like-comeback-go-from-slim-to-zero/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000In the history of chief executive comebacks, OpenAI boss Sam Altman’s was probably the quickest at five days. Steve Jobs’s return to Apple in 1997 was probably the most successful. It propelled the company to where it is today. The iPhone maker was reportedly 90 days away from bankruptcy.

For a few days last week and early this week, Jensen Huang looked like he might make a Lazarus-like return to Nvidia, the company he cofounded 33 years ago. Huang’s downfall at the hands of a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has still to play out but his popularity within the industry and with Nvidia staff appeared to give him a fighting chance.

But that door was slammed shut on Tuesday night after the company announced it did not “intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. The thinking was probably that bringing him back would only prolong the crisis. Lines drawn and all that.

For a global tech industry obsessed with cyber threats and risks to digital infrastructure, it’s ironic that Huang allegedly got caught out by a good old-fashioned honey trap. OpenAI actively trains its staff on how not to fall into these traps as part of the company’s counter-intelligence firewall.

Nvidia’s share price is still down by close to a third since October’s all-time high, suggesting there is considerable investor anxiety about the company, driven as much by wider AI market jitters as Huang’s indiscretions.

Nvidia’s relationship with Singapore-based Megaspeed – the data centre company associated with Alice Huang (the suspected honey trap) – is the murkiest part. The relatively obscure company appears to have been able to buy up to $5 billion (€4.5 billion) worth of high-end Nvidia chips at the height of a global chip shortage. The suspicion is that the company was merely a front to circumvent US export restrictions. Instead of smuggling the chips directly into China, Megaspeed seemed to be installing thousands of GPUs (graphics processing units) inside data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, giving Chinese AI companies access to next-level US computing power.

When reporters turned up at the offices of Megaspeed in Singapore, there was nobody there. Workers from neighbouring offices said the Megaspeed office was rarely used.

Former US president Joe Biden had banned exports of Nvidia’s top-tier chips to China in 2022 out of concern that Beijing would have access to the advanced chips to train its AI models.

The “who knew what, and when” element of the scandal within the US administration – with US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick at the centre – looks set to run. Lutnick is facing criticism for a delay in adding Megaspeed to the blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security. Nvidia itself had put Megaspeed on a “no sell” list last year.

Bessent points finger at Lutnick as Nvidia row ignites Washington blame game

The New York Times has uncovered a web of overlapping financial relationships between several Asian chip importers and Lutnick’s former finance business Cantor Fitzgerald.

The twin tracks of diplomacy and business get messier and messier under Trump. Maybe it was always this way, but the conflicts of interest have never been so obvious. The US president reportedly purchased millions of dollars worth of Nvidia stock from a personal account in advance of his administration loosening restrictions on chip exports to China in May last year.

Nvidia itself made a $25 million contribution to Trump’s new White House ballroom a few months later.

Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer said the administration “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset”.

Huang had conducted a three-year behind-the-scenes campaign to reopen the Chinese market to advanced chip sales, arguing that it served US interests to have China reliant on US technology.

“That’s probably the most important strategic reason to be in China,” he said in an interview with CNBC last year.

Everyone spies on everyone – but as Jensen Huang may be discovering, China does it best

Trump and Lutnick made their political careers as China hawks, but they’ve been anything but in office.

Huang’s departure and speculation about his comeback have invited comparisons with Apple’s Steve Jobs. Jobs, however, left Apple after a management power struggle and returned when the company was struggling and needed him to chart a course forward. Huang, by contrast, faces controversy involving personal conduct and corporate governance.

And his former company isn’t exactly struggling. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported a doubling of revenue to $115.8 billion for the three months to October 25th, with profits also doubling from a year ago to $65 billion.

Much will depend on Nvidia’s future business performance, but for the moment, Huang seems to have been cut loose.

]]><![CDATA[Some retailers are not complying with gift voucher laws, says Irish consumer watchdog]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/some-retailers-are-not-complying-with-gift-voucher-laws-says-irish-consumer-watchdog/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/some-retailers-are-not-complying-with-gift-voucher-laws-says-irish-consumer-watchdog/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Ireland’s consumer watchdog has identified retailers in Ireland who are not complying with laws around gift vouchers, despite the fact that the legislation has been in place for almost six years.

Until the end of 2019, the voucher industry – which is worth hundreds of millions of euro annually – was not governed by any regulations.

The Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Act, which came into force in late 2019, set a minimum expiry date of five years for vouchers and banned contract terms that required them to be spent in a single transaction.

It also made it clear that if a consumer did not redeem the full amount of the voucher in an initial purchase, businesses were required to reimburse any remaining balance of more than €1 by way of cash, electronic transfer or voucher.

The law also banned contract terms that limit the number of vouchers that could be used in a single transaction.

However, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has said that, using recent data from consumer reports to its helpline, it has “identified a number of traders whose gift vouchers may not comply with legislation introduced in 2019”.

It said it has written to traders around Ireland to remind them of the rules around gift vouchers, highlighting a number of issues and drawing attention to the core provisions of the consumer law around gift vouchers.

It called on traders who have sold vouchers valid for less than five years in the post-2019 period to engage with the CCPC and propose remedies for affected consumers.

The CCPC did not name any retailers who were in breach of the law, and the letter has been sent to a wide range of businesses, including hotels, restaurants, takeaways, dentists, sports retailers, clothes shops, salons and spas.

In July of this year, JD Sports issued refunds of €250,000 to consumers following a CCPC investigation that came in the wake of a report in The Irish Times that it had sold gift vouchers valid for only one year, instead of at least five years.

In recent weeks, The Irish Times also revealed that British-based fashion retailer Flannels, which is owned by Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group, had sold vouchers that came with a two-year expiry in line with its UK policies but contrary to Irish law.

“We are still hearing from consumers who are experiencing issues with gift vouchers,” said the CCPC’s director of communications and consumer information Aoibhín de Búrca.

“As we approach one of the busiest times of year for the purchase and use of gift vouchers, we are reminding traders of their consumer protection obligations.”

She stressed that “Irish gift voucher legislation is clear, and traders selling vouchers must follow the law. The legislation is there for consumers, and we want consumers to know what their rights are, and to get the full protection and value of the legislation.”

]]><![CDATA[No employees and prototypes within days: AI agents supercharge start-ups]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/no-employees-and-prototypes-within-days-ai-agents-supercharge-start-ups/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/no-employees-and-prototypes-within-days-ai-agents-supercharge-start-ups/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 04:54:00 +0000After entrepreneurs Claudio Reiter and Leon Busch built their first two fully automated biotech labs, the Helsinki-based pair decided to go one better: they instructed an AI agent to complete another on its own.

“We thought it was a bit arrogant to assume humans know best how to build the lab that will teach AI wet-lab science [where scientists work with physical chemicals]. Why not let AI build its own? So we captured what we learned and now an agent can manage a lab build itself,” says Reiter.

The agent is co-ordinating a budget of roughly $500,000 (€455,000), handling everything from procuring instruments to instructing contractors. Other agents are running simple undergraduate-level experiments for their human masters, who plan to ultimately base the company between San Francisco and Zurich.

Reiter believes that within months “the complexity of the experiments they can do will rise until they can meaningfully contribute to scientific research and make discoveries that humans never could”.

Such arrangements are becoming more common and offer a glimpse of how AI is upending start-up culture, traditionally characterised by large teams working long hours and financed by venture capital. Today, a company can be started without either capital or employees. The innovation cycle in start-ups, always rapid, now looks faster than ever – especially for companies whose own products are AI-related. Founders can use AI agents to write code and handle almost any role, from registering a company to designing the product and making marketing videos.

“It’s never been easier to start a company,” says Ziv Reichert, a partner at London-based venture capital firm Phoenix Court.

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman remarked in 2024 that in a “group chat with my tech CEO friends there’s this betting pool for the first year that there is a one-person billion-dollar company.”

Founders say the game-changing moment for start-ups happened late last year, when new tools such as Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.5 and its Claude Code made coding cheaper, faster and easier than ever before.

Toby Mather, co-founder of AI start-up Rig, which helps groups integrate company data into reports, apps and AI tasks, wrote in a February newsletter titled “Opus Babies”: “Opus 4.5 appeared on November 24 [2025]. We have since completed 18 months’ of ‘old world’ development in three months.”

The end of maths as we know it? Seismic impact of AI has mathematicians worried

Using the new tools, even people who cannot write code can develop software and build products. More and more, entrepreneurs simply speak aloud to AI agents, telling them what to create.

Helena Gagern, who cofounded a tech hub and runs a VC fund for European start-ups called The Embassy in San Francisco, was stunned when she recently caught up with an entrepreneur whose new start-up already had a drug in animal testing – but not a single employee.

“He left his company with the insight, ‘I think I can rebuild every single thing that humans are doing in my company right now with AI’,” she says. “Everything – in terms of disease to work on, the research, the trial design – was driven by AI agents. That was for me the eye-opening moment in terms of how far you can push building a company with practically zero humans working on it.”

She adds that while many start-ups in San Francisco are still raising large sums from venture capitalists, “we’ve seen companies make tens of millions within the first year of operating without raising VC money”.

Vincent Huguet, who in 2013 cofounded Malt, a European platform on which freelance AI engineers and data scientists advertise for work, says that just as computer hardware stopped being a barrier to entry when the cloud arrived 20 years ago, now software is not a barrier either. “It can be made by anyone who is a bit geeky,” he notes.

Isabel Greenslade, the New York-based co-founder of Structured AI, which uses AI to review architectural and engineering drawings, recalls suggesting a possible product to potential customers.

Artificial intelligence: ‘One screw-up ... and we will destroy any remaining trust the public has in science’

“We recorded the conversation, we put it in Claude Code and just said, ‘Build their idea.’ It can literally mock up a prototype. Two days later you can come back to them with exactly [the product] they discussed.”

Making prototypes or even products almost instantaneously takes some of the risk out of a start-up, says Jimmy Cockerton, founder of Impact Advantage, a platform that measures companies’ social value. “You can use AI to create a good enough version to say, ‘This is what it would look like,’ so people can see and feel and touch it, and it can feel like it’s more advanced and built than it really is, which enables you to test and get feedback.”

There is also early evidence AI is making start-ups more geographically diverse. A recent study by academics at the University of British Columbia and the Stockholm School of Economics, which examined how AI is changing entrepreneurship in the US, found the average “innovative” company was more likely than before to have been created away from tech hubs such as San Francisco or New York.

A Brookings Institution report last year found that while the Bay Area remains dominant for AI, other centres such as Houston and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami and Gainesville in Florida qualify as “star hubs” with high growth in AI jobs. Brookings also singled out Detroit, Nashville, Tampa and Pittsburgh as fast risers.

Use of AI is also fuelling a rise in start-ups. In the 15 years to 2019, the average number of weekly applications to form new businesses in the US never reached 80,000, but since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 it has almost always been above 100,000, according to data analysed by asset manager Apollo.

Innovators to watch: The long road to building an Irish AI start-up

In the UK, the number of new companies incorporated in the application software sector jumped 40 per cent to 28,100 in the first half of the year, making the sector the most popular for start-ups, according to an analysis of Companies House statistics by data group Beauhurst and NatWest.

In London, one repeat founder has launched a start-up staffed only by himself and his partner. Each man has five screens above his desk on which AI agents constantly complete complex tasks.

Saving on wages was only part of the lure, he says. “We asked ourselves, ‘Do we need other humans? Won’t they just slow us down?’” He is also glad not to have to engage in frequent meetings.

However, he warns the pace at which his agents produce, including overnight, can be exhausting for people who have to keep checking the agents’ work and giving them new tasks. Reichert, at Phoenix Court, agrees: “I can synthesise way more information than I could before, so there’s way more decisions that I can be taking. I’ve never been busier.”

Even though the use of agents keeps staffing numbers in check at some start-ups, many will eventually require employees, argues Malt’s Huguet, because products, websites and marketing materials made by AI can be mediocre and samey and can result in so-called “slop companies”.

“The overall level of the playing field has risen, but once you’ve reached the basic level, the difference will be made by the people in your team,” he says. New companies will also need persuasive salespeople to woo clients who are being deluged by spam from AI agents.

AI has added an extra competitive edge to the already cut-throat world of start-ups, given the ease with which rival companies can be created.

Joan Burkovic, chief executive of GetMint, a French company that tracks companies’ visibility on AI platforms, says a business now needs to renew itself constantly: “Our product and technology evolve several times a week,” he says. “A company’s rise can be very fast. But the fall can be all the faster.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448884/">

   <description>Die Verhandlungen bei der 31. UNO-Klimakonferenz (COP31) im türkischen Antalya sind auch am Samstag, einen Tag nach dem geplanten Ende der Konferenz, festgesteckt. Im Mittelpunkt der Auseinandersetzung steht die Frage, ob die weltweite Abkehr von fossilen Energieträgern in der Abschlusserklärung erwähnt wird. A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm.

Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private.

InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w

— IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026

Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service.

The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland.

UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests.

The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted.

In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels.

🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę!

Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono.

❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać

🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI

— UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026

The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers.

According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period.

Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer.

 

UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said.

The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree.

UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision.

“Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny.

“If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”.

When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices.

The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska.

Poland has signed memorandums with four of its neighbouring countries – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania – pledging to strengthen regional cooperation on natural gas supplies and the security of infrastructure.

The initiative comes amid Poland’s efforts to use its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity and transmission links to establish itself as a regional energy hub, helping its neighbours, especially landlocked countries to the south, diversify supplies and reduce their reliance on Russia.

The two memorandums of understanding were signed in Warsaw during a ministerial meeting at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC), co-organised by the US Department of Energy, Poland’s energy ministry and the Global Energy Centre run by the Atlantic Council.

Rozpoczęliśmy 7. edycję Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC) – jednego z kluczowych forów współpracy energetycznej Stanów Zjednoczonych oraz krajów Europy Środkowo-Wschodniej. ⚡️

W Warszawie spotkali się przedstawiciele rządu Stanów Zjednoczonych, państw… pic.twitter.com/7t8kLluubF

— GAZ-SYSTEM (@GAZ_SYSTEM) November 18, 2026

One of them, signed by Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – who collectively form the Visegrad Group – establishes a framework for closer collaboration between their gas transmission system operators and more effective use of existing infrastructure.

In late 2022, for example, a new gas interconnector opened between Poland and Slovakia. However, since then, the pipeline has seen very little use, as Bratislava has continued to rely on Russian gas supplies. Hungary has also remained reliant on Russian gas.

By contrast, Poland quickly phased out its imports of Russian energy after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It now receives most of its gas via a pipeline that runs from Norway through Denmark and through LNG that arrives by sea, sourced mainly from the US and Qatar.

From autumn 2027, the EU will ban its member states from importing Russian gas. In September, Hungary’s energy minister said that his country will be ready to meet that deadline. Slovakia, however, is challenging the import ban at the European Court of Justice.

As part of the new memorandum signed this week, the four Visegrad countries will assess the impact of phasing out Russian supplies on regional energy security.

 

The second memorandum, signed between Poland’s Gaz-System and Lithuania’s Amber Grid and KN Energies – which operate gas and LNG infrastructure in the two countries – focuses on strengthening the resilience and security of energy infrastructure around the Baltic Sea.

It provides for closer coordination between the companies, including information-sharing on threats and incidents, joint risk assessments, exchanges of expertise on infrastructure protection and crisis response, and joint training sessions and exercises.

“The LNG terminals in Poland and Lithuania serve as critical supply hubs for…Central and Eastern Europe, significantly enhancing energy security and bolstering regional resilience,” said Sławomir Hinc, CEO of Gaz-System.

But that “security depends on the resilience of every link in the chain”, added his counterpart at Amber Grid, Nemunas Biknius. “This regional agreement will enable us to strengthen that chain in a structured and coordinated way.”

Poland has declared its ambition to become a hub for supplying gas to the CEE region, including Ukraine, in particular by expanding imports of LNG from the United States.

In addition to its existing LNG terminal in Świnoujście, which opened a decade ago, it is planning to build two further floating storage and regasification units that will be located in the Bay of Gdańsk. The first of those, under construction in South Korea, is due to open in 2028.

Last year, a record amount of natural gas was traded in Poland, surpassing the levels seen before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis that followed.

Poland’s rule-of-law crisis has taken another twist, after the Supreme Court (SN) issued a resolution effectively opposing the government’s position towards another top court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), and endorsing that of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

The SN found that TK rulings are only valid if issued by judges the president has sworn in and that they take effect even if the government refuses to publish them. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five TK judges, while the government has refused to publish 85 previous TK rulings.

However, the government’s justice minister argues that the new SN resolution is itself invalid because it was issued by judges who were appointed unlawfully.

Połączone izby Sądu Najwyższego o wyrokach Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jako podstawie wznowienia postępowaniahttps://t.co/DzgL6aDTGK pic.twitter.com/GpiGbWMvNn

— Sąd Najwyższy (@SN_RP_) November 18, 2026

On Wednesday, the SN issued a resolution in response to questions over the validity of rulings issued by the TK.

It found, among other things, that a valid TK ruling can only be issued by a panel of judges who, after being elected to the tribunal by parliament, have “taken an oath before the president, that is, in his presence”.

Those latter words relate to a key dispute that has arisen around the TK. The government’s majority in parliament has this year chosen eight new TK judges, who would now form the majority on the 15-seat tribunal.

However, Nawrocki has refused to receive the oath of five of those judges, citing concerns over the method of their appointment or their qualifications.

Those five judges have instead arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies before a notary and then forwarded their oaths to the presidential chancellery. They and the government argue that this meets the requirement for them to take up their seats.

However, Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former government, reject that position and say that the judges cannot take up their seats on the court until the president receives their oath in person. The Supreme Court has now effectively endorsed their stance.

 

Meanwhile, the SN also addressed another contentious issue. Since March 2024, the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – has refused to publish any of the 85 TK rulings issued in that time.

That is because, under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, three judges were unlawfully appointed to the TK.

The current government argues that TK rulings only take force when published in the official Journal of Laws. Indeed, so did the former PiS government when, in 2016, it refused to publish TK rulings that contradicted its judicial policies. However, the SN has now deemed that valid TK rulings enter force even if not published.

“In a situation where the body responsible for publishing TK rulings fails to fulfil this obligation…these abuses by the executive power cannot affect the universally binding force of TK rulings,” said SN judge Aleksander Stępkowski, quoted by the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily.

However, the validity of the SN’s resolution is itself contested as it was issued by judges whose own status is questioned.

That is because they were appointed to the court through the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS) after it was overhauled by PiS in a manner that brought it under political control and rendered it invalid, according to Polish and European court rulings.

The current government has generally rejected decisions issued by such “neo-judges”, as it calls them. And that position was reiterated on Thursday by justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who wrote that “the neo-judges in the Supreme Court have adopted a so-called resolution”.

“Any decision issued with the participation of even one person appointed through the politicised National Council of the Judiciary after 2017 is a non-existent judgement,” he added.

Neosędziowie w Sądzie Najwyższym podjęli nibyuchwałę połączonych trzech izb (III CZP 41/26), uznając, że nieopublikowane rozstrzygnięcia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego mają moc powszechnie obowiązującą, a za wyrok TK można uznać tylko taki wydany przez osoby, które złożyły ślubowanie…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026

The SN’s resolution comes as the TK itself is embroiled in a crisis. At the end of October, the eight new TK judges chosen by parliament this year took control of the tribunal and announced that its chief justice, Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties.

Święczkowski, supported by Nawrocki and the SN’s chief justice, Zbigniew Kapiński (also a “neo-judge”), has rejected that move as an illegal “coup d’état” and claims he is still in charge of the tribunal. However, police have prevented him from entering the building.

On Wednesday, just as the SN was issuing its resolution, the eight government-backed TK judges announced that they had lifted Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution at the request of Żurek.

The administration of Kraków’s new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has signalled that the city will withdraw from plans to build a metro system and will seek to shrink the size of the recently introduced Clean Transport Zone, which imposes additional costs on older, more polluting cars.

“We won’t, like the previous administrations, make any promises regarding the metro,” deputy mayor Karol Wałachowski told local news service LoveKrakow. “We’re withdrawing from this project until central [government] or European funding becomes available.”

The draft municipal budget for next year presented by Gibała allocates no funds towards preparation work for the metro, notes LoveKrakow. Instead, the new administration wants to establish seven new tram routes.

For decades, Kraków has discussed the possibility of building a metro system, which would be just the second in Poland after Warsaw’s. In 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the idea.

However, only in 2024 did the then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, who came to office that year, announce plans to build a metro. The city unveiled the planned route in 2025 and then, in July this year, it launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project.

But the idea now looks set to be abandoned after Miszalski was dismissed in a recall referendum earlier this year and Gibała was elected last month to replace him.

While Gibała has often said that he would, in theory, like Kraków to have a metro system akin to Warsaw’s, he has argued that it would be impossible to build without significant funds from the European Union or Polish government.

During this year’s election campaign, Gibała told news service Wirtualna Polska that he wanted to “honestly tell Kraków residents that, regardless of whether [Monika] Piątkowska [his opponent] or I win, there won’t be a metro anytime soon. We won’t build it without government funding”.

The issue has become tied up in national politics. Gibała is an independent while Piątkowska, his defeated rival, was from Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party.

Poland’s government has announced plans to introduce a maximum price for natural gas to protect households from the continued impact of the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran earlier this year. The measure would be funded by a new special levy on certain energy companies.

To enter into force, the bill must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record amount of legislation.

Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk noted that gas prices have been at elevated levels due to the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, which is normally a major conduit for both oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).

Tusk pointed out that the European gas benchmark price recently surpassed €100 per megawatt-hour (MWh), which was its highest level in four years. The figure has since fallen to around €85/MWh, though that is still more than double the level in January and February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Such costs are “unacceptable for any Polish family”, said the prime minister. “We can’t allow people to suffer because of decisions made abroad… about war in the Middle East. We don’t want Polish families to pay for it.”

Mrozimy ceny gazu. pic.twitter.com/lLSQZA3R8h

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 17, 2026

The government therefore wants to introduce a maximum price of 197.29 zloty (€44.15) per MWh (which is the level of the current state-regulated gas tariff) for the whole of 2027. The energy ministry estimates that this will save households that use gas for heating up to 1,863 zloty over the year.

As well as individual households and housing cooperatives, the maximum price will also apply to entities providing important public services, such as schools, nurseries, hospitals and shelters.

Companies selling gas to such consumers will then receive compensation from the state to cover the difference if the maximum price is below what the level of gas tariffs would normally be at that time.

 

The costs of this compensation “will be largely covered by a new monthly gas levy” charged to “energy companies holding licences to trade natural gas with foreign countries and selling high-methane natural gas on the domestic market”, says the government.

The levy would amount to 10% of net revenues from domestic sales of high-methane natural gas in 2027. Companies holding capacity rights amounting to less than 10% of the total capacity at entry points to Poland’s gas-transmission system would be exempt.

While the legislation is unlikely to face obstacles in parliament, it remains unknown what Nawrocki’s position will be. The president has previously pushed for the government to lower energy prices. However, he also blocked a windfall tax on energy companies to subsidise fuel-price cuts, before eventually relenting.

In response, the government has reintroduced measures to lower prices at petrol stations https://t.co/icGEST8NAo

Earlier this year, analysis by Allianz, the world’s largest insurance company, found that Poland was among a group of 11 countries “most at risk” from a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Poland has become a growing consumer of gas in recent years. As the country has moved away from its traditional reliance on coal, gas has increasingly been used for both electricity generation and home heating.

Last year, gas accounted for a record 13.2% of electricity production, up from just 2.7% in 2015. The latest figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that in 2024 almost 21% of households use gas for heating, up from 10% in 2015.

The majority of gas consumed in Poland is imported – around 82% last year, according to the energy ministry. Around 43% of imports arrive in the form of LNG, delivered to a terminal at Świnoujście on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast.

Last year, most of that LNG came from the United States (accounting for 30.7% of Poland’s total gas imports) and Qatar (11.2%). However, LNG exports from Qatar have been severely impacted by the difficulties around the Strait of Hormuz.
