]]> In last month’s UK Budget, the Chancellor halved the lifetime limit on Business Asset Disposal Relief and introduced a new Founders’ Relief. Both take effect on 6 April 2027, and the details of the new relief are out for consultation until 30 November.

If you’re still building, your choices on where to incorporate, how to hold equity and which reliefs investors can use need to hold up as the rules change, and they could change again before April. Use the next five months to check your structure against both reliefs and fix what doesn’t work while it’s still cheap.

What the Budget has changed

The new Founders’ Relief will tax up to €11,948,000 of lifetime gains at 10%, but the proposed rules are strict. You must have held at least 25% of the company’s ordinary share capital, together with corresponding voting and economic rights, when the original trade or preparations for that trade commenced; held your shares for at least five years; and been a UK resident for the five tax years before the sale.

The company must be a trading company with €11,948,000 turnover and 15 full-time staff in the accounting period before the sale, and a substantial UK presence for the previous five. It must also pass two of three tests: 25% annual turnover growth, 25% annual headcount growth, or €1,792,200 of qualifying R&D spend. In practice, the relief won’t apply to one of five equal co-founders or any company with turnover below €11,948,000.

Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR), the long-standing relief that lowers Capital Gains Tax for owners selling their business, is being cut back. The rate has already risen from 10% to 14% in April 2025, then to 18% in April 2026. Now the lifetime limit halves from €1,194,800 to €597,400. For a qualifying individual whose gains would otherwise be taxed at 24%, the maximum BADR tax saving will fall from €71,688 to €35,844, assuming the full lifetime allowance remains available. Any BADR or Investors’ Relief you claim from April 2027 also reduces the Founders’ Relief available to you later.

The good news is that the Budget makes it easier to raise money and reward staff. The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme (SEIS) and the Enterprise Investment Scheme (EIS) keep their 50% and 30% income tax relief for investors. From next April, technical changes will allow SEIS and EIS investments on the same day and treat certain investment-limit and payment breaches more proportionately.

The Company Share Option Plan (CSOP), for companies that have outgrown or don’t qualify for Enterprise Management Incentives (EMI), becomes EMI2. From April 2027, its per-employee limit doubles from €71,688 to €143,376 and no longer counts against the €298,700 EMI limit. Where both schemes apply, a key hire could hold up to €442,076 of tax-advantaged options.

If you’re building in the UK: get the early decisions right

What you keep on exit is mostly determined at incorporation and at your first rounds.

Focus on these three things this quarter:

  • Your share structure. Founder holdings, share classes and option schemes are cheap to set up correctly and expensive to fix later.
  • Your SEIS and EIS eligibility. You can lose it through share rights, the timing of a round, or changes in your business activities.
  • Your option scheme. Check it against the EMI limits, or look at EMI2 if you’ve outgrown EMI or work in a sector it excludes.

Entering the UK from the EU: what changes, and what doesn’t

If you’re not a UK tax resident, gains on your shares are generally taxed where you live rather than in the UK, with limited exceptions, so no UK relief applies to you today. That changes if you move, and Founders’ Relief has two five-year clocks to understand before you do.

The first is personal: you must have been a UK resident for five continuous tax years before the sale. If you relocate to London planning to exit in three years, you won’t qualify, however well your company meets the other tests.

The second belongs to the company, which needs a substantial UK presence for the five accounting periods before the sale. It doesn’t have to be UK-incorporated, as a business trading here through a permanent establishment can be in scope. But the UK presence must be real and sustained, so when you enter the market matters.

Be careful about putting your EU company under a new UK holding company. You can meet the 25% test through a holding company, but the consultation doesn’t yet say how the other conditions apply to a newly created one. Take advice before restructuring. 

More broadly, a UK subsidiary, branch or holding company each has different tax and investor consequences, and changing your mind later is costly. If you want UK investors to claim SEIS or EIS, the company needs a UK permanent establishment, so build that in from the start.

It’s best to structure first, and then raise.

On exits and timing

Our clients are already asking if they should sell sooner, but for most, it’s better to stay patient. Rushing a sale at the wrong price can cost far more than any tax relief. If you’re mid-deal, check the CGT disposal date and the proposed BADR anti-forestalling provisions. Certain unconditional contracts signed before 6 April 2027 but completed afterwards may fall within the reduced €597,400 lifetime limit unless the relevant statutory exceptions are satisfied.

Build for change

The UK remains one of the best places in Europe to build and grow a business, but the rules on what founders keep have changed significantly in recent years. You can’t plan for a Budget that hasn’t happened, but you can build a business that reacts quickly when one lands.

That means a simple structure, a clean cap table and regularly reviewed option schemes. It means a small team with clear ownership, so rule changes become quick decisions rather than delayed tasks. And it means you need a tax team that knows your business well enough to advise you within days of a Budget.

Start now by checking which reliefs you qualify for today and which you could qualify for by April. That will show you where your structure needs work. If the proposed Founders’ Relief rules would unfairly exclude your business, you have until 30 November to respond to the government’s consultation and help shape the final rules.

]]> Wilco, a Madrid-based startup building AI voice and messaging agents for healthcare clinic groups, has announced its launch and a new €2.5 million funding round.

The round was led by Samaipata, the European venture capital fund known for backing marketplace and software businesses across the continent. ABAC Nest Ventures, the venture arm of Abac Capital, joined the round, alongside a cohort of executives from the technology and healthcare sectors.

“Today we are launching Wilco to help healthcare groups treat more patients,” the company said in a post on LinkedIn.

Wilco was founded on the premise that clinics routinely lose patients between the first enquiry and the actual appointment. To convert enquiries into actual appointments, Wilco deploys AI agents that call, message and follow up with patients via phone and WhatsApp, from the moment an initial enquiry comes in through to a signed treatment plan and return visit.

The company says 60 to 80% of the people who contact a clinic never make it to a consultation, which is the result of unreturned calls, unconfirmed appointments, and unanswered quotes. “Our AI Agents & Humans-in-the-loop stay with every patient from the first call to the signed treatment plan,” the company added.

The platform is designed to cover the full patient journey across four stages: reaching every new lead, ensuring they attend their appointment, helping them accept a treatment plan, and bringing them back for follow-up care. It serves clinics across six specialities, including dental, medical aesthetics, veterinary, physiotherapy, ophthalmology and dermatology and its clients include some of the largest clinic groups in Spain, among them Vitaldent, Clínica Baviera, and WM Clinics.

While AI agents designed to help healthcare clinics is not new, Wilco says it distinguishes itself via its forward-deployed engineers, who work directly with each clinic’s operations and IT leads to build, test, and launch workflows before a single real patient interaction takes place. The company says they typically go live within three to eight weeks, depending on the integration required for the clinic’s management software.

These engineers remain embedded with the client after launch, refining the system based on outcomes reconciled with the clinic’s own records.

“Around artificial intelligence there is a lot of noise, but the problem for clinics is that they invest in attracting the patient and, too often, they lose them before they reach the consultation. Our job is to make sure that patient opens the door and accepts their treatment plan,” Francisco Hernández Parga, founder and CEO of Wilco, told Forbes España.

Wilco plans to use the proceeds to reinforce its engineering, deployment and sales teams and is actively hiring across these verticals. The funding will also be used to expand its geographic reach beyond Spain into the broader European market, as well as into the United States and Latin America.

Wilco sees AI agents helping healthcare clinics as a starting point and is preparing for a fundamental shift in how patients and clinics will interact in the future. “Today the patient calls the clinic. Soon their AI agent will. We are building for that,” the company said.

]]> Bending Spoons, a Milan-based technology company that acquires and transforms digital businesses, has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Mailchimp, the email marketing automation platform, from Intuit, in a deal valued at €3.35 billion ($3.68 billion)

The all-cash transaction also comes with a reinvestment clause, where Intuit will invest €335 million ($368 million) of its proceeds back into newly issued Bending Spoons equity. Alongside the Mailchimp acquisition, the Italian company has announced a further €1.18 billion ($1.3 billion) private placement of ordinary shares, selling 32.5 million shares to institutional investors in an oversubscribed round that drew participation from both new and existing investors.

“Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences. We’re honoured to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together. After closing, we’ll invest substantially in the business, building on the powerful, easy-to-use tools customers already value and rely on,” said Luca Ferrari, CEO and co-founder, Bending Spoons.

Founded in Milan over a decade ago, Bending Spoons has built a reputation for being one of Europe’s prominent acquirers of digital technology businesses, often snapping up established brands at a fraction of their previous valuations. In this case, Intuit paid €10.92 billion ($12 billion) for Mailchimp in 2021, and this deal represents a 70% drop in valuation in just five years, despite revenue growth.

This shouldn’t come as a surprise. Bending Spoons acquired Brightcove for €212 million ($233 million), which once commanded a valuation of $933 million at its peak. It acquired Evernote for only $200 million ($1 billion valuation at its peak) and Eventbrite, which was valued at $1.76 billion at IPO, for just €430 million ($505 million). It bought Airtable for €1.17 billion ($1.285 billion), Vimeo for €1.1 billion ($1.38 billion), Miro for €1.17 billion ($1.36 billion), and AOL for €1.37 billion ($1.45 billion). These businesses once commanded $200 billion in valuation at their peak, and Bending Spoons acquired them for $6.4 billion.

With every acquisition, Bending Spoons has argued that it can sustainably build these businesses by implementing deep transformations and ongoing optimisations, and reinvesting in additional acquisitions, thereby continuing the compounding cycle. The transformation has often meant deep reorganisation of teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetisation. However, users of these services have often found themselves left with enormous subscription fees and limited freemium features.

AI has also been a central feature of Bending Spoons’ transformation of businesses it acquires. Mailchimp will now join a breadth of businesses that span productivity, media, and marketing technology. It also represents one of its largest and most high-profile acquisitions to date.

Mailchimp was founded in Atlanta in 2001 by Ben Chestnut and Dan Kurzius, and it was originally built as a side project within their web design agency, The Rocket Science Group. Designed as an affordable alternative to the expensive email software, it gave small businesses access to the same digital marketing tools previously enjoyed only by larger corporations.

After its acquisition by Intuit in 2021, the platform turned into an always-on marketing platform serving millions of customers around the world, spanning email, social media, landing pages, and advertising, with AI as a copilot.

“Mailchimp has helped millions of businesses grow and acquire customers through email marketing automation, and we are grateful to the Mailchimp team for what they have built and the impact they have had on customers and Intuit,” said Jack Tam, Senior Vice President, Intuit.

Under the terms of the agreement, Bending Spoons will acquire the Mailchimp business by purchasing 100% of The Rocket Science Group, LLC and other assets and liabilities associated with the email marketing business. The deal is subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close in early 2027.

Citi and J.P. Morgan acted as co-lead financial advisors to Bending Spoons, while Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE, Succursale Italia and Unicredit are serving as additional financial advisors on the transaction. Freshfields US LLP is acting as legal counsel to Bending Spoons, with EY-Parthenon providing financial due diligence and EY STP handling tax due diligence services, the company said in a statement.

The Mailchimp deal follows multiple capital activities for Bending Spoons. In October 2026, Berkshire Hathaway completed a fresh €300.92 million ($330 million) investment in the company, taking its total stake to 4%, following its €547.14 million ($600 million) investment during Bending Spoons’ July 2026 IPO.

Bending Spoons’ acquisition of Mailchimp underscores the Italian company’s growing clout in the digital tech landscape and its ability to compete for marquee American digital businesses.

The company says its software provides a digital twin for heating networks, giving clients insights and support to manage increasingly complex networks. It also lets clients simulate different settings before applying them to the physical network, including hydraulic and physics modelling.

It helps DHC and industrial companies cut heat losses and fuel use, unlock full-system flexibility on electricity markets and integrate renewable heat, all while safeguarding security of supply.

“The EIB’s backing is a strong endorsement of what our team and our customers have built together, and it gives us the foundation to keep investing in the platform for the long term. It means we can bring our Digital Twin to more district heating and cooling and industrial companies across Europe, helping them run their networks more efficiently and integrate more renewable heat,” said Hervé Huisman, CEO of Gradyent. 

The EIB financing is supported under the European Commission’s InvestEU programme. The company plans to use this financing to support the continued evolution of Gradyent’s software suite, aiming to provide clients with the tools to optimise the operational performance of their district heating and industrial heating networks.

Cecilia Thorfinn, head of the representation of the European Commission in the Netherlands, said, “This financing is an example of how Europe is turning its climate ambitions into concrete investments that modernise district heating and cooling and decarbonise industrial heat networks. Earlier this month, Eneco, one of the Netherlands’ largest energy companies and a pioneer in virtual power plant technology, deepened its partnership with Gradyent to unlock the full flexibility potential of its heat and energy production and distribution assets in Utrecht.

Building on an existing collaboration, Eneco now uses Gradyent’s real-time Digital Twin to optimise energy trading and heat and energy production, alongside Eneco’s Myriad Virtual Power Plant (VPP).

Gradyent’s team consists of 150+ energy specialists, engineers, data scientists, and consulting alumni. Investors include Capricorn Partners, Eneco, ENERGIIQ, and Helen Ventures. It works with heating companies in Europe, including E.ON, Eneco, Ennatuurlijk, Helen, Uniper, and Wien Energie.

]]> Vetaion, a Munich-based company that automates the manufacturing of custom electrical control cabinets, has closed a €5.7 million pre-Seed financing round to scale its production in Munich and grow its team.

The round was co-led by Visionaries Tomorrow and UVC Partners, with participation from 2100 Ventures and leading industrial companies such as Viessmann Generations Group. Numerous angel investors also participated, including founders and executives of well-known companies such as Heraeus, Isar Aerospace, Flix, and RobCo.

“Many people see control cabinets as a craft, not a case for venture capital. We see a problem that AI and automation can solve. What convinced us above all was the team and its pace: I visited Vetaion on site twice within just a few weeks. The progress between my visits was astonishing – one of the highest execution speeds I have seen,” said Johannes von Borries, Managing Partner at UVC Partners.

Founded in 2025, Vetaion is automating the manufacturing of custom-built control cabinets. It turns 2D schematics into 3D models to automate the production of electrical control cabinets.

The company calls control cabinets the nervous system of every electrical installation, stating that every automated or electrical installation needs a control cabinet, whether it’s a factory, a wind farm, or a data centre. 

The company estimates that Europe needs more than five million control cabinets every year. Inside the cabinet, power is distributed and protected; the control system sits there, and hundreds of wires lead to motors, sensors, and drives.

It notes that control cabinets are almost always custom, designed for their specific purpose, and built by hand. Vetaion says demand for these electrical control systems in Germany and Europe keeps growing. 

Explaining why control cabinets are becoming a bottleneck, it says the industry has long assumed control cabinet manufacturing couldn’t be automated. The main reason is that every cabinet is unique: no two are built alike, so no fixed production sequence can be programmed.

“Then there are the many wires inside: they are flexible, and a production robot has to treat them differently from rigid components. As a result, every single step of the process is still designed around manual labour,” the company mentioned in the press release. 

It also highlighted that manual labour rests on electricians, and the skills shortage makes them scarcer year after year. Also, since control cabinets are too large and too heavy to ship, they have to be built where they are needed. The supply chain for the entire electrical infrastructure stalls when skilled workers are missing on the ground.

“Europe’s share of global manufacturing has fallen from 25 to 16% in recent years. We have forgotten how to make things and have preferred to rely on suppliers abroad. If we do not bring that capability back, it will be lost for good, and we will not be able to deliver the infrastructure build-out that the megatrends of AI, robotics, and the energy transition require,” said founder Nikolaus von Bary. 

Vetaion claims to transform control cabinet manufacturing. Instead of printed schematics, tape measures, and hand drills, its cabinets are guided by software and built by robots, saving time and reducing costs.

The company converts 2D circuit diagrams into 3D models. Once a cabinet exists as a three-dimensional model, robots can take over component placement and wiring, and the company is developing those solutions in-house. With VetaionOS, the German startup is building its own operating system to automate one-off product manufacturing.

It highlights that the entire team sits in Garching directly above the production floor and can trace every step of the build. It reports that the lead times for a control cabinet fall from several months to under four weeks, and the manual work involved drops to a tenth.

Vetaion responds to project inquiries with a firm quote within 24 hours, provided a PDF circuit diagram and an Excel bill of materials are available.

With this capital, it plans to scale operations and increase automation to meet growing customer demand.

“We are currently hiring Europe’s most ambitious experts to bring AI and robotics into batch size 1 manufacturing. Anyone who wants to shape the future of automated production in our own factory, with direct feedback cycles, will feel right at home at Vetaion,” added von Bary.

Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas.

The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:28:26 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 From ‘bonkers’ flying scooter concept to crewed flight tests: CoolFly’s next steps https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/coolfly-personal-evtol-urban-dream-st-flight-tests/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57481 CoolFly’s unusual stand-up flying scooter drew attention at CES 2026. Now the Chinese company said its seated Dream ST is ready for delivery.

The post From ‘bonkers’ flying scooter concept to crewed flight tests: CoolFly’s next steps appeared first on AGN.

]]> CoolFly Aircraft tells Aerospace Global News its seated Dream ST personal electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft is ready for delivery, following a series of crewed demonstrations in China and overseas. 

The Hangzhou-based company attracted attention at CES 2026 with its Urban solo stand-up flying scooter. At the time, Aerospace Global News described the stand-up flying machine as a bit “bonkers”, with some possibly useful applications in emergency response and an appeal to daredevil racing.

The company took the critique well, calling it “fair.” They also reached out with a ten-month update that caught our attention. CoolFly supplied new performance figures, details of its safety testing, and a clearer picture of who it expects to buy its aircraft.

Seated Dream ST advances

CoolFly has returned with updates on its somewhat less harrowing Dream ST seated personal eVTOL. Dream ST is a single-seater open cockpit aimed at the ultralight market.

“Today, Dream ST is ready for delivery,” Alex Chen, CoolFly’s brand marketing lead, told AGN.

The company’s more intrepid stand-up Urban aircraft, meanwhile, is undergoing further development. “Urban is moving to its next version: we’re still optimising some parameters and expect to roll it out to all markets after that update,” Chen said.

From CES display to crewed demonstrations

CoolFly launched Urban, the seated Dream ST and Dream Pro, and its NA80 flight-control system at an event in Hangzhou on 13 August. Chen said the launch included crewed flights. 

The company performed crewed Dream ST flights in France, as well as Dream ST and Dream Pro test flights in Canada.

In October, the company said Dream ST completed a crewed island-to-island flight in the Maldives.

Urban also performed demonstrations carrying humanoid robots in Zhuhai and Dongguan. 

The company had additional static display appearances at EAA AirVenture Oshkosh and IFA Berlin.

Chen said CoolFly has flown all its models with pilots in China.

An earlier version of Urban also flew with a pilot in Harbin in February, in temperatures of –30°C. According to Chen, the chilly demonstration led CoolFly to rethink its batteries.

“Harbin pushed us hard on batteries. At –30 °C, battery output drops sharply,” Chen said. “We developed a new ultra-low-temperature battery thermal management system for that flight, and it’s now used across all of our models.” 

What the aircraft can do

CoolFly puts Dream ST’s empty weight below 115kg (approximately 253lb), with a maximum payload of 95kg, a top speed of 100km/h and 16 minutes of flight with a 70kg pilot. 

Dream Pro has a claimed 120kg payload, the same top speed and 40 minutes of flight with a 70kg pilot.

CoolFly has not released updated Urban specifications, as some parameters are under development. 

Chen said all three eight-motor aircraft use independent propulsion units, main and backup batteries and dual flight controllers, each with three inertial measurement units. CoolFly says it has tested controller switchover and single-motor and propeller failures, with the aircraft remaining controllable. 

“Safety is built in three layers,” Chen said, specifying redundancy, active assistance and passive protection. On the dual control system, he said: “If one detects a fault, the system can switch within milliseconds.” CoolFly said it has verified that switchover in testing, alongside simulated or actual single-propeller and motor failures. 

Active safety includes “an extensive sensor suite for perception and obstacle avoidance, plus intelligent features that lower pilot workload, such as one-key takeoff and landing and intelligent hover.”

Urban also features enclosed propellers, a protective structure, and foot grips to keep the standing pilot somewhat more stable. Dream Pro incorporates airbags. Chen said pilots are supplied with a helmet and airbag suit. Those measures may address the differences between an open personal eVTOL and a conventional enclosed light aircraft, but their effectiveness would depend on the circumstances of an incident.

Can it fly in the US without a pilot’s licence?

Technically, yes. CoolFly is designing Dream ST for US ultralight rules under FAA Part 103. Those rules permit qualifying single-occupant recreational aircraft to operate without aircraft registration, an airworthiness certificate or a pilot certificate. In effect, the FAA is saying, if you are willing to try it, go for it, but the agency makes no guarantees of airworthiness or your ability to control the craft. Powered ultralights must weigh less than 254lb empty and meet other operating and performance limits. 

Dream ST’s listed empty weight (253 lb) is close to that threshold. Its stated top speed of 100km/h is also close to the Part 103 limit of 55 knots (approximately 102km/h). 

However, Part 103 is not an FAA type approval, and the recreational-use restriction limits potential commercial applications.

“Outside the US, ultralight rules are set country by country,” Chen said. CoolFly works with dealers on national requirements in Europe and said its aircraft have CE and FCC certifications. Neither designation, by itself, establishes compliance with aviation operating rules or substitutes for any approval that a particular country may require.

Chen said that Dream Pro is not being positioned as a Part 103 ultralight, and added: “We’ll share Urban’s regulatory approach closer to its wider rollout.” 

Dealers, deliveries and CES 2027

CoolFly expects recreational flyers to be its first customers, followed by tourism and event operators. Chen said discussions about emergency-response applications have taken place, but no agreements have been finalised.

“Our first and largest group of users is people who are passionate about flying sports and outdoor recreation,” Chen said. Tourism sites and event organisers are the next market CoolFly wants to reach, with trained staff on hand.

CoolFly described Dream ST as ready for delivery, but did not disclose order numbers or confirm delivery dates.

“We sell through local dealers, who handle sales, delivery, training and support,” Chen said. “In the US, we’re currently selecting dealer partners, and pricing will follow once they’re in place.” The company is also recruiting dealers in Europe, Australia and the Middle East. 

Chen identified three hurdles that CoolFly must clear to take off: navigating differing national rules, obtaining local support and “earning public trust in personal flight, which is why we fly in public.”

CoolFly will exhibit Dream ST and Dream Pro at CES 2027 (LVCC North Hall, Booth #15927). 

“We’ll have Dream ST and Dream Pro on the stand, and visitors can sit in Dream,” Chen said. 

For the flying scooter that first caught attention at CES 2026, the next test will be whether revised Urban specifications, regulatory requirements and customer deliveries can meet the promise of the public demonstrations. If nothing else, CoolFly will likely draw crowds again in Vegas.

]]> 5 things pilots do before take-off that passengers never see https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/5-things-pilots-do-before-take-off-passengers-never-see Sat, 21 Nov 2026 13:45:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56893 Plenty happens behind the cockpit door before an aircraft leaves the stand. Pilots have a long list of checks, calculations and preparations to complete, often while keeping a close eye on the clock.

The post 5 things pilots do before take-off that passengers never see appeared first on AGN.

]]> There’s much more to getting an aircraft ready for departure than starting the engines and taxiing to the runway. Before every flight, pilots have several important tasks to complete, many of which passengers never see.

We chatted exclusively to serving airline captain Pete Wilson, who told us all about five of them.

1. Take-off and emergencies briefing

Once the flight management computer (the onboard computer used to programme and manage the flight) has been loaded with the flight plan and take-off performance data, the pilot flying briefs the pilot monitoring on the take-off and possible emergencies.

This covers the taxi route, take-off configuration and V-speeds. These determine whether a take-off can be rejected with enough runway remaining to stop (V1), or must continue even if an engine fails.

The crew also discuss the Standard Instrument Departure route, cleared altitude and how they would handle emergencies, such as an engine fire before V1 or engine failure after V1, including possible diversion airports.

Any special procedures, such as de-icing or using an external air supply to start an engine if the APU isn’t working, are also covered, along with potential threats like bird strikes and bad weather.

Finally, as they line up on the runway, many pilots mentally rehearse what they would do if something went wrong during take-off.

Read: Why Airbus is testing extra-long wings on an A321neo Read: Why Airbus is testing extra-long wings on an A321neo

2. Paperwork

How many times have you heard the flight deck say, “We’re almost ready to go, just waiting on the last few bits of paperwork…” ?

Much of it is now done digitally on the crew’s iPads, but one of the last physical documents needed is the fuel receipt.

After refuelling, the refueller either passes it to the dispatcher (turnaround coordinator) or rolls it up and holds it up to the cockpit window on the end of a long pole for the crew to take.

The receipt shows how many thousands of litres of fuel have been added, so the crew can calculate its weight.

The aircraft’s technical logbook must also be completed and signed by the captain, either on paper or digitally.

All this feeds into the final load sheet, which includes the aircraft’s take-off weight, fuel load, centre of gravity position and passenger numbers. It also lists any animals or dangerous goods in the cargo hold, such as electric wheelchairs containing lithium batteries, which must be correctly secured.

3. Checking the weather and FlightRadar24

While on the ground, the crew use their iPads to carry out last-minute checks.

FlightRadar24 shows how busy the airport is and whether there’s a queue for take-off. Apps such as Windy provide the latest weather along their route, helping identify storm clouds they may need to avoid.

The aircraft’s weather radar won’t be switched on yet and, even when it is, only looks in the direction the aircraft is pointing. With many aircraft now equipped with inflight Wi-Fi, these checks can continue once airborne.

Read next: What is clear-air turbulence and why is it so dangerous for pilots? Read next: What is clear-air turbulence and why is it so dangerous for pilots?

4. Keeping an eye on the time and what’s going on around them

Getting an aircraft away on time involves a lot of coordination, often under time pressure. The flight may have an air traffic control take-off slot to meet, and missing it could mean waiting hours for another one.

The crew must keep track of the turnaround: has the pushback tug arrived, is loading finished, has the refueller turned up, where are the toilet service truck and cleaners, and how long will boarding take? They may also be waiting for delayed connecting passengers or need an engineer.

Things need to be chased up, with close coordination between the crew, ground handling company and airline’s operations department. If a delay is unavoidable, arranging it early makes it more likely that any ATC slots can be updated.

5. Fixing problems and aircraft resets

It’s not unusual for aircraft to develop minor technical faults when first switched on. With so many onboard computers and sensors in a modern airliner, the occasional problem is inevitable.

Many faults can be resolved by resetting circuit breakers. There’s a list of systems that can be reset, specifying whether this is permitted only on the ground or also in flight.

The crew must inform the maintenance control team of any resets. If one doesn’t work, engineers may be sent to investigate, or maintenance control may guide the crew through another procedure over the phone.

Believe it or not, sometimes the best solution is simply to de-power the aircraft, wait a few minutes and then turn it back on again!

]]> Flight review: How good is Cathay Pacific’s new Aria Business Suite really? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/flight-review-how-good-cathay-pacific-aria-business-suite Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:18:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57188 I tried out Cathay Pacific's newly revamped Aria Business Suite on a flight from London Heathrow to Hong Kong, putting its latest Boeing 777-300ER business class to the test. How does it compare with the competition?

The post Flight review: How good is Cathay Pacific’s new Aria Business Suite really? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The gradual rollout of the new Aria Business Suite represents a significant investment in the long-haul business class offering of Cathay Pacific. So can its latest cabin compete with established products from British Airways, Qatar Airways and Emirates?

In early November 2026, I travelled on a late-evening flight (CX254) from London Heathrow to Hong Kong aboard a Boeing 777-300ER to experience the new suite first-hand. It was a brilliant chance to assess its design, technology, dining and sleep quality on a long overnight sector.

Overall, it proved an impressive experience, with just a couple of areas deserving attention.

Inside the new Cathay Pacific Aria Business Suite on the Boeing 777-300ER

On boarding, I was shown to seat 19K (immediately behind a bulkhead – ideal for extra privacy).

The cabin has a contemporary feel, with darker finishes and carefully thought-out lighting. The seats themselves follow a reverse herringbone layout, with added privacy doors, and are based on a heavily modified version of the Super Diamond design from Collins Aerospace.

The enclosed design is a key part of the Aria Business Suite. Rather than just offering a larger seat, Cathay has created a more private space where passengers can work, dine or relax.

The seat converts into a fully flat bed, with practical storage for headphones, bottled water and personal belongings, plus universal AC, USB-A, and fast-charging USB-C.

Inflight entertainment comes through a huge 24-inch 4K touchscreen (the largest in business class as of 2026), alongside a separate control panel for the seat and lighting. A vast array of blockbuster movies, current TV shows, kids entertainment and games are all at your fingertips. Individual spotlights and a generous pull-out tray table finish off the setup.

The amenity kit provided was exceptional too, packed with luxury Bamford goodies including toothpaste, toothbrush, mouthwash, body gel and balm, earplugs, pillow mist and an eye mask.

One disappointment was the clarity of the flight deck announcements, which were particularly quiet and muffled. Unfortunately Cathay isn’t alone in that though.

Another niggle is around connectivity. The complimentary Intelsat 2Ku-powered Wi-Fi was adequate for browsing and streaming, but noticeably slower than the Starlink connections I have experienced on the likes of BA. WhatsApp messages tended to buffer for quite a while before eventually sending, and I noticed my phone would randomly stop charging at times too. Maybe it was just a quirk with my seat.

Also read: Cathay orders 14 more Airbus jets as fleet investment tops $19 billion Also read: Cathay orders 14 more Airbus jets as fleet investment tops $19 billion

How Cathay Pacific Aria Business Suite compares with British Airways Club Suite and Qatar Qsuite

The Aria Business Suite enters an increasingly sophisticated and competitive market. British Airways’ Club Suite introduced enclosed seating with sliding doors to its Boeing 777 fleet back in 2019 – a considerable improvement over the previous Club World.

Cathay follows a similar philosophy, prioritising individual passenger space and privacy. Both products reflect the industry’s move away from traditional open-plan business class cabins.

Qatar Airways’ Qsuite is another important benchmark, with its distinctive enclosed design and flexible seating arrangements. Emirates offers a different interpretation of premium travel aboard the Boeing 777, with its own emphasis on privacy, materials and service.

Against these competitors, Cathay’s Aria suite is a credible contender. Its combination of enclosure, storage, entertainment and sleeping comfort makes it an interesting addition to the international business class market.

Business class dining and inflight service

Dinner was a real treat. Rather than serving everything together on a single tray, the cabin crew delivered individual courses, creating a more relaxed, restaurant-style experience.

I started with celeriac soup, followed by chicken wellington with broccoli and carrots. The chicken was tender, the pastry well prepared and the portion very generous.

A cheese selection of stilton and cheddar followed, accompanied by crackers and grapes. I finished with a praline chocolate and English tea. I was absolutely stuffed!

The leisurely pace made a difference, giving me time to enjoy each course without feeling rushed.

So did I sleep well in the Aria Business Suite?

The real test of any business class seat comes when it’s time to sleep. After dinner, the cabin lighting was dimmed and the seat converted into a fully flat bed.

I’m not exactly short at 5ft 8”, but had loads of room to spread out. I soon got comfortable under the super soft Bamford duvet and managed an impressive eight hours of snoozing. To be honest, it was the best sleep I’ve ever had on an aircraft in all the years I’ve been flying – my bed at home isn’t as cosy as that!

Cathay Pacific business class breakfast and Hong Kong milk tea

Breakfast was another part of the journey that didn’t disappoint. On boarding, I pre-ordered the lighter option, comprising two poached eggs, smoked salmon, sourdough toast, asparagus and hollandaise sauce.

Pastries, tea and fresh pineapple with lime completed the meal. Everything was tasty, nicely presented and served at the right temperature.

A particularly enjoyable discovery was Hong Kong milk tea, recommended to me by a member of the cabin crew. Creamy, very sweet and richer than expected, it was a great introduction to a local favourite.

Read: Qantas unveils new lie-flat business class suites for A321XLR and 787 Read: Qantas unveils new lie-flat business class suites for A321XLR and 787

Cabin crew service and passenger experience

The crew were extremely friendly and attentive throughout without being intrusive. They literally couldn’t do enough for you and everything was done with a genuine smile. The in-flight manager also came over to chat to me, recommending various attractions in Hong Kong, including the Symphony of Lights, the Star Ferry and the city’s historic trams. It was a welcome personal touch.

I was also impressed by the lavatories, which remained exceptionally clean and well-stocked, even towards the end of the flight. It’s definitely the little things that count on a flight of 12 hours plus.

Is Cathay Pacific Aria Business Suite one of the best Boeing 777 business class products?

Cathay Pacific’s Aria Business Suite is a strong addition to its long-haul offering and gives it a serious contender in the Boeing 777-300ER business class market.

The private suite design, large entertainment screen, useful storage and comfortable bed all make for a well-thought-out experience. The food and drink offering is another highlight, with plenty of choice throughout the flight (I highly recommend the Australian red wine).

There are a few things that could be better, particularly the Wi-Fi speed and the clarity of cabin announcements, but neither had a major impact on the overall experience.

Ultimately, a business class cabin needs to deliver over the course of a long flight, not just look good when you first step on board. After arriving in Hong Kong, I felt well rested and ready to get on with the day.

Would I fly Cathay Pacific’s Aria Business Suite again?

Absolutely. It’s undoubtedly a thoughtfully designed premium cabin that puts Cathay Pacific firmly in the conversation alongside the leading international airlines. With a few tweaks it would be perfect.

]]> Exclusive: Virgin Atlantic CEO talks Manchester expansion and Airbus A330neo introduction https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/exclusive-virgin-atlantic-manchester-expansion/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57119 Virgin Atlantic, faced with constraints in Heathrow, has set its sights on Manchester. Its Airbus A330neos will debut next summer.

The post Exclusive: Virgin Atlantic CEO talks Manchester expansion and Airbus A330neo introduction appeared first on AGN.

]]> London Heathrow Airport (LHR) is notoriously slot-constrained. Virgin Atlantic, the airport’s second-largest operator after British Airways, has grown considerably in recent years. However, the operator now says it is unable to expand further as it is limited by LHR’s capacity, CEO Corneel Koster told Aerospace Global News in an interview.

Virgin Atlantic plans to introduce the Airbus A330neo to its Manchester operation as of next year and will bolster frequencies on some of its core long-haul connections to the United States. Koster says the Manchester operation will continue to expand “step by step” over the coming years.

Heathrow capacity constraints

Virgin Atlantic has expanded its Heathrow hub rapidly in recent years. This year, it launched new routes to Phuket and Seoul Incheon, and bolstered its Cancun, Bangalore, Montego Bay, Cape Town and Toronto flights according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Further growth from Heathrow may be a challenge, though. Koster said: “I currently don’t have Heathrow slots to expand. We have grown a lot in the last couple of years though.

“Virgin Atlantic is the fastest-growing airline in the last couple of years at Heathrow. SkyTeam is the fastest growing alliance. But eventually it’s going to top off when slots are no longer available. We’ll still look for opportunities here and there, but I see no immediate growth for a little bit.”

Its joint-venture with Delta Air Lines provides additional feeder connectivity to and from the United States in particular for the rest of Virgin’s network. Crucial as it is for the carrier, it criticised Heathrow’s recent terminal occupancy changes that plan to put the two in different terminals.

Separately, Virgin Atlantic is in favour of expansion at London Heathrow Airport, including the construction of a third runway, but only at the right price.

Koster told the conference: “If you then look at expansion, they want to spend eye-watering amounts with guaranteed returns on expansion. We’re all for expansion. We absolutely need expansion with Heathrow, but we need it to be done in an affordable way.”

British Airways’ CEO Sean Doyle echoed Koster’s sentiments about affordable expansion. Later in the day, easyJet CEO Kenton Jarvis confirmed the airline would consider operating out of Heathrow if the conditions were right.

Manchester growth and Aer Lingus’ base closure

Aer Lingus closed its operational base in Manchester in April 2026. Virgin Atlantic was quick to respond, increasing its overall capacity to fill some of the void.

“There’s no airline who serves Manchester as consistently in long haul as we do,” Koster proudly told Aerospace Global News on the sidelines of the Airlines 2026 conference in London.

“We’ve been there over 30 years. You will see us expanding our Manchester base step by step as well.”

Last week, Virgin Atlantic made adjustments to its Manchester network. It decided to suspend its Las Vegas route as of next summer, instead concentrating on New York-JFK, Orlando and Atlanta flights which will all see an increase.

Its Las Vegas route lagged its other American destinations in 2025 by seat load factors, according to information from the US Department of Transportation. It achieved 77% loads, compared to an overall average for 80% for its American destinations.

Next year, flights to New York-JFK will rise from daily to 10x weekly between April and June, according to schedules filed with aviation analytics firm Cirium. Orlando flights will reach up to 17x weekly catering to high leisure demand during the holiday peak.

Manchester-Atlanta flights will also see additional capacity investments, moving from daily to 11x weekly in June and July.

Manchester will get A330neos from March 2027

Virgin Atlantic will be introducing the Airbus A330neo at its Manchester hub from March 2027, debuting on its New York-JFK flights. From June, the aircraft will also be deployed on flights to Orlando and Atlanta.

Koster described the A330neo as a “fantastic aircraft.”

“Our new A330neos have been already operating out of Heathrow. They’re going to make a debut in Manchester next year,” he confirmed. “And our crews and our customers in Manchester can’t wait because those aircraft are scoring very well in customer experience.”

Aer Lingus’ Manchester closure signalled challenges in its commercial performance. The airline admitted that despite its best efforts, “operating margin performance continues to significantly lag” its Dublin-based operation. When asked, Koster said Virgin Atlantic’s Manchester flights are generally performing well.

“There’s a lot of demand from the Greater Manchester area. There’s business, there’s visiting friends and relatives, there’s a lot of holiday demand to places where we’re strong like Orlando. We’ve always made it work and I’m sure we will make it work for many, many years to come and grow at a steady pace. If we now look at our route results out of Manchester, they do well.”

Its LHR base enjoys higher premium demand compared to Manchester, Koster admits. He adds, though, that “premium demand is certainly growing out of Manchester too.”

Long-term plans: While Asia flights are not ruled out, near-term growth will be transatlantic

When asked, Koster shared his thoughts on the Manchester hub. He pointed to the lack of connecting traffic at Manchester as something that would otherwise have helped “maintain a stronger and a wider network.”

“If we could connect more out of Manchester, we would,” he admits. “The Manchester Airport is not necessarily fully laid out and processes don’t fully work for very short connections yet. We’re regularly talking to the Manchester Airport authorities who are very receptive to our needs to try to optimise processes to deliver better connectivity. They’re receptive to those needs and they’re working on it, but they still have a way to go.”

When asked whether the carrier would expand into other areas such as Asia to facilitate long-haul connecting traffic, he said: “If that is workable from a route result perspective and if we have the aircraft to do so, absolutely. Step by step. And we’ll keep growing and we’re still taking deliveries of lots of A330neos.”

He concluded: “The initial growth you’ll see out of Manchester will be modest, but step by step, and it will be on the Atlantic.”

]]> The Irish flag carrier will roll out the transformation across 10 Airbus A330 aircraft from next year, with new Business Class suites, a new Premium Economy cabin and a redesigned Economy cabin.

Aer Lingus unveiled its all-new in-flight experience on 18 November, showcasing the major transformation for transatlantic flights on its Airbus A330 fleet. The project introduces the airline’s first-ever Premium Economy cabin, alongside reimagined Business Class and Economy products.  

When will Aer Lingus’ new cabins enter service?

The first refurbished aircraft will take to the skies on 1 October, 2027, initially on select Dublin-New York (JFK) flights. More North America routes will follow as further aircraft refurbishments are completed.

The nose-to-tail transformation of 10 A330s represents one of the carrier’s most significant investments in the onboard passenger experience. Alongside the three redesigned cabins, it brings new seating, dining and inflight technology.

Why the Irish carrier’s transformation matters

The upgrade comes as Aer Lingus faces tough trading conditions. The airline’s profits have fallen 57% as fuel prices surged. It is cutting capacity by 6% and dropping underperforming routes.

The refurbishment, and particularly the introduction of a Premium Economy cabin, is essential for the airline to stay competitive on the transatlantic market. The overhaul also modernises ageing A330 interiors, with the airline investing in higher-yielding seats, while trimming costs elsewhere.

Aer Lingus eyes up to 500 job cuts as it works to trim costs Aer Lingus eyes up to 500 job cuts as it works to trim costs

Inspired by Ireland

Aer Lingus’ distinctive Irish identity runs through the new interiors. The colours, materials and design draw on Ireland’s lush landscapes, coastlines and cultural heritage. Botany Weaving, in Dublin’s Liberties, has developed bespoke, locally sourced fabrics with subtle Ogham-inspired details.

Lynne Embleton, CEO, Aer Lingus described the ambition of the redesigned cabin interior as “simple.” It’s about giving customers “greater choice, comfort and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus,” she continued.

“This investment is much more than the introduction of a new cabin,” she said. “It is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy and, for the first time in Aer Lingus’ history, introducing Premium Economy.”

What passengers can expect from Aer Lingus’ Premium Economy

The introduction of Premium Economy marks a milestone for the Irish carrier, providing passengers with more choice on Atlantic crossings. The dedicated four-row cabin features 28 next-generation Recaro R4 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. Every seat has an integrated footrest and privacy-enhancing seat wings, with a 380-inch pitch, 18-19 inches of width, and a 9-inch recline.

Customers will be served a three-course meal and complimentary drinks throughout the flight. They will also receive bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones.

Aer Lingus means business

The Business Class cabin has 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 layout, meaning every passenger will have direct aisle access and a private suite with a closing door. Each seat converts into a fully flat bed, expanding to 78 inches in length.

The Business Class menu focuses on seasonal Irish ingredients combined with contemporary cuisine inspired by the airline’s transatlantic network. Passengers can also help themselves to snacks and refreshments from a self-service bar.

Elevated economy experience

Economy passengers also benefit from the refurbishment, with new ergonomic seating that offers greater comfort and personal space. The dining menu has also been refreshed and a new self-service snack bar is available.

How next-generation technology will transform the passenger experience

Every refurbished A330 aircraft will have Panasonic Astrova in-flight entertainment, with larger 4K HD screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity and USB-C charging. Meanwhile, customised mood lighting is designed to reduce the effects of jet lag and create a more relaxed onboard environment.

Free, ultrafast WiFi connectivity, already available across all Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes, ensures passengers stay as connected at 30,000 feet as they are on the ground.

The reveal follows Aer Lingus’ recent launch of ‘The Irish Airline’, a North American brand campaign aimed at introducing Aer Lingus to a wider US audience.

]]> Russia’s rare An-72P border patrol aircraft spotted in new exercise footage https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/russia-an-72p-patrol-aircraft-returns/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:27:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57429 New footage appears to show the FSB's little-seen An-72P conducting live-fire exercises, raising questions about renewed use of the specialised border patrol aircraft.

The post Russia’s rare An-72P border patrol aircraft spotted in new exercise footage appeared first on AGN.

]]> Fresh footage published on Russian social media appears to show one of the country’s rare An-72P armed patrol aircraft taking part in a live-fire exercise.

The specialised variant, developed for the Soviet KGB’s border troops and now operated by the FSB’s Border Service Aviation branch, has rarely been seen in recent years, prompting speculation that the type is returning to more active use.

Rare An-72P patrol aircraft appears to return to FSB service

On 18 November, the Russian Telegram Channel, Fighter-Bomber posted a video of an Antonov An-72P patrol aircraft in flight carrying out live-fire exercises. The family is distinctive due to its high-mounted Lotarev D-36 Turbofans.

According to reporting by Ukraine’s Militarnyi news outlet, it appears that the rare An-72P patrol aircraft has been restored to service with the Russian Border Service Aviation of the Federal Security Service (FSB).

One documented 2001 incident involved an An-72P firing on a fishing vessel (“Albatros-101”) after it refused to stop.

Reprising its old KGB role

Nicknamed Cheburashka, the An-72P is a specialized patrol variant of the Soviet-era An-72 military transport aircraft, developed by Antonov.

It was developed at the request of the Soviet Union’s KGB border troops to patrol maritime borders and intercept vessels caught violating territorial waters. Historically, it was particularly noted for operations around the disputed Kuril Islands.

Militarnyi writes, “Unlike the standard transport variant, the An-72P, which made its maiden flight in 1984, was equipped with weapons for engaging surface and ground targets. In particular, the aircraft can carry a UPK-23-250 gun pod fitted with a twin-barrel 23 mm GSh-23L cannon.”

In temporarily occupied Crimea, @usf_army operators, jointly with @DI_Ukraine, hit an Orion UAV depot (4 drones destroyed), an An-72P patrol aircraft, and a P-37 radar. https://t.co/WRrgPmOrSi

— Defense of Ukraine (@DefenceU) April 2, 2026

In addition, it carries two underwing pylons able to carry UB-32M pods loaded with 64 S-5 unguided aircraft rockets as well as 100 kg aerial bombs. Other capabilities include limited troop/paratroop transport, life rafts/buoys, and STOL performance for remote areas.

Ukraine has claimed to have destroyed one An-72P in Crimea. Some claim the airframe was an old, abandoned ex-Ukrainian example parked at the base.

So far, two An-12s, one An-22, and eight An-26s appear in Oryx’s visually confirmed data.

Dutch F-35As intercept three Russian aircraft during Baltic Air Policing scramble Dutch F-35As intercept three Russian aircraft during Baltic Air Policing scramble

Russia’s fleet of Antonov An-12, An-26, An-72-series aircraft

AGN has previously reported on a Dallas Analytics analysis that suggests Russia is having major issues maintaining its legacy An-series fleet, for which it has no replacement.

Reporting on leaked Russian documents, Dallas Analytics wrote, “Russia currently operates approximately 368 An-series aircraft (An-12, An-26, An-72) belonging to the Ministry of Defence, the National Guard, and the FSB Aviation branch, of which 143 require repairs.”

The documents carried warnings that without urgent measures, the fleet would be forced out of service. Without Ukrainian Antonov support and expertise to help maintain the aircraft, the fleet is becoming increasingly unserviceable.

On 17 November 2026, a Russian Air Force Antonov An-12 transport aircraft crashed near Yagunovo, Kemerovo Oblast, Russia. At least 17 people on board died. Representative photo of An-12BK, 15 red. https://t.co/ltE1Yb5Xy2

— The Military Watch (@MarcinRogowsk14) November 17, 2026

Still, it remains unclear how dire it is for the entire fleet. Instead of a complete retirement, it may be more reasonable to see an increasing share of the fleet cannibalized to keep an ever-shrinking share of the fleet operational.

Separately, earlier this week, a Russian Air Force An-12 cargo aircraft reportedly crashed in Kemerovo, Siberia, killing all 17 occupants.

]]> Bell completes first MV-75 fuselage as US Army’s next-gen tiltrotor takes shape https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/bell-completes-first-fuselage-us-army-mv-75-cheyenne-ii/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:31:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57432 Bell Textron has completed the first fuselage of the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II tiltrotor at its Wichita facility, advancing the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft programme toward structural testing and first flight.

The post Bell completes first MV-75 fuselage as US Army’s next-gen tiltrotor takes shape appeared first on AGN.

]]> Bell Textron has completed the first fuselage of the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II, bringing the next-generation tiltrotor a step closer to flight testing.

Designed to fly twice as fast and twice as far as existing Army helicopters, the aircraft is being developed to carry troops and supplies over much greater distances.

The fuselage was built at Bell’s Wichita Assembly Center in Kansas and has been delivered to its Amarillo facility in Texas, where it will be joined with the aircraft’s completed wing structure and engine nacelles.

The milestone, announced on 16 November, comes two years after Bell selected Wichita as the manufacturing centre for the fuselage of the MV-75, which is being developed under the US Army’s Future Long Range Assault Aircraft (FLRAA) programme.

The aircraft is intended to transform how the Army moves troops, equipment and supplies across large distances, particularly in areas where conventional helicopters face limitations in speed and range.

Bell said the fuselage was assembled in four major sections covering the forward, middle and rear portions of the aircraft, followed by the joining of the structures and installation of the outer skins.

The Wichita facility uses advanced drilling and manufacturing equipment intended to shorten production times while maintaining structural accuracy.

“This achievement is a testament to the dedication and agility of Bell and the entire MV-75 team, who rapidly established infrastructure and moved with purpose to design and assemble the first fuselage,” said Adam Blackford, general manager of Bell’s Wichita Assembly Center.

“The completion of this fuselage reflects our unwavering commitment to delivering the MV-75 Cheyenne to our warfighters,” Blackford said.

What happens next?

The completed fuselage will be joined with the wings and nacelles at Amarillo before being placed in a purpose-built structural test fixture.

Bell will use the fixture to calibrate strain gauges and apply controlled loads to the aircraft’s structure. These tests are intended to establish whether the airframe can withstand the forces it will encounter during operation. The work is an essential step before flight testing begins.

Other parts of the aircraft have also been progressing through manufacturing and testing. In October, Bell announced that the first nacelle structures had been completed and successfully fitted to the wings.

The company also began testing the MV-75’s gearboxes at its Drive System Test Lab in Grand Prairie, Texas.
The gearboxes form part of the aircraft’s drive system and support electrical generators, hydraulic pumps and cooling equipment for the engines and nacelles.

Meanwhile, Bell is testing flight-control computers, electronic components, displays and other systems at its Weapon System Integration Lab in Arlington, Texas.

These ground tests allow engineers to identify problems with the aircraft’s software and electronic systems before they are installed in a flying prototype.

Why the US Army wants the MV-75

The MV-75 is being developed to address a longstanding limitation of military helicopters as their ability to take off and land vertically comes at the expense of speed and long-distance performance.

The US Army’s UH-60 Black Hawk has served as the backbone of its assault and utility helicopter fleet for decades. It carries troops, transports supplies, evacuates casualties and supports a wide range of military operations.

The MV-75 is designed to perform many of those missions over substantially greater distances.

Unlike a conventional helicopter, the MV-75 uses a tiltrotor configuration, with large propellers mounted at the ends of its wings.

During take-off and landing, the propellers face upwards, allowing the aircraft to operate much like a helicopter.

Once airborne, they tilt forwards, enabling the aircraft to fly like a fixed-wing aeroplane.

This arrangement allows it to combine vertical take-off capability with the higher cruising speeds and longer range associated with conventional aircraft.

Bell says the MV-75 will offer more than twice the speed and range of existing Army rotorcraft.

The aircraft is derived from Bell’s V-280 Valor demonstrator, which was developed to prove the tiltrotor concept for future military operations.

The V-280 was designed around a cruising speed of approximately 280 knots, significantly faster than the Black Hawk.

The Army has also cited a range of approximately 2,440 nautical miles for the MV-75. The greater range is intended to allow military units to operate from bases farther away from hostile forces, reducing their dependence on forward airfields and refuelling points.

It could also enable commanders to move troops rapidly between widely separated locations without relying on the same number of intermediate stops required by conventional helicopters.

How the MV-75 differs from the Osprey

The MV-75 follows the same basic tiltrotor principle as the Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey, which has served with the US Marine Corps and Air Force for years.

However, the two aircraft use different designs. On the V-22, the engines and propellers tilt together, while the MV-75 keeps its engines fixed and tilts only the rotor assemblies. The newer aircraft is also being developed specifically for the Army’s long-range assault missions, rather than as a direct replacement for the Osprey.

From V-280 Valor to MV-75 Cheyenne II

The programme has its origins in the US Army’s Future Vertical Lift initiative, which was established to develop aircraft capable of replacing several existing helicopter types.

The Army launched the FLRAA competition in 2019, seeking an aircraft that could provide a substantial improvement in speed, range and operational flexibility.

Bell competed against a Sikorsky-Boeing team offering the Defiant X compound helicopter.

In December 2022, the Army selected Bell’s V-280-based design, awarding the company the contract to develop the future aircraft.

The decision represented one of the most significant changes in US Army aviation procurement in decades.

Rather than adopting another conventional helicopter, the Army chose a tiltrotor design intended to operate across much larger battlefields.

The MV-75 is not expected to replace every Black Hawk. Instead, it will take over part of the assault and utility mission while existing helicopters continue to serve in other roles.

The 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) has been identified as the first Army division scheduled to field the new aircraft.

The division specialises in moving troops by air and is expected to be among the first formations to develop operational tactics around the MV-75’s greater speed and range.

Why is it called Cheyenne II?

600The Army formally named the aircraft MV-75 Cheyenne II in April 2026, continuing its tradition of naming helicopters after Native American tribes.

The name honours the Northern Cheyenne Tribe in Montana and the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma.

The number 75 refers to 1775, the year the US Army was established.

The Cheyenne II designation also recalls the Lockheed AH-56 Cheyenne, an advanced attack helicopter developed for the Army during the 1960s.

That earlier programme was cancelled before the aircraft entered operational service.

“In naming the MV-75 Cheyenne II, we honour the enduring contributions of the Cheyenne people to our Nation – both their distinguished service in uniform and their legacy as steadfast protectors of their way of life,” said Colonel Jeffrey Poquette, the Army’s FLRAA project manager, when the name was announced.

“The name also reflects a connection to the bold vision of the AH-56 Cheyenne, while ‘II’ signifies a new era of innovation and capability.”

A different approach to Army aviation

Beyond its flight performance, the MV-75 is being designed with a modular electronic architecture intended to make future upgrades easier.

Bell says the MV-75’s open-system architecture will allow new equipment and capabilities to be integrated without extensive redesign of the aircraft.

The Army also expects the platform to undertake medical evacuation, tactical resupply and humanitarian assistance missions in addition to transporting assault troops.

Its ability to operate over longer distances could be particularly useful in regions where military units are dispersed across islands, remote terrain or areas with limited infrastructure.

]]> Chemical used to fight wildfires corroded US air tankers, NTSB reveals https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/chemical-fight-wildfires-corroded-us-air-tankers-ntsb-reveals/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:02:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57492 An NTSB investigation found extensive damage to two aircraft after they carried a newly approved fire retardant, exposing serious shortcomings in how firefighting chemicals are tested.

The post Chemical used to fight wildfires corroded US air tankers, NTSB reveals appeared first on AGN.

]]> A fire retardant approved by the US Forest Service caused extensive corrosion in two firefighting aircraft, damaging critical wing structures, engines and electrical systems during the 2023 wildfire season, a federal investigation has found.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the chemical, Fortress FR-200, had been cleared for use without adequate testing of its effects on aircraft structures. The findings have prompted two safety recommendations calling for tougher approval standards.

The investigation involved a BAe 146 operated by Neptune Aviation Services and an MD-87 operated by Aero Air. Both aircraft participated in a Forest Service trial of the magnesium chloride-based retardant.

The first indication of trouble came from maintenance inspections. What initially appeared to be deposits inside a retardant tank eventually led investigators to uncover damage extending well beyond the aircraft’s firefighting equipment.

A strange discovery inside the aircraft

On 16 July 2023, maintenance crews entered Neptune Aviation’s BAe 146 retardant tank after repeated problems with its liquid-level indication system. The aircraft had completed 64 drops of the new chemical.

Inside, technicians found black residue, hard crystalline deposits and a gelatinous substance resembling yoghurt. Much of the softer material washed away with water, but the crystals remained attached to components.

The problems persisted. By early August, after 107 drops, further deposits had accumulated around tank floats, switches and structural fasteners.

Aero Air’s MD-87 was showing different signs of deterioration. After just 20 loads of FR-200, inspectors found pitting on metal test samples inside its tank. In August, they discovered corrosion on two steel springs used to secure a tank ventilation door. One had fractured.

The full extent of the damage emerged during detailed inspections after the firefighting season.

On the MD-87, corrosion had affected primary wing structure, fuselage components, landing gear assemblies, electrical connectors, control cables and engines.

One structural component near the wing root had suffered corrosion extending through more than half its thickness in an affected area. Aero Air replaced the damaged section, along with more than 90 electrical connectors and several control cables.

Engine inspections revealed further problems. Technicians rejected 61 parts or modules from one engine and 53 from another because of excessive corrosion or contamination.

The speed of deterioration was particularly concerning. Aero Air reported that corrosion found on some flap components would ordinarily take 18 to 24 months to develop.

The MD-87 had entered tanker service less than three months earlier.

Investigators found no corresponding corrosion on comparable aircraft that had not carried FR-200.

Earlier warning signs

The investigation found that concerns about similar chemicals had emerged two years earlier.

During a 2021 evaluation, another Fortress product, FR-100, produced thick deposits when it came into contact with a conventional phosphate-based retardant.

The material became gel-like when wet and clay-like when dry. Operators reported problems with tank sensors, valves, flow meters and seals, alongside corrosion of hardware and deterioration of protective coatings.

The evaluation recommended additional testing of aircraft materials and further investigation of the chemical reactions.

Despite those findings, FR-200 received full Forest Service approval in December 2022.

Its operational evaluation had been conducted using a smaller, single-engine airtanker fitted with a fibreglass tank. That meant the tests did not adequately examine how the chemical would affect the combinations of metals and structural components found in larger aircraft.

The two large airtankers subsequently carried FR-200 during the first part of the 2023 season before alternating it with a conventional phosphate-based retardant.

The NTSB found that existing qualification procedures failed to assess the corrosion risks adequately, including those associated with mixing products based on different chemicals.

How the chemical gained approval

The Forest Service had revised its qualification requirements in 2020 to encourage competition and allow alternatives to traditional phosphate-based retardants.

Fortress subsequently introduced FR-100 and FR-200, the first new products added to the agency’s approved list in more than two decades.

However, the NTSB found that laboratory testing relied heavily on small, isolated metal samples rather than complete aircraft structures.

It did not adequately assess joints, fasteners, connected metals or the effects of repeated exposure to different chemicals.

The investigation also clarified that while the Federal Aviation Administration approves aircraft for aerial firefighting operations, the Forest Service decides which retardants may be carried and released.

Investigators demand tougher testing

The Forest Service suspended approval of FR-100 and FR-200 in May 2024 and removed both from its approved list that December.

It has since commissioned additional testing covering 20 aircraft materials and assemblies designed to better represent operating conditions.

However, the NTSB warned that these measures would not resolve the underlying problem unless the qualification rules themselves were changed.

The agency issued two recommendations calling for more realistic corrosion testing, developed with aircraft operators, manufacturers and technical specialists, and for those procedures to become mandatory when approving future retardants.

The concern extends beyond the cost of replacing damaged parts.

Corrosion can weaken an aircraft’s structure and, if undetected, eventually cause structural failure.
