    The Music Mission team owns Spotify's end to end proposition for music creators and the experiences they create for fans. The team is dedicated to building tools and services to enable creation, promotion, expression, and monetization at scale.

    We're looking for a Senior Data Scientist to join the Artist-First AI Music lab. Our team explores and advances generative technologies for music to create new experiences for fans and artists, with a focus on listening experiences that center and celebrate artists and creatives. All of our products will put artists and songwriters first, through these four principles:

    Partnerships with record labels, distributors, and music publishers: We'll develop new products for artists and fans through upfront agreements, not by asking for forgiveness later.

    Choice in participation: We recognize there's a wide range of views on use of generative music tools within the artistic community. Therefore, artists and rightsholders will choose if and how to participate to ensure the use of AI tools aligns with the values of the people behind the music.

    Fair compensation and new revenue: We will build products that create wholly new revenue streams for rightsholders, artists, and songwriters, ensuring they are properly compensated for uses of their work and transparently credited for their contributions.

    Artist-fan connection: AI tools we develop will not replace human artistry. They will give artists new ways to be creative and connect with fans. We will use our role as the place where more than 700 million people already come to listen to music every month to ensure that generative AI deepens artist-fan connections.

    For more information, see this press release: https://newsroom.spotify.com/2025-10-16/artist-first-ai-music-spotify-collaboration/

    ","id":"babebec3-0061-4c39-a4ad-c51a54d23567","lists":[{"text":"What You'll Do","content":"
  • Lead foundational measurement and insights work for generative music experiences, developing the frameworks that help Spotify understand how creators, listeners, and rights holders engage with generative AI music.
  • Design and run large-scale analyses and evaluations of generative music systems, from prompt interpretation to model output quality, using Spotify's unique behavioral datasets, annotations, and experimentation platforms.
  • Partner with Engineers and AI Researchers to integrate evaluation signals into model development loops, debugging workflows, and product iteration, making sure scientific rigor informs technical direction.
  • Identify the behavioral and market dynamics that shape sustainable consumer demand and creator participation, and translate them into clear strategic recommendations.
  • Build practical, scalable metrics and decision systems that define what "good" looks like for AI music: credibility, user delight, safety, creator alignment, and ecosystem trust.
  • Bring together model, user behavior, and ecosystem signals into clear narratives that shape product strategy, cross-functional alignment, and long-term priorities across Spotify.
  • Create the datasets, dashboards, and long-term measurement systems that give Spotify a lasting, comprehensive understanding of product health and impact.
  • Work closely with Product, Design, Research, Legal, Trust & Safety, Marketing, Policy, and Licensing teams, bringing statistical rigor and principled measurement to help build artist-first systems that scale responsibly.
    • "},{"text":"Who You Are ","content":"
  • You have a track record of using insights to shape strategy for major company initiatives involving many different partners.
  • You have significant hands-on experience in advanced analytics or data science, ideally in a domain involving LLM evaluation, user-generated content, or complex user behavior.
  • You communicate clearly, form well-founded, evidence-backed points of view, and can bring together messy, multimodal signals (quantitative, qualitative, and model telemetry) into clear narratives for senior executives, researchers, engineers, and the music industry.
  • You're proficient in advanced analytics with Python and SQL, have analyzed large datasets, and use AI tools (e.g. Cursor, Copilot) to increase your productivity and impact.
  • You have experience developing metrics frameworks for complex products that help teams measure impact and reason clearly about priorities.
  • You have experience with machine learning frameworks, designing and assessing multimodal or embedding-based models, and validating them against LLM judges or human ground truth, with an understanding of how to evaluate models beyond offline accuracy.
  • You have a solid grounding in experimental design and causal inference, such as A/B tests, quasi-experiments, and power analysis.
  • You thrive when tackling loosely defined problems in ambiguous, zero-to-one spaces.
    • "},{"text":"Where You'll Be ","content":"

","description":"

    We’re looking for a Senior Digital Learning Experience Designer to join our Learning & Inclusion team, the group responsible for creating learning experiences that help every Spotify band member grow, belong, and do their best work.

    You’ll bring together instructional design, visual design, storytelling, and broader learning and development expertise to create inclusive and effective experiences at scale. You’ll partner with subject-matter experts, people leaders, and Learning & Inclusion colleagues on company-wide initiatives, from leadership development to programs that bring Spotify’s values to life.

    ","id":"9d1c90b5-a8a4-4218-b2f3-7bbaefae7fd1","lists":[{"text":"What You'll Do","content":"
  • Lead the end-to-end design of learning experiences, from needs analysis and curriculum architecture through development, launch, and evaluation.
  • Partner with subject-matter experts and stakeholders to identify performance needs and turn them into clear learning objectives and practical solutions.
  • Design learning journeys across live, digital, blended, and self-directed formats using evidence-based learning principles.
  • Create engaging learning materials, including eLearning, facilitator guides, participant resources, job aids, presentations, and micro-learning experiences.
  • Use visual design and storytelling to make complex ideas clear, memorable, and engaging while creating experiences that feel unmistakably Spotify.
  • Build interactive digital learning experiences using AI-assisted workflows and authoring tools such as Articulate Storyline or Rise, Adobe Captivate, or similar platforms.
  • Design inclusive learning experiences that reflect different perspectives, reduce barriers to participation, and support a culture of belonging.
  • Pilot and iterate on learning experiences using learner feedback, stakeholder input, and performance data.
  • Define meaningful measures of success and evaluate learning effectiveness, knowledge transfer, learner experience, and behavior change.
  • Manage multiple learning projects from initial scoping through delivery while creating clarity around priorities, timelines, and stakeholder expectations.
  • Explore emerging approaches in learning design, including AI-assisted authoring and adaptive learning, and apply them where they can meaningfully improve the learner experience.
    • "},{"text":"Who You Are","content":"
  • You have 5+ years of professional instructional design experience and a portfolio demonstrating thoughtful work across multiple learning formats.
  • You apply learning science principles such as cognitive load, retrieval practice, spaced learning, and adult learning theory to practical design decisions.
  • You know how to uncover learning and performance needs, translate them into measurable objectives, and design learning journeys that build knowledge and skills over time.
  • You create meaningful practice through scenarios, simulations, assessments, and other interactive experiences rather than relying on passive content.
  • You have strong visual and UX design judgment and understand how typography, hierarchy, layout, and visual storytelling can make learning clearer and easier to navigate.
  • You have experience with rapid authoring tools such as Articulate 360, Captivate, Lectora, or similar platforms, along with design tools such as Figma, Adobe Creative Suite, Canva, or equivalent.
  • You can create clear storyboards, scripts, facilitator guides, and supporting materials that help others confidently deliver consistent learning experiences.
  • You use learner feedback and data to evaluate effectiveness, iterate on your work, and connect learning experiences to meaningful outcomes.

  • Lead the end-to-end design of learning experiences, from needs analysis and curriculum architecture through development, launch, and evaluation.

  • Define meaningful measures of success and evaluate learning effectiveness, knowledge transfer, learner experience, and behavior change.
  • Manage multiple learning projects from initial scoping through delivery while creating clarity around priorities, timelines, and stakeholder expectations.

  • Explore how AI, automation, and emerging advertising technologies can improve our products, customer experiences, and product marketing practices and identify opportunities to rethink how Spotify develops, positions, and scales its advertising solutions.

    Spotify's Global Organic Social team shapes how Spotify connects with audiences across its owned social channels, bringing fans closer to the music, podcasts, audiobooks, and experiences they love.

    We're looking for a Social Strategy Manager to help grow and engage communities around podcasts, books, and fitness on Spotify. You'll develop social strategies that celebrate creators, connect with fans, and bring cultural moments to life, from major podcast releases and book launches to fitness experiences.

    As part of our Global Organic Social team, you'll work with Creative, Communications, Marketing, Partnerships, and other teams to turn business priorities into compelling, platform-native social campaigns. You'll balance long-term strategy with timely cultural opportunities, using creative judgment, audience insights, and performance data to shape work that makes an impact.

    ","id":"d9e57c3c-1c0a-483b-a783-6d1c9f2ce057","lists":[{"text":"What You'll Do","content":"

  • Lead organic social strategy for high-impact campaigns, creator partnerships, and cultural moments across Spotify's podcasts, books, and fitness experiences, from initial planning through launch and evaluation.

  • Turn integrated marketing objectives into creative, platform-native social strategies that engage audiences, strengthen fandoms, and support business goals.

  • Manage complex social campaigns across internal teams and agency partners, coordinating briefs, timelines, creative development, approvals, and delivery.

  • Partner with Creative, Communications, Marketing, Product, Content Partnerships, Paid Media, Legal, and external agencies to develop integrated campaigns and culturally relevant social experiences.

  • Identify emerging audience behaviors, creator trends, and cultural opportunities, developing proactive social programming that keeps Spotify and its creators connected with fans between major campaigns.

  • Shape social creative and content capture strategies for podcasts, long-form video, live events, and experiential activations, providing clear direction and actionable feedback to creative and production partners.

  • Develop social strategy frameworks and best practices, sharing recommendations with cross-functional teams and senior stakeholders to strengthen how Spotify approaches organic social marketing.

  • Define campaign success metrics alongside analytics partners, evaluate performance, and turn audience insights into recommendations that improve future campaigns and ongoing social programming.

    • "},{"text":"Who You Are","content":"

  • You have 7+ years of experience in organic social media strategy, social marketing, or a related role within consumer, entertainment, technology, or media brands.

  • You have experience developing social strategies for integrated marketing campaigns, balancing business objectives, audience needs, and platform-native creative ideas.

  • You understand how audiences engage with podcasts, books, fitness, and creator-led content, and you're interested in building meaningful connections between creators and their communities.

  • You have strong editorial judgment and a practical understanding of internet culture, emerging trends, and how to identify relevant opportunities for brands.

  • You understand major social platforms, including Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, and emerging channels, and know how to adapt content strategies to different audience behaviors.

  • You can manage complex projects, collaborate across functions, and guide agency partners through creative development, production, and campaign execution.

  • You use social analytics and performance insights to set goals, evaluate results, and make informed strategic recommendations.

  • You communicate ideas clearly, build trusted relationships with stakeholders, and make thoughtful decisions when priorities shift or information is evolving.

","description":"
    Our mission on the Advertising Product & Technology team is to build a next generation advertising platform that aligns with our unique value proposition for audio and video. We work to scale the user experience for hundreds of millions of fans and hundreds of thousands of advertisers. This scale brings unique challenges as well as tremendous opportunities for our artists and creators.

    Spotify is building the next generation of advertising, investing in the technology and capabilities that enable advertisers to reach audiences, deliver relevant experiences, and achieve measurable business outcomes across audio, video, and beyond.

    As our advertising business evolves, the scale, intelligence, reliability, and efficiency of our technology platform will be fundamental to our ability to compete and grow.

    We are seeking a VP, Head of Engineering, Advertising to define and lead our global advertising engineering strategy, strengthen and scale our technology platform, and shape the architecture and engineering capabilities required for Spotify Advertising's future.

    Reporting directly to the SVP of Advertising, you will be a member of the global Advertising leadership team, operating within a business with end-to-end P&L accountability. You will lead a large, multidisciplinary organization spanning Advertising Engineering and Insights, working closely with Product, Data, and Commercial leadership.

    This is an opportunity to shape the future of a sophisticated advertising technology platform, advancing real-time decisioning, machine learning, AI, and engineering excellence while building the technical foundation for a significantly larger business.

    We are looking for an exceptional engineering executive who combines deep technical and architectural judgment, experience leading at scale, strong commercial instincts, and the ability to build outstanding engineering organizations.

    ","id":"2c51f265-b95b-4b47-b467-e0fdc7744b5c","lists":[{"text":"What You'll Do","content":"

  • Set the engineering strategy and architecture. Define the long-term technical vision, investment priorities, and target architecture for Spotify’s advertising platform — balancing near-term delivery with future scale. Own build-versus-buy decisions, technical debt prioritization, and the transformation required to get from where we are to where we need to be.

  • Scale our advertising technology. Lead engineering across Ads Manager, Spotify Ad Exchange, ad serving, programmatic integrations, data infrastructure, and machine learning-based optimization.

  • Raise the bar on platform reliability. Advance standards across availability, latency, delivery accuracy, data quality, observability, incident management, and production resilience.

  • Advance intelligent advertising. Develop capabilities across real-time decisioning, auctions, bidding, targeting, relevance, pacing, pricing, and optimization to improve advertiser outcomes, monetization, and listener experience.

  • Fundamentally rethink how we develop and operate technology through AI. Redesign engineering workflows — not just adopt tools into existing processes — to deliver measurable improvements in productivity, quality, and speed across development, testing, debugging, and operations.

  • Partner across the Advertising leadership team. Work closely with Product, Data Science, and Commercial leadership to connect technical investments to customer value and business growth. Bring engineering perspective to major business decisions.

  • Build and develop the engineering organization. Attract exceptional technical leaders, strengthen succession, and foster a culture of ownership, accountability, and continuous improvement.

  • You have a track record of designing, scaling, and materially improving high-volume, low-latency, data-intensive platforms, with strong architectural judgment and operational discipline across reliability, observability, and incident management.

  • You combine long-term strategic vision with a pragmatic, results-oriented approach to execution.

Tech.eu https://tech.eu en Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:09:29 +0000 hourly 1 <![CDATA[Startup ecosystem calls to withdraw and re-table EU Inc proposal, Isomorphic Labs bags $5B, and inside Plural's €1B fund]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/startup-ecosystem-calls-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/startup-ecosystem-calls-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/#comments This week, we tracked more than 65 tech funding deals worth over €6 billion and over 4 exits, M&A transactions, rumours, and related news stories across Europe.

This week, I've gone straight from the scale and intensity of Slush in Helsinki to Yerevan, Armenia, where a much different startup ecosystem is taking shape. It's an interesting contrast. While conversations at Slush centred on scaling European tech companies, unlocking institutional capital and removing regulatory barriers, Armenia is focused on building the foundations of a globally competitive startup ecosystem where previously diaspora has been its main competitive advantage.

AI is a common thread, but the conversations are markedly different — from infrastructure, commercialisation and technological sovereignty in Helsinki to the opportunities AI presents for smaller ecosystems to compete on the global stage. Despite their different stages of maturity, both face familiar challenges: retaining talent, accessing capital, commercialising technical expertise and building internationally successful companies without founders feeling compelled to relocate.

Stay tuned for lots of stories.

Want to stay in the know? If email is more your thing, you can always subscribe to our newsletter and receive a more robust version of this round-up delivered to your inbox.

❗ Want to explore the data in more detail? The free, open-access Tech.eu Funding Explorer offers deeper insights into funding rounds, investor activity, company profiles and market trends.

Either way, let's get you up to speed.

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/startup-ecosystem-calls-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:09:29 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/startup-ecosystem-calls-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/feed 0 true <![CDATA[AI startup founded by two Irish YC alumni gets backing from Stripe's Collison brothers]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ai-startup-founded-by-two-irish-yc-alumni-gets-backing-from-the-collison-brothers/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ai-startup-founded-by-two-irish-yc-alumni-gets-backing-from-the-collison-brothers/#comments Paul Graham, the Y Combinator co-founder, said the two young Irish entrepreneurs reminded him of Patrick and John Collison, the Irish brothers who founded and run the $160bn payment giant Stripe.

Ryan Morrissey and Bence Redmond, the co-founders of AI startup Hoplite, might not be brothers but, like the Collison brothers, are Irish, have ties to Limerick, and attended Y Combinator.

During their time at Y Combinator, Morrissey says they biked all over San Francisco to set users up for their startup, over 240 rides, a tactic Graham called the “Collison installation”.

Morrissey met Redmond at the University of Limerick and dropped out at 19, before the pair joined YC’s summer 2026 batch. Morrissey even interned at Stripe.

Morrissey says: “I first met John as an intern at Stripe, and Paul Graham later reconnected us during YC. John’s most valuable advice was to focus on startups rather than chase large enterprise contracts too early, and to back the companies that haven’t hit hyperscale yet but have the potential to.”

Now, the Collison brothers are leading a $5.5m funding round in Hoplite, with John Collison saying Hoplite is at the forefront of changes to software development.

The investment round also includes Relational Capital, Upside Ventures, Y Combinator, Graham and Fin co-founder Des Traynor.

Hoplite, founded in 2026 and based in San Francisco and Dublin, is a startup that is trying to make it easier for software teams to run several AI coding agents at once. Running agents like Claude Code or Codex on a laptop can mean juggling separate copies of the codebase, managing development environments and keeping the machine on while they work. 

Hoplite’s tech allows software teams to run multiple AI coding agents in the cloud. Developers connect their GitHub repository and bring settings from tools such as Claude Code or Cursor. Each agent gets its own workspace, where it can edit code.

Morrissey, CEO, said: “The models are good enough. What's missing is the infrastructure around them - the setup, the machine. “The most interesting software in the world is increasingly built by very small teams and their agents. We now give them the same leverage large companies have. We built the version that just works."

John Collison said: "AI is completely changing how software development is happening, and Ryan and Bence are at the forefront of that change.”

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ai-startup-founded-by-two-irish-yc-alumni-gets-backing-from-the-collison-brothers/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:08:00 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ai-startup-founded-by-two-irish-yc-alumni-gets-backing-from-the-collison-brothers/feed 0 false <![CDATA[OakNorth wins US banking licence]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/oaknorth-wins-us-banking-licence/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/oaknorth-wins-us-banking-licence/#comments OakNorth, the UK SME lender, has won a US banking licence, it said today, allowing it to offer services beyond lending including checking and savings accounts to businesses in the US, which now accounts for 40 per cent of its lending business.

The digital bank, which is backed by Japanese investor SoftBank and GIC, the Singaporean state fund, said it’s the first foreign digital bank to secure a US banking licence, after winning regulatory approval from the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

OakNorth applied for US regulatory approval through its acquisition of Community Unity Bank, an FDIC-insured lender in Michigan, which it acquired in 2025. 

Earlier this year, the Federal Reserve told OakNorth to move its domicile from Jersey to the UK to clear its purchase of Community Unity Bank.

The UK challenger bank, which launched in the UK in 2015 and has lent over $24bn, first entered the US market in 2023 and has provided $3.5bn in lending to American businesses.

In the US, the bank supports established and entrepreneur-led businesses typically generating $5m–$100m in annual revenues, typically providing financing ranging from $5m to $50m.

It says this market faces challenges in accessing financing. OakNorth says the US licence will allow it to offer a wider range of services beyond lending, including checking and savings accounts, and payments.

Fintech Wise and European challenger bank Bunq have this year been rebuffed in their efforts to land US banking licences, while Revolut has secured conditional approval for a US banking licence from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency but is still waiting for regulatory approval from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Federal Reserve.

Rishi Khosla, CEO and Co-founder of OakNorth, said: “The US is home to some of the world's most ambitious entrepreneurs, yet too many businesses in the lower mid-market remain underserved by traditional community/regional banks. These businesses are vital to the American economy, creating jobs, driving investment and supporting growth in communities across the country.

“Securing a US National Banking Charter now enables us to support more of their banking needs, helping them focus on what they do best – building successful businesses."

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/oaknorth-wins-us-banking-licence/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:27:14 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/oaknorth-wins-us-banking-licence/feed 0 true <![CDATA[Archer raises $10M to connect recruiters and job seekers with AI]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/archer-raises-10m-to-connect-recruiters-and-job-seekers-with-ai/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/archer-raises-10m-to-connect-recruiters-and-job-seekers-with-ai/#comments Archer (formerly hackajob) has raised $10 million in new funding in a round led by Volition Capital, with participation from existing investor AVP. The company develops an AI-powered recruiting platform designed to connect employers with suitable candidates while helping job seekers discover relevant opportunities.

Founded by Mark Chaffey and Razvan Creanga at King’s College London, hackajob initially operated as a reverse hiring marketplace where companies applied to software engineers. The platform grew to one million users before the company began developing Archer in 2025, adapting its approach to the growing use of AI in recruitment.

Developed in collaboration with customer Sainsbury’s and publicly launched in September, Archer uses AI to automate candidate sourcing, qualification and introductions. Unlike recruitment tools focused primarily on employers or job seekers, the platform serves both sides, recommending candidates to recruiters and relevant positions to applicants.

The growing use of AI in recruitment is changing the dynamics of the hiring process, creating new challenges for both employers and job seekers.

As AI tools simplify job applications, application volumes have tripled, while the average likelihood of securing an interview has declined from approximately 15 per cent to 2 per cent. With around 47 per cent of workers using AI to prepare applications, CVs are becoming increasingly standardised, making it more difficult for recruiters to identify suitable candidates.

Candidates adopted AI far faster than employers did, and now both sides are stuck in an arms race that no one is winning. Hiring should be human-led. Archer does the sourcing and qualifying, so recruiters can spend their time on conversations that matter,

said Mark Chaffey, CEO and co-founder of Archer.

To identify potential candidates, Archer combines its own network of 1.5 million job seekers with targeted job advertisements and direct outreach through email, WhatsApp and iMessage. Its sourcing capabilities also draw on 25 million professional profiles across the US, UK and India.

The platform evaluates candidates based on their suitability for a role, professional experience, contextual skills, behaviour and achievements, while explaining why particular opportunities may be relevant to them. To reduce fraudulent applications, Archer restricts users to a single profile, analyses online signals and incorporates identity verification.

According to the company, candidates introduced through Archer are five times more likely to reach an interview, based on customer benchmarks. The platform currently serves approximately 120 enterprise customers, while annual recurring revenue has increased fivefold over the past 12 months.

Sean Cantwell, Managing Partner at Volition Capital, highlighted the shift in recruitment spending from services towards software as an opportunity for Archer. He also pointed to the company's growth among enterprise and financial services customers as evidence that its transition towards AI-powered recruitment has gained traction.

Archer will use the new funding to expand its go-to-market teams in New York and London and support further development of its AI recruiting platform.

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/archer-raises-10m-to-connect-recruiters-and-job-seekers-with-ai/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:11:26 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/archer-raises-10m-to-connect-recruiters-and-job-seekers-with-ai/feed 0 true <![CDATA[Ukrainian drone engineering meets German manufacturing as QFI ramps up production]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ukrainian-drone-engineering-meets-german-manufacturing-as-qfi-ramps-up-production/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ukrainian-drone-engineering-meets-german-manufacturing-as-qfi-ramps-up-production/#comments Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics are expanding their industrial cooperation through a programme for long-term support capacity in Ukraine aimed at systems developed by Frontline Robotics and produced in Germany by Quantum Frontline Industries (QFI).

The programme is the next stage of the partnership the two companies established in December 2025 through (QFI), their joint venture for manufacturing Ukrainian-developed unmanned systems at scale.  

QFI began manufacturing Frontline Robotics’ Linza 3.0 multi-purpose drone in Germany in February 2026.

With its first contract for the delivery of 10,000 Linza systems to Ukraine approaching completion, the joint venture has secured a larger follow-on contract with the National Guard of Ukraine for 2027, covering both Linza multi-purpose drones and Zoom reconnaissance drones. QFI plans to expand its production capacity fivefold in 2027.  

“The additional commitment represents a further step to strengthen Ukraine’s domestic defence-industrial base and build long-term capacity to support Ukrainian-developed unmanned systems. Through QFI, we’ve shown what Ukrainian engineering and German manufacturing can achieve together. As our co-production scales in Germany, the infrastructure that supports these systems in Ukraine needs to grow alongside it,” said Matthias Lehna, Vice President at Quantum Systems and Managing Director of QFI.  

This contractual commitment will support operator training, a dedicated support line and local maintenance services in Ukraine. As QFI expands production in Germany, these services will support Ukraine’s Defence Forces as more systems enter service.

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ukrainian-drone-engineering-meets-german-manufacturing-as-qfi-ramps-up-production/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:49:53 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/20/ukrainian-drone-engineering-meets-german-manufacturing-as-qfi-ramps-up-production/feed 0 true <![CDATA[EU–INC calls on von der Leyen to withdraw and re-table EU Inc proposal]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/eu-inc-calls-on-von-der-leyen-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/eu-inc-calls-on-von-der-leyen-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/#comments EU–INC and Startups for Europe are calling on European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to withdraw and re-table the original EU Inc proposal, warning that compromises made by EU Member States threaten to undermine one of Europe’s most important economic reforms for startups and scaleups.

The announcement comes as Europe’s leading policymakers, founders and investors gather at Slush in Helsinki to discuss the state of EU Inc. After two years of campaigning for a single European company standard, EU–INC and Startups for Europe remain strong supporters of the European Commission’s original proposal.

The Commission delivered a solid framework that could finally give European founders a genuine alternative to incorporating in Delaware, and allow companies to start and scale under one common European standard.

But the Council’s negotiating mandate of 19 October has weakened or removed some of the very provisions that would make EU Inc a true European standard:

  • Free choice of registration – Weakened: Founders can choose where to incorporate, but national authorities have more room to challenge that choice in certain circumstances, creating legal uncertainty.
  • Employee stock options – Restricted: The scheme stops at 750 employees or €150 million in turnover, excluding successful scale-ups where ESOPs are most valuable.
  • Central EU register – Removed: The 27 national registers remain, preserving the fragmentation EU Inc was meant to overcome.
  • Simplified insolvency – Removed: Different insolvency rules across Member States make winding down a company harder, costlier and less predictable for investors.

The demand for a single European company standard is clear.

In September, President von der Leyen warned against turning EU Inc from a speedboat into a heavy tanker. EU–INC and Startups for Europe say that warning is now becoming true.

The organisations judge EU Inc by one simple test: Would a founder choose it over a Delaware C-Corp?

The Commission's original proposal passes that test.

The Council's mandate does not.

EU–INC and Startups for Europe warn that proceeding directly to final negotiations, known as trilogues, risks further compromises rather than restoring the provisions already lost. If the proposal continues on its current course, Europe risks adopting an EU Inc that founders won't use.

Andreas Klinger, Co-Initiator of EU–INC and investor, warns that the consequences go far beyond the regulation itself:

“Founders don't need a European regulation that delivers on paper but fails in practice.

They need a company structure that makes it easier to build, raise capital and scale across Europe. The Commission's original proposal delivers that. But if we strip away the things that make it work, founders will simply incorporate elsewhere. We have one chance to get EU Inc right, and we can’t waste it.

We risk more than Europe's competitiveness. We risk losing the trust of an entire generation of founders who still believe they can build global companies in Europe.”

A call to Member States to change course – and get EU Inc right

EU–INC and Startups for Europe are asking the Commission to withdraw, negotiate, and re-table its original proposal. Not to abandon EU Inc, but to give it the time and chance to succeed.

The call follows a joint letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, in which both organisations reaffirm their strong support for the Commission's original proposal and call for Member States to reconsider their positions.

For Simon Schaefer, President of Startups for Europe and Co-Initiator EU-INC, the responsibility now lies with Member States to put Europe's collective interests ahead of national compromises:

“A truly European company standard requires Member States to look beyond their national interests. We cannot spend years negotiating one of Europe's most important competitiveness reforms only to end up with another patchwork of national rules.

This is an opportunity for Member States to reconsider their positions and make sure EU Inc delivers on its original promise.”

Backed by more than 26,000 EU–INC co-signatories, the campaign remains committed to its original mission: One Europe. One Standard. One that founders can actually use.

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/eu-inc-calls-on-von-der-leyen-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:00:00 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/eu-inc-calls-on-von-der-leyen-to-withdraw-and-re-table-eu-inc-proposal/feed 0 true <![CDATA[€100B in company value, one shared ambition: European tech leaders demand political reform at Slush]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/100b-in-company-value-one-shared-ambition-european-tech-leaders-demand-political-reform-at-slush/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/19/100b-in-company-value-one-shared-ambition-european-tech-leaders-demand-political-reform-at-slush/#comments More than 35 European tech founders and business leaders issued a joint declaration at Slush 2026, calling for three fundamental shifts in European technology policy to strengthen the continent's global competitiveness. Representing more than €100 billion in company value and 115,000 jobs, the signatories pledged their long-term commitment to building and scaling technology companies in Europe.

“We share one conviction: Europe can lead the next era of technology, and we want to make it happen.”

The declaration challenges the prevailing narrative of European decline, pointing to the continent's scientific excellence, private wealth and strengths in advanced manufacturing, energy, aerospace, robotics, quantum, climate technology and AI. The EU accounts for around 22 per cent of global scientific publications, compared with 17 per cent for the US, according to the declaration. Yet Europe has struggled to translate these strengths into global technology leadership.

“Europe was never short of talent, technology or capital. It was short of the political determination and the boldness to put them to work.”

The signatories identify three political priorities to address this imbalance.

Mobilising European capital to fund technology growth

The declaration argues that Europe's investment challenges stem not from a shortage of capital but from how it is allocated. European households alone hold more than €12 trillion in savings, alongside substantial pools of capital managed by pension funds and institutional investors.

However, much of this wealth finances innovation and infrastructure overseas, while European technology companies struggle to secure large growth rounds domestically.

“Europe funds the earliest, riskiest phase of deep tech and research-backed innovation – and then foreign capital steps in and captures the growth. This must end.”

The signatories call for the accelerated implementation of the Savings and Investments Union, alongside investment in critical technology infrastructure, including access to frontier AI and greater European compute capacity.

“European savings should finance European innovation, and European citizens should participate in the wealth it creates.”

Completing the Single Market through EU Inc

Despite the scale of Europe's Single Market, founders continue to face fragmented corporate, tax and employment rules when expanding across member states.

The declaration identifies EU Inc, an optional, digital-first European company structure, as a critical first step towards removing these barriers. It would enable founders to incorporate once and operate across member states without establishing separate local entities, while harmonising employee share options and investment processes.

“A startup founded in Paris, Berlin, Warsaw or Milan should be able to hire, raise capital, sell and scale across the continent as easily as an American company expands across the United States.”

The signatories also advocate for deeper integration of European capital markets, including the creation of a pan-European stock exchange.

“The objective is one market, one rulebook and one launchpad for global companies.”

Simplifying regulation while protecting competition

The declaration takes a dual approach to regulation, calling for reduced administrative burdens alongside stronger enforcement of competition rules. It argues that excessive regulation and the abuse of market power by dominant technology platforms are both significant barriers to European innovation.

“The re-establishment of fair digital competition and smart simplification are not opposing agendas but two sides of the same coin.”

The signatories call for policymakers to prioritise reducing red tape, particularly in fast-moving sectors such as AI, while enforcing the Digital Markets Act (DMA) to prevent dominant platforms from restricting access to critical digital markets. They argue that fair competition could enable European companies that are already competitive under existing conditions to emerge as global leaders.

European founders pledge to double down on Europe

The declaration concludes with a commitment to work with the European Commission and national governments to translate these priorities into policy. The signatories frame technological leadership as fundamental not only to economic prosperity but also to democratic resilience and political independence.

“We bring the experience of those building Europe’s technological sovereignty and competitiveness every day, and we are prepared to double down on Europe. We call on Europe’s political leaders to match this ambition.”

These improvements have increased generation success rates and processing speeds, making the platform more efficient and reliable.

The company is also developing its own AI models to offer more cost-effective solutions for specific content creation tasks. These include Flint Image, which generates multiple images per request, and Lockstep, a video model that allows users to replace characters in existing footage while preserving their movements.

The platform has seen growing adoption, processing approximately one million runs per day and serving more than 750 paying organisations. Its customers include advertising platform Wask, which uses each::labs to power its AI creative feature and generate content at scale.

]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/visage-technologies-launches-eur31m-eu-backed-project-to-develop-adaptive-training-technology/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:32:05 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/visage-technologies-launches-eur31m-eu-backed-project-to-develop-adaptive-training-technology/feed 0 true <![CDATA[Beyond the 15-minute delivery race: Glovo's next chapter in quick commerce]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/beyond-the-15-minute-delivery-race-glovos-next-chapter-in-quick-commerce/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/beyond-the-15-minute-delivery-race-glovos-next-chapter-in-quick-commerce/#comments The days of racing to deliver groceries in 15 minutes — I once clocked a 7-minute delivery from the non-defunct Gorillas here in Berlin — may be over, but quick commerce is constantly evolving. What began as a race to get food to customers faster is developing into a broader retail model, spanning everything from pet food and pharmacy products to fashion and electronics.

During a recent visit to Glovo's Yellow Park headquarters in Barcelona for its Startup Campus, I spoke with Connie Kwok, VP of Q-Commerce at Glovo, about how the sector is changing, where the next opportunities lie and the practical challenges of making almost anything available on demand.

Having spent eight years at Amazon before joining Glovo, Kwok believes quick commerce will fundamentally change how people shop. But as delivery platforms expand beyond their original focus on restaurants and groceries, they face new challenges, from managing fashion returns and fragmented retail inventory to determining where autonomous delivery robots make commercial sense.

With quick commerce now accounting for around 22 per cent of Glovo's business, the question is no longer simply how fast a product can reach someone's door, but how delivery platforms can become a viable part of everyday retail.

Glovo began in Barcelona in 2015 as an on-demand service that lets customers order almost anything from local businesses or send packages across the city. It later evolved into a marketplace connecting customers with restaurants and retailers, then expanded into groceries, pharmacies, fashion, pets, and other retail categories.

Glovo operates across 21 countries in Europe, Ukraine, Central Asia and Africa, connecting customers with restaurants, supermarkets and retailers through its on-demand delivery platform.

From pharmacies to pet food: Building new shopping habits

According to Kwok, pharmacy is typically the next category customers adopt after groceries. However, it is a particularly complex market because regulations vary significantly between countries. In Spain, for example, Glovo can offer over-the-counter medicines, but the user experience is complicated by the need to connect customers to individual pharmacy websites.

"That allows us to work with independent pharmacies, which is important, but it adds complexity. We operate in 21 countries, each with different regulations, and we have to respect those local requirements."

Another category Kwok is particularly excited about is pet products.

"I'm a dog owner myself, and it's easy to understand the appeal of having a 15-kilogram bag of dog food delivered to your door within 30 minutes.

What's especially interesting is the repeat purchase rate. Once customers discover they can order pet food through the platform, they tend to come back.

People generally feed their pets the same food consistently, so once that purchasing habit is established, it opens opportunities for accessories, clothing and other pet products."

Petcare is already proving to be a promising category for Glovo. In 2024, the company reported 51 per cent growth in petcare across its markets, alongside an expanded partnership with Mars covering food, snacking and pet products.

"Our app was built to sell pizzas. It wasn't built to sell shoes"

Glovo has also started delivering fashion products, launching Adidas and Birkenstock in Morocco. According to Kwok, retailers have largely driven the expansion by approaching Glovo rather than the other way around. Morocco is an interesting market because its retail infrastructure differs from that of many European countries.

"There aren't shopping malls everywhere, so having products delivered offers customers another way to access brands.

But fashion is a much more considered purchase than groceries.

We often say that our app was built to sell pizzas. It wasn't built to sell shoes.

There are a lot of improvements I'd like to make to the user experience before we can fully support these categories."

Returns are among the biggest challenges in online fashion retail.

"Technically, we can send a courier to collect a product, but what happens when it arrives back at the retailer? Someone needs to inspect it, determine its condition and establish who is responsible for any associated costs.

We still need to work through that entire process."

Kwok spent considerable time in China, where she observed delivery models that allow customers to try on clothes while the courier waits before committing to a purchase.

"Customers can order several sizes, try everything on and return what they don't want immediately.

Logistics costs are considerably lower in China, which makes that kind of service easier to offer. I'd love for us to reach that point. It would be an amazing customer experience."

The inventory challenge: From live APIs to WhatsApp updates

One of Glovo's biggest operational challenges is inventory accuracy, particularly given the different levels of digital maturity among retailers across its markets.

Kwok explained: 

"Take supermarkets as an example. Even when a partner provides live stock updates, there are still customers physically shopping in the store.

If there are three apples left on the shelf, should we show three apples available in the app, or only two, anticipating that someone in the store might buy one?"

In Spain, many supermarket partners are integrated with Glovo through APIs, providing live inventory data. However, the same supermarket chain may operate very differently in an African market, where stock updates are sometimes sent once a week through WhatsApp.

"That's the reality of operating across 21 countries with very different levels of technological development. In some markets, we can solve problems relatively quickly with technology. In others, we still need people," explained Kwok.

Where stock updates are infrequent, Glovo deploys people into stores to conduct random inventory checks. Those checks provide additional data that machine learning models can use to improve stock predictions. "It's also about helping retailers understand where they should invest in technology. That's something I'm quite proud of, because we're helping improve the capabilities of the wider retail industry."

Ukraine provides another example of how Glovo has adapted its technology to local conditions. In a previous interview with Tech.eu, Maryna Pavliuk, GM of Glovo Ukraine, explained how the company developed integrations with city services providing real-time blackout information to help maintain operations during power outages caused by Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and also deploying walking delivery employees for short deliveries when other modes of transport were unsafe due to snow.

Despite the challenges of operating during wartime, Ukraine has become one of Glovo's five largest markets globally, with quick commerce growing from 17 to 28 per cent of its business in just over two years. The platform operates across 40 Ukrainian cities and works with more than 12,000 partners, over 85 per cent of which are SMEs.

Beyond delivery: Helping retailers digitise and access financing

Glovo's expansion into retail also presents opportunities for smaller businesses that lack sophisticated ecommerce infrastructure. Through its Glovo Local programme, the company had supported more than 11,000 SMEs by November 2025, reporting an average 20 per cent increase in online sales among participating businesses. The programme provides digital tools, training and support to help local retailers reach customers online.

In May 2025, Glovo partnered with Berlin-based fintech finmid to provide small businesses with access to financing directly through its platform. Launched in Spain, Portugal and Poland, the service allows eligible merchants to receive funding within 24 hours, using transaction and business performance data to assess eligibility. Businesses can use the capital for equipment, renovations, marketing or cash flow, with the companies reporting sales increases of up to 20 per cent among merchants accessing financing.

This support extends also to couriers. Glovo's G-Learning programme offers couriers online courses, language learning through Busuu and entrepreneurship training delivered with Impact Hub. The Start Programme has operated in countries including Spain, Georgia, Ghana and Italy with over 7000 graduates. 

Why delivery robots won't replace human couriers completely

Glovo began with its founders delivering food orders by bicycle. Since then, last-mile logistics have evolved considerably, and autonomous delivery technology has emerged as a potential alternative to human couriers. Glovo's sister brand in South Korea has been testing a delivery robot called Dilly.

However, Kwok believes autonomous delivery is best suited to extremely densely populated cities such as Seoul.

"Even Barcelona struggles to achieve that level of density."

There are also practical challenges. Robots need to navigate public spaces, use elevators and manage the final handoff to customers. Collecting orders from restaurants and supermarkets presents another obstacle. Robots require designated places to park and receive orders because they cannot simply enter shops.

"Robots could certainly help reduce delivery costs, but I don't believe there will ever be a time when they're the only solution. 

I think the future will involve a hybrid model combining autonomous technology and human couriers."

Beyond the basket: The expanding role of delivery platforms

Glovo is not alone in exploring how existing delivery infrastructure can support a wider range of services.

Wolt expanded into peer-to-peer secondhand delivery through a partnership with Finnish resale marketplace Bought. Launched in June 2025, the service enables consumers in Finland to purchase secondhand clothing and other items from sellers within a 7.5-kilometre radius and have them delivered in as little as an hour. Once a buyer and seller agree on a collection time, a Wolt courier picks up the item directly from the seller and delivers it to the buyer.

For Glovo, the bigger opportunity may lie in becoming an essential partner to the businesses it once simply delivered for. Whether that means helping a small shop secure financing, giving a supermarket better visibility of its stock or connecting brands with customers in underserved markets, its ambitions increasingly extend beyond the doorstep.

As Kwok sees it, the future isn't necessarily about getting things to people faster, but changing what they can access in the first place.


]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/beyond-the-15-minute-delivery-race-glovos-next-chapter-in-quick-commerce/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/beyond-the-15-minute-delivery-race-glovos-next-chapter-in-quick-commerce/feed 0 true <![CDATA[From Wi-Fi challenger to NATO defence technology: Oledcomm's Li-Fi revival]]> https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/from-wi-fi-challenger-to-nato-defence-technology-oledcomms-li-fi-revival/ https://tech.eu/2026/11/18/from-wi-fi-challenger-to-nato-defence-technology-oledcomms-li-fi-revival/#comments Li-Fi is hardly new. I first started writing about the technology more than a decade ago, when the idea of transmitting data through light rather than radio waves promised to transform wireless connectivity.  But despite the early excitement, Li-Fi never achieved mainstream adoption.

But now, the technology is finding renewed relevance in an unexpected place.

French optical wireless communications company Oledcomm is developing light-based communications systems designed to address the vulnerabilities of conventional radio-frequency communications, particularly in military environments where electronic warfare and jamming are increasingly prevalent.

Oledcomm has been selected for the Mission Track of NATO's Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) after participating in the programme's initial Challenge phase.

I spoke with Benjamin Azoulay, President and CEO of Oledcomm to learn more.

What is Li-Fi?

Li-Fi, short for Light Fidelity, is an optical wireless communication technology that transmits data by rapidly modulating light, including infrared LEDs. An optical access point sends a modulated signal to a dedicated receiver, enabling wireless connectivity without conventional radio-frequency transmission.

The signal is largely confined to the illuminated area, which can be useful in sensitive environments. Oledcomm also uses laser-based optical links for longer-distance communications, including between vehicles, drones and satellites. 

From consumer Li-Fi to defence

I remember there was a lot of excitement about Li-Fi in the 2010s, particularly around IoT, but it never really took off.

Azoulay said Oledcomm experienced the same trajectory. The company emerged from a university lab in Paris, where two professors had been working on Li-Fi.

"Everyone was talking about it. They created a lot of IP, and they created Oledcomm to bring it to market. The dream at that time was to bring Li-Fi to the mainstream and replace Wi-Fi."

As lighting shifted towards LEDs, the ambition was to turn light fittings into internet access points. "Everyone dreamed of every light on Earth having data communication capabilities and becoming an internet access point." But Wi-Fi advanced rapidly, while major chip and device manufacturers prioritised cellular technologies rather than Li-Fi. Azoulay concluded around 2020 or 2021 that mainstream adoption remained years away. Discussions with the French Ministry of Defence helped redirect towards defence and space. Electronic warfare, radio-frequency detection and jamming became increasingly prominent concerns following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The ministry financed Oledcomm's first military-grade product.

Why light-based communications matter on the battlefield

On the battlefield, conventional radio-frequency communications can expose military personnel and equipment to detection and attack. Azoulay explained:

"When you emit on the radio, the enemy's electronic warfare systems take seconds to detect you, geolocate you and probably hit you with an FPV drone. So now everyone is looking for solutions to continue communicating, which is vital, but without being detected."

What we say at Oledcomm is that light is the new radio because it has zero electromagnetic radio-frequency footprint. It's undetectable. It's totally immune to jamming."

Optical communication avoids conventional radio-frequency emissions, although its performance depends on maintaining an unobstructed optical link. 

Making the technology suitable for military use required more than repackaging civilian equipment. The hardware had to withstand shock, vibration, and extreme temperatures, while the software needed stronger security protections.

"We developed software called LiFi Manager with post-quantum-resistant encryption. Now, with DIANA's help, we're applying for NATO Secret accreditation for our products."

Beyond defence, Li-Fi has potential applications in secure offices, industrial settings, education, healthcare and transport, particularly where radio-frequency emissions or signal containment are concerns.

From orbit to soldier: Oledcomm's four products

Oledcomm's concept is a network connecting military personnel, vehicles, drones and command centres without conventional radio-frequency links.

"Our concept is a tactical bubble. We call it a one-kilometre bubble, a completely RF-silent tactical bubble," said Azoulay.

"Outdoors it's lasers, indoors it's Li-Fi."

The company has developed four optical communications products:

SOLARIS – Mobile command centres: An indoor Li-Fi system connecting up to 32 users in approximately ten minutes. It uses point-to-multipoint connectivity in military shelters and mobile command centres.

CLOVIS – Vehicle-to-vehicle communications: A mesh networking system connecting military vehicles over distances of up to one kilometre, with data transmission speeds of 1 Gbps. Azoulay said Oledcomm had secured a contract with the French Army, with delivery planned for the end of 2026.

LISA – Drone-to-vehicle communications: An optical communications system enabling drones to act as relays for military vehicles operating in radio-jammed environments or under radio-silence requirements. The drone can be positioned approximately 300 metres to one kilometre above the vehicle.

LUCI – Satellite-to-satellite communications: A laser communications system designed to maintain links between fast-moving satellites, with stated transmission speeds of up to 400 Gbps over distances of up to 8,000 kilometres.

"With those four products, we can deliver the promise that we always call 'from orbit to soldier, everything in light'," said Azoulay.

Lessons from military deployment

Oledcomm has deployed its technology with two brigades and one division of the French Army, according to Azoulay. It has also conducted tests with the UK Ministry of Defence, supported by its participation in NATO DIANA's UK accelerator.

One important lesson has been that practical usefulness to soldiers matters more than the technology alone. Optical communications require line of sight, which can be challenging in mobile environments.

"If there's an obstacle between the emitter and the receiver, you don't see each other, and you cannot communicate anymore," Azoulay explained.

During deployments with France's 7th Armoured Brigade, personnel changed the layout of tents and tables inside mobile command centres to preserve the optical link. Oledcomm also uses pointing, acquisition and tracking systems to maintain connections between moving vehicles, drones and satellites.

The company has revised its products three or four times in response to field feedback.

"So this field learning is absolutely critical for success."

Commercialising military communications

Oledcomm's business model combines hardware sales with annual service contracts covering cybersecurity, software updates, maintenance and training. Depending on customer requirements, the company can provide one-to-one replacement of faulty equipment, in some cases within 48 hours. It also offers annual training to account for personnel turnover within defence ministries, where staff typically rotate every three years.

Cybersecurity and encryption software are updated annually.

Azoulay sees accreditation as a significant barrier to entry for competitors. It can take years after a product is developed to secure the approvals required for defence deployment. Oledcomm is also pursuing partnerships with established defence contractors to integrate its technology into existing vehicles and drones, rather than developing complete military platforms itself.

"It's better to have someone who already has the contract, who already has the product, the vehicle or the drone, and we can add intelligence to it by embedding Li-Fi," explained Azoulay.

"This is our approach, which I think makes sense instead of trying to sell a full solution directly. For a small company, it's extremely complicated."

Revenue ambitions and the space opportunity

Oledcomm aims to double its turnover in 2026 and again in 2027, with a longer-term target of reaching €15 million in annual revenue by 2030.

"We're still small. We're talking about a few million, but moving towards €10 million in turnover to start with. My goal is to be a €15 million company in 2030," said Azoulay.

He sees different growth dynamics in defence and space. In space, the main limitation of radio-frequency communications is bandwidth, with growing demand from satellite constellations, AI applications and proposed space data centres.

"With lasers, and it's not exactly Li-Fi, it's lasers, it's light, we're able to reach 400 gigabits per second, terabit-per-second connectivity.

In space, there's huge demand. It's exploding now."

Azoulay pointed to Europe's IRIS² satellite constellation, which he said will comprise 330 satellites equipped with three laser communication terminals each, representing potential contracts worth €150 million to €200 million for the terminals alone.

He estimates that the space laser communications market will reach €9 billion by 2032, with around 30 per cent potentially accessible to smaller suppliers as major satellite operators develop their own terminals.

Defence presents a different challenge, with longer procurement cycles driven by operational testing and security accreditation.

"You need a minimum of two to three years to enter a new defence application because of accreditation and testing. Nobody will buy it before testing it in an operational exercise."

Military exercises involving brigades or divisions, field reports and accreditation can all be required before procurement decisions are made.

"So the time to market in Li-Fi is quite long, probably longer than in space."

Oledcomm is targeting expansion into the UK, Germany and the US. It already has a small US subsidiary and is beginning to increase investment there.

The value of NATO DIANA

Azoulay praised the support Oledcomm received through NATO's DIANA accelerator programme, particularly from the UK-based team, which helped the company access opportunities and prepare pitches.

"The key point is that we had a team who were really treating the innovators as stars, doing everything they could to open doors for us, to help us be brilliant in making our pitches."

Staff were highly engaged, even contacting participants at weekends to check their preparations for demonstrations and events.
